This behavior is consistent with asymmetric vortex entry and motion governed by the magnetic stray fields generated near the bridge edges. At 3 K with the remanent magnetization perpendicular to the current, increasing the W-N thickness from 18 to 28 nm widens the current interval between the dissipation thresholds for opposite polarities from about 0.3 to 1.55 mA. All three bilayers exhibit diode efficiencies of approximately 75-80% in this configuration.

items.title: Causal discovery from Bayesian symbolic regression
items.summary: Causal discovery from observational data is central to scientific reasoning, yet established constraint-based and score-based methods often recover only a Markov equivalence class and provide no signal in bivariate or strongly autocorrelated regimes typical in some areas of science. Here, we recast causal discovery as a Bayesian symbolic regression problem. Given a set of candidate parents for each target variable, the Bayesian symbolic regression samples closed-form expressions from a posterior over symbolic models. The fraction of sampled expressions in which each candidate variable appears defines a posterior inclusion probability that we use as the causal score. This replaces pointwise model selection by an ensemble of plausible mechanisms. We evaluate the method on coupled nonlinear bivariate dynamics, on the CauseMe benchmark suite spanning linear, chaotic, nonlinear, higher-dimensional and high-noise settings, and on a four-variable biogeoscience structural causal model under Gaussian, heavy-tailed and mixed-noise regimes. Our approach is competitive with, and often outperforms, specialized causal discovery algorithms. Additionally, the method returns closed-form mechanisms leading to explicit causality and interpretability.

items.title: Deriving Tsallis Entropy from First Principles
items.summary: The kinetic approach for q-distribution is extended through a "bottom-up" procedure to the corresponding entropic formula. In this way, the validity of Tsallis' formula, S_q(W) = k_B ln_q(W), is established from first principles. The resulting q-entropy is additive and the zeroth law of thermodynamics is automatically satisfied because the conventional identification beta = 1/(k_B T) remains valid. Entropy, energy, and all relevant quantities for both discrete and continuous cases are evaluated using standard (linear) averages. The "bottom-up" and "top-down" approaches yield the same q-distribution for velocities. The standard results are naturally recovered in the limit q -> 1.

items.title: N-Layer quasi-geostrophic modons in a vertically sheared flow
items.summary: Modons, or dipolar vortices, are a form of propagating vortex solution consisting of two counterrotating regions of fluid and moving together under self-advection. They are common features of the upper ocean that can remain stable over long times, thereby transporting fluid over large distances. Here, we present a semi-analytical method for finding modon solutions in a vertically-sheared background flow using the multi-layer quasi-geostrophic framework. This method works for arbitrarily many fluid layers and builds on our previous studies of multi-layer modon solutions. We present three example of modons in a background flow, highlighting the effect of varying relative potential velocity between layers and the impact of depth-dependent potential vorticity gradients arising from surface deformation and velocity shear.

items.title: Mechanisms of Zener diode and ohmic contact resulting from a heavily doped p-n junction: A novel explanation in terms of impurity-photovoltaic-effect resulting from infrared self-emission at room-temperature
items.summary: In textbooks, a quantum-mechanical tunneling mechanism based on electron-wavefunction is used to explain Zener diode as well as ohmic contact resulting from a heavily doped p-n junction. In this study, an attempt in particle description is made to explain these devices. Any object at room-temperature emits infrared (IR) photons. The process of heavy doping can cause many defects. The self-absorption of the IR emission could be achieved through sub-band-gap excitations due to defects, creating carriers. In a heavily doped p-n junction device, some of the IR-generated carriers diffuse into the junction which has a built-in field. The built-in field sweeps out the carriers, creating IR photocurrent. The reverse leakage current of the p-n junction is regarded as the IR photocurrent according to a precedent where impurity-photovoltaic-effect is used to explain circuit devices (arXiv:2510.18226). Heavy doping results in not only a great many IR-generated carriers but also an avalanche effect at low voltage, producing Zener breakdown. Additionally, the impurity-photovoltaic-effect can make a reasonable contribution to explaining the temperature dependence of Zener breakdown. If the doping is very heavy, the heavily doped p-n junction can be altered to create an ohmic contact, which can also be explained in terms of impurity-photovoltaic-effect. Not only quantum mechanics, but also this photovoltaic mechanism in particle description can explain the above devices. Considering the wave-particle duality, the combination of quantum-mechanical and photovoltaic mechanisms is suggested to explain these devices. Each mechanism plays a big or small role in the explanation.

items.title: Sensitivity of diffusion MRI to white matter pathology: a comparison between ROI-based effect size and TBSS analysis under different diffusion protocols, field strengths and post-processing strategies
items.summary: We investigated how much more advanced diffusion MRI acquisitions and more complex processing increase sensitivity to group-wise white matter (WM) differences due to pathology, and how the choice of statistical analysis affects this sensitivity. Data were acquired with DTI and DKI protocols at 3T and 7T in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), athletes with persistent post-concussive symptoms (PPCS), and healthy controls (HC). Seven processing pipelines combining denoising, Gibbs removal, eddy current and motion correction, and Gaussian smoothing were applied. Sensitivity was assessed with two methods: a region-of-interest-based (ROI-based) effect size analysis over 72 WM tracts segmented by TractSeg, quantified by Cohen's d, and tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS), quantified by the fraction of significant voxels in the WM skeleton. The ROI-based analysis found significant group differences for both SLE versus HC and PPCS versus HC, whereas TBSS found differences only for SLE versus HC. Both analyses agreed that the diffusion protocol affected sensitivity more than field strength or post-processing. Regardless of pipeline, DTI-derived fractional anisotropy (FA) yielded a 0.26 higher effect size and 25% more significantly different voxels between SLE and HC than DKI-derived FA, and 3T yielded a 0.2 higher effect size and 21% more significant voxels than 7T. Smoothing reduced sensitivity in both analyses (by up to 12% in TBSS for SLE versus HC). Overall, TBSS appears less suited to localized pathology such as neurotrauma, whereas the ROI-based analysis showed no bias with respect to the nature of the pathology. Advanced protocols such as 3T-DKI and 7T-DTI may need further optimization before surpassing conventional 3T-DTI in sensitivity to WM pathology in SLE.

items.title: Parker Solar Probe Flies Through the Sun's Magnetic Poles Near 10 Solar Radii
items.summary: During the peak of the Sun's magnetic cycle, the solar corona can be complex and dominated by dynamics, while hidden below, the dipole component of the its photospheric magnetic field steadily reverses with respect to the rotational axis. Here, we use Parker Solar Probe (\emph{Parker}) data from two of its closest approaches in mid-2025 to show that the large-scale field at solar maximum resembled a simple tilted dipole. Similar to how Ulysses provided a complete scan of the solar rotation-aligned dipole at solar minimum, \emph{Parker} sampled the full range of magneto-latitudes, probing both magnetic poles below the Alfvén surface. Concurrent in situ data at larger distances reveal that both hemispheres contain solar wind with asymptotic speeds near 800 km s-1, yielding a picture similar to the Ulysses latitude scans but now in the equator near solar maximum. This contrasts with the disordered structure observed by Ulysses during its solar maximum latitude scan, which we attribute to the long timescale of data collection. Overall, we find the coronal field is organized as a dipole, but the fast solar wind streams are deformed by non-dipolar substructure: the positive dipole axis is aligned with one coronal hole, the negative centers over a pseudostreamer, and significant mass flux enhancements are observed at magnetic separatrixes. Our measurements suggest that even at solar maximum, the solar corona can still exhibit structure nearly as ordered as solar minimum. Moreover, by sampling rapidly and close to the Sun, the detailed imprint of source region structure can be determined in the solar wind.

items.title: Magnetized plasma modulator for polarization-tunable ultrahigh-power single-cycle lasers
items.summary: Ultrahigh power lasers with tunable polarization and few-cycle duration have long been considered the holy grail of high-power laser science, as they push light-matter interactions into an entirely new physical regime. Yet such pulses remain far beyond the reach of conventional solid-state optics and technologies. Here, we introduce a novel magnetized plasma modulator that boosts linearly polarized lasers from petawatt to exawatt powers while simultaneously enabling tunable polarization, offering a promising approach for high-power laser development. This is achieved in density-tailored plasmas by combining dispersive compression of a chirped picosecond laser pulse with magneto-chiral group-velocity splitting in a few-Tesla magnetic field. It can generate circularly or elliptically polarized pulses with extremely high compression ratios (over 1000) and extremely short durations (down to the single-cycle level) in a compact and efficient manner. These findings demonstrate a feasible pathway toward exawatt-class few-cycle lasers with tunable polarization, opening new avenues for a wide range of cutting-edge research and applications.

items.title: Frequency tuning capability of self-powered piezoelectric tuned mass dampers
items.summary: Tuned mass dampers suffer from frequency shift sensitivity. This paper investigates the use of tunable piezoelectric tuned mass dampers (PE-TMD) by studying their behavior with tunable resistive and capacitive loads to adapt their resonant frequency. An analytical model is developed to assess the influence of key dimensionless parameters-electromechanical coupling coefficient, mass ratio, and quality factoron vibration attenuation, frequency tuning capability, and energy harvesting. The study reveals trade-offs between attenuation, tunability, and energy harvesting. It provides design guidelines for autonomous PE-TMDs and identifies key challenges for their practical implementation, including the interest of high coupling coefficients, whose the implication is limited is with growing mass ratio. Notably, it highlights the necessity of high coupling coefficient, the influence of which on frequency tuning is limited as the mass ratio grows.

items.title: Data-Driven Conservation Laws for Newtonian Systems: Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Eisenhart-Duval Geometry
items.summary: We introduce a Physics-Informed Neural Network approach for the data-driven reconstruction of the symmetries and conservation laws of Newtonian dynamical systems, based on the geometrization of the dynamics through the Eisenhart-Duval lift. Within the Eisenhart-Duval lift, the symmetry conditions reduce to the linear Killing or Conformal Killing equations of the extended metric. We combine a Hamiltonian neural network, which reconstructs the potential function from the data, with a random-feature neural network, which solves the symmetry conditions for the collineations of the extended geometry. From the learned vector fields we construct the Lie algebra and, through Noether's theorem, the corresponding conserved quantities, while the derivation of the curvature invariants for the extended geometry provide allow us to perform an independent consistency test. We apply the method to the one-dimensional Ermakov-Pinney equation and to the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator, with and without a quartic perturbation, by using different level of noise in the phase-space data. For the Ermakov-Pinney equation, the three Killing vectors of the flat extended plane, and the corresponding nonlocal conservation laws, are recovered for, while for the harmonic oscillator, the ten conformal Killing vectors which form the $so(3,2)$ Lie algebra are determined for noise levels up to $10\%$. When the quartic term is added, the broken symmetries are identified as approximate symmetries.

items.title: Physics design of a dual-ring light source toward MHz-rate free-electron laser radiation
items.summary: Combining the high peak brilliance and short pulse duration of free-electron lasers (FELs) with the high repetition rate of diffraction-limited storage rings (DLSRs) is a promising direction for accelerator light sources. In this paper, we propose a dual-ring light source concept that, at MHz repetition rates, delivers pulses with a pulse durations and peak power intermediate between those of FELs and DLSRs. Such a light source can be realized as an upgrade of an existing DLSR by adding an isochronous ring equipped with transverse gradient undulators (TGUs) and connecting the two rings via bunch compression and decompression systems. We present the conceptual layout and show that bunch compression shortens the electron bunches to ps-scale durations; multi-turn radiation in the isochronous ring raises the repetition rate to 1.36 MHz from a single TGU; and the long TGUs enhance the brilliance, delivering $10^{7}$--$10^{9}$ photons per pulse across the soft and hard X-ray range, an increase of 2--4 orders of magnitude over the original DLSR. The dual-ring light source thus provides a cost-effective route to MHz FEL operation based on existing storage-ring infrastructure, combining the high repetition rate of a DLSR with the short pulses and high brilliance of a linac-driven FEL.

items.title: HFR distorted-wave photoionization of Te III: a preliminary benchmark for large-scale atomic data production to model nebular-phase kilonovae
items.summary: The shortage of photoionization cross sections for heavy elements remains an obstacle to non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) modeling of nebular-phase kilonova ejecta, where hydrogenic prescriptions have often been adopted in the absence of ion-specific calculations. We present a first preliminary benchmark of direct photoionization cross sections for doubly ionized tellurium, obtained using the distorted-wave (DW) approximation within the pseudo-relativistic Hartree-Fock (HFR) method implemented in the Cowan codes, in which a semi-empirical adjustment based on the observed energy levels is performed. For the photoionization from the ground level of Te III to the ground level of Te IV, comparison with Dirac R-matrix data shows encouraging agreement in the magnitude and overall decrease of the non-resonant background in the lower photon-energy region, approximately below 4 Ry (autoionizing resonances are absent from the present direct treatment). These preliminary results support HFR distorted-wave calculations as a promising and computationally tractable approach for large-scale production of photoionization cross sections, with lanthanides and actinides as longer-term targets, in light of their importance to kilonova modeling and of the severe lack of atomic data for these species.

items.title: Longitudinal beam dynamics II. Lecture 2: intensity effects and beam instabilities
items.summary: In this lecture, dealing with intensity effects, the equations of longitudinal motion with induced beam voltage are analyzed. This allows us, first, to describe the single-bunch potential well distortion and the loss of Landau damping. Then the linearized Vlasov equation is used to derive step-by-step the Lebedev equation. This matrix equation is then applied to find the thresholds, growth rates and spectra of an unstable multi-bunch beam. The lecture is concluded by a discussion of possible beam-instability cures.

items.title: Retweeting patterns reveal partisan asymmetries in information sharing and signal state-level electoral outcomes in the 2020 US presidential election
items.summary: As social media has become a primary source of political information, concerns are growing that online information consumption may intensify political polarization and reshape democratic processes. Yet how large-scale online information consumption organizes polarized political ecosystems and relates to offline voting remains unclear. Here we reconstruct partisan information ecosystems from more than 500 million tweets generated during the 2020 US presidential election, integrating information diffusion across media outlets, influencers, and social peers. Contrary to the conventional expectation that broader information exposure promotes moderation, we find that retweeting a wider range of political information is associated with stronger political polarization. We further show systematic asymmetries in political information ecosystems: the Republican ecosystem is highly concentrated and ideologically biased, whereas the Democratic ecosystem is more dispersed and primarily organized around relatively moderate left-leaning sources. Finally, we demonstrate that several shared retweeting signatures robustly map onto state-level electoral outcomes despite cross-state heterogeneity. Our findings reveal asymmetric political information ecosystems as a key organizing principle of online political communication and identify collective retweeting patterns as a scalable signal of real-world voting behaviours.

items.title: Longitudinal beam dynamics II. Lecture 1: single and double rf systems
items.summary: In the first part of this lecture, the main characteristics of synchrotron motion, namely, synchronous particle and phase, bucket area and emittance, are introduced. The equations of longitudinal particle motion in a single rf system of a proton synchrotron are rederived and the phase equation is analyzed for small and large amplitude particles. The particle motion below and above transition energy is also considered. The main applications and operation modes of a double rf system are discussed in the second part of the lecture. The intensity effects and beam instabilities are the subject of the following lecture.

items.title: VNA-Only Calibration of Waveguide Thermistor Mounts with Self-Consistent Determination of the Thermistor-Port Impedance
items.summary: A method is presented for determining the calibration factor and the effective efficiency of waveguide thermistor mounts from vector-network-analyzer reflection data alone, without a microcalorimeter, extending the three reflection-coefficient method of the coaxial case. In waveguide the thermistor is coupled to the line through a matching structure and the reference impedance of the thermistor port, $Z_0$, is not known a priori; it is inferred through a power-consistency relation between pairs of states, under the convention that it is real. The method reproduces the factory certificates (U = 2 %) of four K486A mounts within 1.0 % rms and the PTB-traceable values (U = 0.85 to 0.98 %) of a fifth within 0.34 % rms; its expanded measurement uncertainty is 0.5 to 1.16 % (k = 2) for the best specimen and below 2 % for the five. A mount with its waveguide-to-coaxial adapter is calibrated directly, without characterizing the adapter, from the model factor of the mount and the geometric factor measured through the adapter. The scattering matrix implied by the solution is not passive; a minimum-norm correction of the thermistor impedances along the two directions invisible to the calibration factor - the ratios of the efficiencies of the three states - brings it to the floor of passivity, where the efficiency depends on the load only through its mismatch factor, leaves the result unchanged, and gives the sensitivity of the efficiency to the bias resistance in closed form: below $4\times10^{-5}$ $Ω^{-1}$ in band mean, proportional to the mismatch of the operating state and to the loss of the mount.

items.title: Boosting bottom-up milling of glass with GHz laser bursts
items.summary: Burst-mode laser processing has gained increasing attention in material machining due to its potential to enhance processing efficiency and quality. However, most studies have focused on conventional top-down machining strategies, while investigations of bottom-up milling (BUM) remain limited. In this work, we optimize processing parameters for high-efficiency glass milling using a bottom-up approach with GHz bursts. The results show that the highest BUM efficiencies are achieved when employing high pulse counts ($\geq$ 20). To the best of our knowledge, we report the highest glass milling efficiency, reaching more than 250 $μ$m$^3$/$μ$J for both soda-lime glass and fused silica. Furthermore, increasing the burst repetition rate while maintaining a parameter set associated with high milling efficiency enables a material removal rate larger than 8 mm$^3$/s.

items.title: Why fluid relaxation modes matter: Nonlinear frequency response, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in of electrostatic microbeams with squeeze-film damping
items.summary: The squeeze film between an electrostatically actuated microbeam can both induce damping and add stiffness to the structure. In addition, the dynamics of the film can interact with the nonlinear response of the microbeam. This paper extends a reduced-order model built on the complex modes of the coupled fluid-structure problem to the computation of periodic responses and their stability for clamped-clamped microbeams. Periodic orbits are continued in the frequency domain, and their stability is determined from their Floquet multipliers. The robustness of the response is assessed through basins of attraction, integrity measures, and dynamic pull-in maps in the plane of the excitation parameters. The model is validated against the measured and computed frequency response of a microswitch. Closed-form expressions are derived for the fluid relaxation modes, together with a correction for strongly coupled films, and define a parameter that characterizes the regime of the film. The approach is applied to different microbeams including cases where fluid modes relax on the timescale of the oscillation. For all simulated devices, a single fluid mode is necessary and sufficient, whereas adding coupled modes cannot replace it, whether the fluid modes respond quasi-statically or carry their own dynamics. Removing the fluid mode displaces both bifurcations that bound the pull-in band, changes the size of the basins of attraction and the position of the attractor within them, misses an abrupt erosion of the safe basin under increasing excitation, and shifts the whole region of dynamic pull-in in the excitation plane. The reduced model, with three real unknowns, makes these global analyses affordable for a fully coupled fluid-structure system.

items.title: The role of administrative costs in policies to improve cooperation
items.summary: We use an agent-based model for studying policies of an abstract government to increase the level of cooperation. In situations where defection is the rational choice, agents receive a bonus if they choose to cooperate. The government taxes agents' payoffs from a repeated prisoner's dilemma game to establish a budget that covers the payment of bonuses, but also the administrative costs involved. We consider costs to identify cooperators, and costs to mitigate the consequences of defective behavior. Governmental interventions are fallible, i.e. cooperators and defectors are correctly identified only with a certain accuracy. Hence, the critical bonus needed to let agents cooperate depends on the accuracy, but also on the current level of cooperation. We analyze the cost constraints for the government to pay the critical bonus and different policies to adjust the accuracy dependent on the level of cooperation. We find that perfect cooperation becomes impossible. Instead, high levels of cooperation can be achieved with optimal adjustment policies.

items.title: Quantum Optical Signatures of Band Geometry in Solid-State High Harmonics
items.summary: We develop a general theory of high-harmonic generation (HHG) in solid-state systems, based on a weak-correlation expansion of photonic and matter degrees of freedom. Unlike standard HHG theories, which treat light-matter dynamics through the Schrodinger equation, our approach employs density-matrix evolution, naturally capturing the mixed-state character of both the field and the matter - a critical aspect for describing complex solid-state band structures. We show explicitly that the properties of the emitted fields are governed by the quantum statistics and quantum geometry of the underlying solid. Taking the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model in a one-sided optical cavity as a paradigmatic example, we demonstrate the change in HHG response and quantum-light signatures due to the presence of the cavity. Furthermore, we show that cavity-matter interaction gives rise to squeezed high-harmonic quantum light, whose properties are directly imprinted by the current- current fluctuations and conductance in the material system. Crucially, the observed squeezing does not rely on a separate quartic Kerr mechanism. In the mesoscopic regime, the genuine quantum Kerr term is higher order in the light-matter coupling strength and negligible, while the relevant non-classical effect is governed by current-current fluctuations encoded in the complex susceptibility of the material. Additionally, non-trivial cross-correlations between different far-field emitted modes appear and show bunched and anti-bunched mode pairs. This work establishes a direct link between band geometry and photon statistics, opening new avenues for geometry-sensitive quantum light generation and photon statistics based spectroscopy of solid-state systems.

items.title: Usage of GPUs for ALICE Reconstruction in the ALICE Online Compute farm and in the Grid
items.summary: ALICE, the dedicated heavy-ion experiment at the LHC, records Pb-Pb collisions at an interaction rate of up to 50 kHz. It was the first LHC experiment to leverage GPUs for online data processing during LHC Runs 1 and 2, and its Run 3 online event reconstruction is now almost fully based on GPUs. In order to use its online processing server farm also for offline processing in an efficient way while the LHC is not operating, ALICE has been running the offline TPC tracking on GPUs since 2023. Since then, ALICE has been working on offloading more offline reconstruction steps to GPUs. In particular, porting the track model decoding and ITS tracking to GPUs has improved the throughput by 29%. Starting in 2026, ALICE can use the GPUs at external grid sites beyond the ALICE online computing farm for offline reconstruction. A first production campaign ran on the NVIDIA GPUs of the NERSC Perlmutter cluster, marking the first use of GPUs for LHC offline reconstruction at an external grid site.
authors: David Rohr for the ALICE Collaboration

items.title: Midlatitude cloud radiative effects reinforce storm tracks on seasonal timescales
items.summary: Midlatitude storm tracks play a central role in Earth's climate by transporting heat from low to high latitudes. Their strength is therefore set by the meridional temperature gradients, traditionally linked to differential solar heating. This framework predicts a substantial seasonal reduction in storm activity, as meridional insolation gradients vanish during summer. Yet in the Southern Hemisphere, storm activity decreases by only about 40% from its seasonal maximum. Here, we show that cloud radiative effects contribute to the seasonal maintenance of storm activity by reinforcing the temperature gradients that sustain it. Satellite observations reveal that sunlight reflected by midlatitude clouds in early summer creates a substantial meridional gradient in surface heating, despite the nearly uniform summer insolation. Idealized aquaplanet simulations then show that shortwave cloud radiative effects reinforce meridional sea-surface temperature gradients, thereby strengthening storm activity primarily during late summer and autumn, while longwave cloud effects partly offset this response. To interpret these results, we develop a simple theoretical model linking storms, clouds, and sea-surface temperature gradients. The model captures the seasonal response and demonstrates the importance of two emergent cloud properties: the maximum attainable cloud albedo and the sensitivity of cloud cover to storm activity. Together, these findings indicate that cloud radiative feedbacks help maintain the thermal gradients that sustain storm activity on seasonal timescales. More broadly, they reveal a strong coupling among storms, clouds, and the ocean spanning distinct spatial and temporal scales.

items.title: Mosaic: A Benchmark Suite for Differentiable Physics Solvers
items.summary: Differentiable partial differential equation (PDE) solvers underpin solver-in-the-loop MLtraining, gradient-based optimal control, and inverse problems, yet the practical cost of obtaining correct, usable gradients from a given solver on a given problem is largely undocumented. Integration effort, computational cost, memory, gradient accuracy, and numerical stability vary widely across solvers and are discoverable only by trial and error. We introduce Mosaic, an extensible benchmarking framework for differentiable PDE solvers that standardizes access to solver gradients. Each solver is packaged as a containerized component (Tesseract) exposing a uniform gradient API regardless of language or automatic differentiation (AD) strategy, enabling researchers to evaluate, compare, and build on non-trivial physical solvers. Our evaluation of 14 solvers across fluid dynamics, structural mechanics, and heat transfer demonstrates that the benchmark surfaces practically relevant differences: order-of-magnitude variation in computational cost and memory, alongside setup incompatibilities and instabilities that rule out solvers for specific tasks. Despite this variation, all solvers that produce gradients converge to similar optima on our tasks, indicating that the practical barriers are memory limits, numerical stability, and setup compatibility rather than gradient accuracy alone. Mosaic is open-source and available at github.com/pasteurlabs/mosaic.

items.title: Hidden Distances: How Likert-Scale Spacing Shapes Algorithmic Voting Advice
items.summary: Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) are algorithmic recommenders that match voters with political candidates on policy preferences. They are widely adopted across many multi-party democracies; in Denmark, 62\% of eligible voters used a VAA ahead of the 2022 general election, and 45\% of VAA users reported following its advice. VAAs typically ask voters and candidates to respond to policy statements on a Likert scale, from ``strongly disagree'' to ``strongly agree'', and recommend candidates whose responses are closest to the voter's. Computing these distances requires assigning numbers to response options, a design choice without an empirical basis, since it is unknown how people perceive the distances between options. Here we show that this seemingly technical choice substantially changes whom voters are matched with. We parameterize the distance between ``(dis)agree'' and ``strongly (dis)agree'' relative to the distance between ``neutral'' and ``(dis)agree'' as $α$, and quantify how it changes recommendations for a popular Danish VAA. We find that moving from equidistant options to doubling this distance can change $37.7\%$ of top candidate matches and $21.9\%$ of top party matches, although no answers change. Low $α$-values favor candidates with strong positions, with some parties receiving up to $ 19.6\%$ more recommendations, while high $α$-values favor moderates. Similarly, female candidates receive fewer recommendations at low $α$ and more at high $α$-values. Our findings demonstrate that undisclosed quantification choices in algorithmic recommenders can carry considerable electoral consequences, and they call for transparency and sensitivity analysis in VAA design. As Likert-based matching also underpins dating platforms and roommate allocation systems, these implications extend well beyond elections.

items.title: Phase-Stabilization-Free Information Processing on Unstable Photonic Processors
items.summary: Hadamard-coded optical receivers commonly require stable interference conditions for absolute codeword discrimination. Here we encode four symbols as differential Hadamard operations: no phase change or a $π$ shift on exactly two of three non-reference input modes. The information is carried by the selected phase-change operation, rather than the absolute optical codeword. We investigate a fixed eight-port intensity-only receiver that reconstructs six coupled trigonometric observables from simultaneous power measurements. Their deterministic sign transformations allow an analytical decoder to identify the applied operation from successive measurements without continuous optical phase stabilization or knowledge of the initial absolute codeword label. An earlier measured signature and sufficiently limited inter-measurement drift remain necessary. We establish exact observable reconstruction, characterize exceptional phase configurations and conditional noise sensitivity, and compare ideal four- and eight-port detection under an equal-photon budget. Experiments on programmable photonic processors yield 96.19\% analytical decoding accuracy; a separate machine-learning analysis reports 98.31\% on a held-out experimental trace. The results demonstrate differential, intensity-only Hadamard operation decoding under the tested conditions.

items.title: Efficient sensitivity analysis for combustion problems via reformulation and adjoint methods
items.summary: Numerical simulations of combustion processes rely on chemical kinetic models, whose predictive capability is typically assessed by comparing measurements of quantities of interest (QoIs) in idealized experimental configurations with the corresponding simulated values. Sensitivity analysis quantifies the influence of model parameters on QoIs, making it a key tool for model development and optimization. Given the large number of parameters involved in detailed kinetic models compared to the number of QoIs, adjoint methods are a promising approach for efficient sensitivity analysis. Ignition delay times (IDTs) and extinction strain rates (ESRs) are among the QoIs of primary importance. However, applying adjoint methods to these quantities is not straightforward and is addressed in this work. The system of governing equations is reformulated via a coordinate transformation that makes the QoI an explicit component of the solution vector. This reformulation enables the application of adjoint sensitivity analysis for both IDT and ESR. A computational complexity analysis demonstrates that the proposed formulation significantly improves algorithmic efficiency compared to conventional approaches. The methodology is verified by comparing adjoint sensitivity coefficients with those obtained from other methods. Execution time measurements show computational cost reductions of up to two orders of magnitude relative to standard direct sensitivity analysis. A benchmark study is conducted across kinetic models of increasing size to assess how far theoretical efficiency gains are realized in practice. While the results show that implementation details can limit performance for smaller problem sizes, the expected asymptotic scaling is observed for larger models. The benchmark thus provides a reference framework for identifying key performance bottlenecks and guiding subsequent optimization efforts.

items.title: Uncertainty-Aware End-to-End AI Weather Forecasting: Disentangling Observation and Model Contributions
items.summary: End-to-end weather forecasting systems produce skillful global gridded and station forecasts directly from raw Earth observations, replacing the numerical weather prediction pipeline, including data assimilation, at a fraction of its cost. These systems are deterministic and issue no uncertainty. Here we render the Aardvark Weather model probabilistic by attaching one stochastic mechanism to each component: learned, input-dependent noise at the observation encoder, aimed at the uncertainty inherited from the observing system, and Monte Carlo dropout in the processor, aimed at the uncertainty of the learned dynamics. The resulting nested ensemble attributes forecast spread to the two sources through a law-of-total-variance decomposition, cross-checked by withholding observation streams. Probabilistic finetuning significantly improves the mean forecast, by 11% on average across variables and lead times. The ensemble is close to calibrated against ERA5 through the medium range, is at least as accurate as the deterministic model at weather stations while beating it in relative economic value at every lead time, and remains considerably behind the operational ECMWF IFS ensemble. The encoder branch behaves as observation-driven uncertainty. Component-attributed uncertainty makes end-to-end forecasts more transparent, a step toward observation-driven digital twins of the atmosphere.

items.title: Deep Learning-based Algebraic Reynolds Stress Closures for RANS Simulations of Turbulent Flows
items.summary: Turbulence is ubiquitous in engineering and science, yet direct simulation is prohibitively expensive. The Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations provide savings exceeding ten orders of magnitude but introduce unclosed terms. Offline-trained machine-learning (ML) closures suffer distribution shift in predictive simulations, while ML methods that bypass the governing equations struggle to generalise from scarce high-fidelity data. We develop a physics-derived deep learning closure for RANS, the Deep Algebraic Reynolds Stress Model (DARSM), which can be trained on one or two flow cases and accurately generalise across an order of magnitude in Reynolds number, to unseen geometries, and across flow regimes. A neural network maps flow invariants to empirical parameters in an implicit algebraic Reynolds stress equation, derived from the Reynolds stress transport equations under the weak-equilibrium assumption, imposing physics-based structure on the ML closure. End-to-end optimisation through the governing PDEs eliminates distribution shift, but both unrolled and implicit automatic differentiation fail on the stiff coupled solver. We derive adjoint equations that exploit the solver's implicit-explicit structure for efficient optimisation. On canonical square-duct and periodic-hill benchmarks, DARSM reduces average test velocity error over baseline RANS by 2-4x across Reynolds number, geometries, and flow regimes, with peak case-level reductions of 12x. The model trained on attached, anisotropy-dominated flows (square duct) accurately generalises without retraining to separated flows (periodic hills), a regime change in the underlying physics. DARSM also outperforms established ML methods: offline training, tensor-basis neural networks, field-inversion machine learning, DeepONets, physics-informed neural networks, and an adjoint-trained source-term closure.

items.title: Optical frequency combs on thin-film lithium niobate: from principles to applications
items.summary: Optical frequency combs, consisting of mutually coherent and equally spaced spectral lines, provide a powerful means of synthesizing, distributing, and processing optical frequencies on chip. Among integrated photonic platforms, thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) is particularly attractive for comb generation because it combines strong electro-optic (EO) functionality, accessible $χ^{(2)}$ and $χ^{(3)}$ nonlinearities, low-loss nanophotonic confinement, and versatile dispersion engineering. This review summarizes the physical foundations and representative realizations of TFLN combs, and discusses their applications in optical communication, microwave photonics, optical computing, and precision metrology. The integration of nonlinear functionality, EO control, and passive photonic components is expected to advance compact, energy-efficient comb sources and broaden the utility of TFLN in integrated photonics and quantum optics.

items.title: Ultrafast Liquid Jet X-ray Total Scattering
items.summary: X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) provide the temporal resolution needed to extend total scattering and pair distribution function (PDF) analysis to investigate structural dynamics on femtosecond-to-picosecond timescales. We recently demonstrated that high-quality total scattering data and PDFs can be obtained from individual XFEL pulses; here, we take the next step towards time-resolved studies of structural dynamics in solution. Using the Materials Imaging and Dynamics (MID) instrument at the European XFEL, we obtain total scattering data up to $Q_{\max} = 16.4\,\mathring{\mathrm{A}}^{-1}$ from both conventional capillary samples and, critically, from samples delivered by a liquid jet. Despite the large air and solvent backgrounds inherent to this setup, PDFs suitable for quantitative structural analysis are recovered from liquid dispersions and molecular clusters in solution. We further demonstrate pump-probe total scattering from $\mathrm{CsPbBr}_3$ nanocrystals in a liquid jet, resolving a fluence-dependent photoinduced isotropic lattice strain. Additionally, empirical potential structure refinement (EPSR) of XFEL total scattering data from an aqueous Keggin cluster reveals site-specific hydration environments and enables three-dimensional mapping of the surrounding solvent structure. Together, these advances open the door to tracking not only ultrafast structural changes in solution, but also the evolving solvent environments that govern molecular behaviour and reactivity.

items.title: Probabilistic wavefield decomposition from array covariance
items.summary: Inter-sensor coherence loss carries information about the wavefield that conventional array processing discards. The array-covariance matrix is modelled using a mixture of energy distributions over slowness with analytical characteristic functions, e.g., skew-normal and angular-harmonic distributions, and inverted using variational Bayesian inference. The posterior supports uncertainty quantification, experimental design, model comparison and hypothesis testing. For a synthetic hydroacoustic T-phase, information is increased by an additional sensor and decreased by noise; the data favour a distributed source over a point source. For an observed thermospheric infrasound return, energy is skewed back towards the source. The method is implemented in the software Topophone2.

items.title: Modelling socio-economic effects of the pandemic in a metropolitan area
items.summary: One of the most notorious measures taken by authorities in every country trying to prevent the uncontrollable spread of the Covid 19 pandemic was to impose severe measures to diminish the mobility of people. In recent publications we proposed a mathematical model to address the consequences of these measures and to predict the infections under different scenarios, for various different countries. In this paper we extend the model, called the BTH--SEIRS-model, to deal with the reduction of mobility in an urban area. The chosen region was the densely-populated metropolitan area around Helsinki, the capital of Finland. This choice obeyed to the fact that there are precise data related to mobility from a mobile telephone company, and that this region was completely isolated from the rest of the country for a short period during the pandemic. We also used public transport data from railways and the accommodation occupation rates in the area of interest. We show that the BTH--SEIRS model is capable of simulating the real infection data as well as the mobility-related economic activity, exhibiting the main trends present in the three indicators used for comparison. Our calculations allow us to highlight the difference of the behaviour of the pandemic in a totally different spatial scale, and to discover the hidden factors that govern the behaviour of people who are forced to commute every day from home to work.

items.title: Beam-beam effects on measurements at electron-positron colliders: LEP neutrino counting and Higgs factories
items.summary: Beam-beam electromagnetic interactions affect the luminosity, collision energy, polarization, and particle backgrounds relevant to precision measurements at electron-positron colliders. We investigate these effects using Fast $e^{\pm}e^{\pm}$ Beam and Luminosity (FeeBL), a new beam-beam simulation framework, and compare its predictions with published results from LEP and proposed future colliders. We reproduce the analytical field-integration calculations of LEP Bhabha scattering and identify an approximately 2% bias in previously published beam-deflection simulations. Applying the corresponding luminosity correction and a revised uncertainty assessment motivated by the observed agreement among the four LEP experiments yields ($N_ν= 2.9965 \pm 0.0040$), compared with the previously reported ($2.9963 \pm 0.0074$). The revised uncertainty is conditional on an assumed common rescaling of experiment specific uncertainties and motivates further investigation of the original uncertainty budgets. We identify and correct implementation errors in the modeling of Breit-Wheeler, Bethe-Heitler, and Landau-Lifshitz pair production, with implications for detector backgrounds at Higgs factories. Simulated beam depolarization and luminosity spectra are compared with existing ILC and HALHF predictions. Finally, we investigate collision energy monochromatization for direct Higgs production, obtaining sub-MeV collision energy peak widths in exploratory linear collider configurations at substantial luminosity cost, while finding significantly weaker narrowing for the FCC-ee configurations studied. We derive a rigid Gaussian beam overlap model and estimate that FCC-ee needs roughly 10 m of horizontal only dispersion to reach widths of $\approx1~\mathrm{MeV}$.

items.title: Variational free complement method with Gaussian expanded complement functions: extensions of general atomic framework including helium and lithium ground states with geminal induced expansion length
items.summary: We expand the previous framework of hierarchical-decontraction Gaussian expanded complement functions approach (arXiv: 2603.16262v2) of the free complement (FC) method to $N$-electron atomic systems including general permutations. We consider the possibility that the Gaussian expansion length depends on the presence of the geminal $g$ function. To be more specific, fewer expansion length shall be used when the two-electron $g$ function is combined with the initial wavefunction. The present approach is applied to the ground states of the helium and lithium atoms. The complement function generations via 2s$\rightarrow$1s channel in the lithium ground state are discussed. Symmetries for the associated $N$-electron integrals are analyzed.

items.title: Predictability of Collective Behavior in Networks of LLM Agents
items.summary: As AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact at scale, anticipating their collective behavior becomes necessary. Unlike humans, individual LLM agents can be probed in {controlled scenarios}; however, the predictability of their collective outcomes hinges on what such measurements capture. We study information cascades on networks of LLM agents that decide whether to share a post given how many of their contacts have shared it. At the same fraction of sharing contacts, an agent's response depends on how many contacts it has and on the post. Responses that ignore the number of contacts mispredict the cascades, increasingly on heterogeneous networks, by an error we derive analytically and that network topology alone cannot reveal. Measured in context, the response predicts, through mean-field theory, the cascades of full LLM simulations, tipping points included. Anticipating the collective behavior of AI agents thus requires evaluating them in their local network context.

items.title: Active learning and explicit electrostatics enable accurate modeling of electrolytes
items.summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) combine near-ab initio accuracy with the computational efficiency of classical force fields, making them promising tools for modeling molecular liquids and electrolytes. Their predictive accuracy depends strongly on the diversity of the training set, while the explicit treatment of electrostatics is increasingly recognized as an important factor in improving their performance. In this work, we assess the impact of incorporating explicit electrostatics and environment-dependence of atomic charges by comparing short-ranged Moment Tensor Potentials (MTPs) with electrostatics-augmented MTPs, including fixed-charge and environment-dependent charge models. To this end, we employ D-optimality-based active learning (AL) to train short-ranged MTPs and extend the AL procedure, previously unavailable for long-range electrostatics-augmented MTPs, to these models, enabling largely automated generation of diverse training sets for pure ethylene carbonate (EC) and ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), their mixtures, and LiPF6 solutions. For EC, EMC, and their mixtures, electrostatics-augmented MTPs achieve accuracy comparable to or better than that of their short-ranged counterparts while requiring fewer machine-learned parameters. For LiPF6 solutions, however, a notable improvement in accuracy is achieved only with environment-dependent charges, which also enhance stability in large-scale molecular dynamics simulations, unlike the fixed-charge model. The resulting short-ranged MTPs and environment-dependent-charge models reproduce experimental densities with mean absolute deviations of 0.2-6% and ionic conductivities with deviations of 11-15%, while capturing the experimentally observed temperature dependence of conductivity.

items.title: One2N: Recursive refinement breaks the resolution barrier for Earth-system AI
items.summary: Earth-system AI models approach kilometre-scale resolution, but halving grid spacing quadruples the grid-point count and end-to-end training cost. We introduce One2N, a recursive incremental framework extending a coarse model through $N$ levels of cross-resolution residual correction. At each level the parent is frozen and excluded from backpropagation, so its activations and optimizer states are never retained; only a tier-specific module is trained. A single refinement level on the NeuralGCM-0.7$^\circ$ baseline yields the two-level One2N-0.07$^\circ$, trained on one 80 GB GPU. Against HRES-0.07$^\circ$ and ERA5-0.25$^\circ$ analyses it matches its parent's tropospheric skill while reducing upper-stratospheric errors and resolving finer structure. Tropical-cyclone track errors nearly match the parent's and are lower than Pangu-Weather-0.25$^\circ$ at medium range; RMSE is lower than that model's on 93.46% of common targets. One2N thus turns an existing forecasting system, or an inexpensively trained coarse baseline, into a reusable foundation for high-resolution development, breaking the resolution barrier.

items.title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
items.summary: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

items.title: Off-focus detection for SNR enhancement in coherent single-pixel imaging
items.summary: Coherent single-pixel imaging (CSPI) enables amplitude- and phase-resolved computational imaging with a single coherent detector, offering particular advantages in spectral regimes where high-performance detector arrays remain unavailable. In conventional Fourier-plane CSPI, the detector is typically placed at the focal point to maximize the collected power. However, this focal position does not necessarily maximize the reconstruction fidelity for image reconstruction in the presence of system nonidealities. Here, we introduce detector position as an additional degree of freedom for CSPI optimization. We show that appropriately selected off-focus Fourier-plane positions can improve reconstruction performance by suppressing fluctuation-sensitive coherent backgrounds while preserving spatially encoded signals. Experimentally, using a programmable liquid-crystal terahertz spatial light modulator and coherent heterodyne detection, we demonstrate improved amplitude and phase reconstruction from selected off-focus channels compared with focal detection. A symmetric off-focus pair with complementary transverse-wave-vector weighting further enhances image fidelity, contrast, and compressive-sampling robustness through coherent channel fusion. These results establish detector-position engineering as a new strategy for enhancing the robustness and information efficiency of CSPI.

items.title: Bayesian Kinetic Model Selection in Dynamic PET via Consistency Models
items.summary: Accurate voxel-wise parametric imaging in dynamic positron emission tomography (PET), particu- larly with total-body PET (TB-PET) scanners, requires se- lecting the appropriate kinetic model for diverse organs and lesions. Conventional nonlinear least squares fitting paired with the Akaike or Bayesian Information Criterion (NLS+AIC/BIC) is computationally slow, sensitive to lo- cal minima, and prone to selecting simple models under high voxel-level noise, whereas classical Bayesian methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and Approx- imate Bayesian Computation (PET-ABC) are too slow for whole-body imaging. In this work, we propose a consis- tency model (CM) that performs simultaneous Bayesian kinetic model selection and parameter posterior estimation. By combining the continuous kinetic parameters and dis- crete model index into one target vector conditioned on the measured time-activity curve (TAC) and input function, the CM samples from the joint posterior distribution p(θ, m|y) in seconds per slice with a GPU workstation of 4 NVIDIA A100. We validated the framework on two simulated and clinical applications: whole-body [18F]FDG TB-PET across seven compartment models, and brain [11C]raclopride PET for detecting smoking-induced dopamine release between two neurotransmitter models. In simulations, the CM achieved 97.97% model selection accuracy in the [18F]FDG applica- tion (vs. 58.67% for NLS+AIC) and 91.4% accuracy in the [11C]raclopride application (vs. 73.5% for NLS+BIC), while closely matching reference MCMC parameter posteriors. In clinical applications, CM generated whole-body FDG model selection maps, in which each regions was assigned litera- ture established sensible kinetic models; CM also success- fully mapped voxels in the brain where dopamine release was induced by smoking.

items.title: X-ray parametric down-conversion probes radiation-induced dynamics in hybrid perovskite MAPbBr3
items.summary: We report minute-timescale time-resolved measurements of X-ray parametric down-conversion (PDC) of X-rays into ultraviolet photons in a MAPbBr3 single crystal under continuous irradiation. Despite the known radiation sensitivity of hybrid perovskites and the high photon flux required to detect the intrinsically weak PDC signal, the nonlinear response remains measurable throughout the irradiation sequence. Both PDC and Bragg diffraction exhibit a slow decay consistent with diffusion-driven damage dynamics on timescales reported for bromide-vacancy and proton migration. However, despite their similar decay rates, the PDC and Bragg signals evolve toward markedly different steady states, while an additional fast decay component is observed in the Bragg response but absent in the PDC signal. Density functional theory calculations identify N 2s states of the methylammonium cation as the most likely contributors to the measured PDC response and show that their Fourier component is only weakly affected by bromide-vacancy formation. These results establish nonlinear X-ray diffraction as a channel-selective probe of radiation-induced dynamics and demonstrate that radiation damage can couple differently to nonlinear and linear X-ray responses.

items.title: Topological phases and scattering protected by projective chiral symmetry
items.summary: The bulk-boundary correspondence states that topological properties of a bulk material guarantee the existence of protected edge modes, oftentimes associated with the attractive property of backscattering immunity. In this Letter, we consider a time reversal invariant classical system with both translation and chiral, or sublattice, symmetries. We show that when these two symmetries anti-commute, the material exhibits a topological phase protected by the same invariant as type D topological superconductors. We realize such a system experimentally and observe the existence of the associated edge modes in an acoustic network. Our measurements are in excellent agreement with theoretical predictions from discrete lattice models. Finally, we show that these edge modes are immune to backscattering for perturbations consisting in two subsequent identical defects.

items.title: Tunable Near-Unity Light Absorption via Surface Exciton-Polaritons in Periodic Gratings of Anisotropic Polarizable Materials
items.summary: Near-perfect light absorption in ultrathin films is hindered by two fundamental obstacles: the momentum mismatch that prevents resonant excitation of surface exciton-polaritons (SEPs) under ordinary illumination, and the 50% absorption ceiling imposed on free-standing conductive sheets by geometric symmetry. Here we show that both obstacles can be overcome simultaneously in a simple, planar geometry. A one-dimensional periodic grating of anisotropic polarizable ribbons composed of J-aggregates supporting bright molecular excitons provides the reciprocal lattice momentum needed to excite SEPs without employing an attenuated total reflection configuration, while a metallic mirror beneath a dielectric spacer folds the reflected field back onto the absorber, breaking the $50\%$ limit through interference between the incident and reflected waves. We develop a semi-analytical matrix formulation to compute the full optical response of such structure, and demonstrate that the absorptance at the first-order SEP resonance can be continuously tuned from near-unity to near-zero by varying the spacer thickness alone. The grating period and filling factor offer additional spectral control, and oblique incidence unlocks a second, out-of-plane polariton branch. These results establish periodic gratings of excitonic media as a versatile, practical and integrable platform for spectrally selective, near-perfect light absorption.

items.title: Fluctuation-Response Relations and Memory in Tissue Cell Number Dynamics
items.summary: The longevity of multicellular systems requires finely tuned feedback mechanisms to control the balance of cellular proliferation and loss. To understand the microscopic details governing feedback during homeostasis, it is crucial to quantify the feedback using a robust, minimally invasive method. Existing methods typically depend on perturbing the system to quantify the response. Such perturbations may alter cell physiology and are often technically challenging to implement. We propose a steady-state fluctuation-analysis framework to measure the dynamic response coefficient of cellular tissues. Under the minimal assumption of crowding feedback and Markovian noise, we derive a corresponding theoretical description. We validate this framework against three models of increasing complexity: a simple stochastic simulation, an agent-based mechanical model of tissue growth, and a multi-scale model of membrane-potential-regulated growth. These tests reveal the suitability of using passive fluctuations to characterize the tissue response parameters. Furthermore, this approach can help discover novel phenomena; in particular, we uncover memory effects arising from the non-equilibrium nature of growth. This work opens new avenues to quantify growth parameters in living tissues.

items.title: Heterogeneous Acceleration of TRIMEG++ code using OpenMP for Gyrokinetic Simulations
items.summary: Turbulent transport largely determines the performance of magnetic-confinement fusion devices such as tokamaks, and gyrokinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations are a principal tool to predict it. Advancing up to hundreds of millions of markers and solving large sparse field systems at every time step makes whole-device simulations among the most expensive in plasma physics. GPUs can accelerate this workload, but porting a complex code requires restructuring its parallelism and memory traffic, ideally without a separate version per vendor. In this work, the gyrokinetic code TRIMEG-C1, whose unstructured triangular mesh and high-order finite elements cover both the confined core and the open-field-line edge of the plasma, is rewritten in C++ as TRIMEG++ and fully offloaded to GPUs with OpenMP target directives, so that one portable code base runs on both AMD and NVIDIA hardware. The particle-to-grid projection is offloaded in its standard and field-aligned formulations, the PETSc-based field solver runs on the GPU through the library's backends, and, together with the previously offloaded particle pusher, every stage whose cost scales with the marker count runs on the GPU. All speedups are node-to-node comparisons against a 256-core CPU node (2x AMD EPYC 9754). On the TCV-X21 tokamak reference case, the offloaded kernels reproduce the CPU results to a relative accuracy of 1e-11, and the full simulation runs 4.1-6.1x faster on a node with two AMD MI300A and 2.1-3.0x faster on a node with four NVIDIA A100, with the speedup growing with problem size. The MI300A, with shared CPU-GPU memory, needs no explicit data transfers, whereas the A100 needs them managed by hand. These results show that directive-based offloading can accelerate a complex gyrokinetic code across GPU vendors, making whole-volume tokamak simulations with hundreds of millions of markers practical on a single GPU node.

items.title: Universal Scaling and Geometric Correction of High-Frequency Mass Transfer in Porous Electrodes
items.summary: Classical film theory predicts a finite diffusion-limited current at porous electrodes. Transient operation can nevertheless produce peak interfacial fluxes above this steady limit, although the time-averaged flux remains bounded. Here, we use a frequency-domain volume-averaging framework to study this transient response in porous media. In the perfectly reactive limit, the spectral Sherwood number approaches $\Shnd\sim\sqrt{\iu\wstar}$ at high frequency, with magnitude proportional to $ω^{1/2}$, phase $π/4$, and a universal leading prefactor. A boundary-layer analysis shows that this response follows from local transient diffusion and is independent of the global pore geometry. Numerical results for parallel plates, circular tubes, and twelve porous microstructures confirm the scaling across variations in particle shape, symmetry, porosity, array arrangement, flow orientation, and flow strength. We also derive the first geometry-dependent correction, which depends on interfacial area, surface curvature, and sharp edges, and verify it without fitted parameters. Comparisons with published impedance measurements for a carbon-felt fiber and a vanadium flow-battery electrode are consistent with the predicted transport response. Finally, we derive bounds on pulse duration and identify operating windows for representative redox couples. These results establish a temporal route to enhanced peak transport in porous electrodes without requiring surface charge, confinement, or electrokinetic instability.

items.title: State estimation of Rayleigh-Bénard convection with reduced-order models
items.summary: In this work, we develop a state estimation framework for two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard (RB) convection that combines a stable Galerkin reduced-order model (ROM) with an extended Kalman filter (EKF). The ROM, constructed from controllability modes of the linearized Boussinesq equations, provides the nonlinear dynamical model for the filter prediction step. Direct numerical simulations (DNS) are used to generate synthetic measurements for data assimilation. We assess filter performance across periodic, quasiperiodic, and chaotic regimes, demonstrating that the filter tracks the most energetic modes with high fidelity and achieves time-averaged reconstruction errors below $16\%$ for velocity and $19\%$ for temperature. We apply the ROM-based EKF to a hybrid simulation scenario where the system state is assimilated from velocity measurements. It is shown that velocity observations alone suffice to reconstruct the state, including the temperature field. Finally, we exploit the Kalman gain matrix to develop a greedy sensor placement strategy that progressively removes the least informative sensors. The algorithm reveals a clear hierarchy among sensor types and can be used to derive skeletal observation configurations. It also provides guidance on which measurement variables and spatial locations are most informative for state correction. The present framework is general, and may be applied to other quadratic Galerkin ROMs for state estimation.

items.title: Amortized Transport-Map Likelihoods for Hierarchical Inverse Problems with Application to Wetting
items.summary: Hierarchical Bayesian models pool measurements, but with the forward model in the likelihood every posterior evaluation costs one forward solve per cell. To reduce this cost, we introduce a simulation-based inference framework in which a triangular transport-map likelihood, trained once per design, serves every cell. We apply it to infer wetting properties from photographs of a stable hole in a thin liquid film. The hole's radius depends, through the nonlinear Young-Laplace equation, on the contact angle and capillary length. One photograph gives rank-one information about them, so we pool many in a hierarchical model whose cells, each a substrate at one volume setting, share the apparatus geometry and the noise scale. A design fixes the number of substrates, the volume settings and the photographs per cell. The map's posteriors agree with direct sampling of the forward model in the wetting properties at a synthetic validation design, and less closely at a larger synthetic scaling design. At the validation design, simulation-based calibration detects no departure for any parameter. There, the map needs several hundred times fewer forward-model evaluations than direct sampling with a gradient-free ensemble sampler for a single posterior, and about five orders of magnitude fewer over a calibration study of 200 posteriors. On real photographs its posterior agrees with direct sampling and is consistent with the measured radii. Trained offline, the amortized map turns new photographs into a posterior with no forward solve. It is thus a major step toward measuring wetting properties in situ without disturbing the liquid.

items.title: Second stability region for gyrokinetics and the L-H transition
items.summary: Using a simple circular tokamak geometry, we show the well-known `second stability region' of MHD-ballooning modes exists for linear gyrokinetics too---whether electrostatic or electromagnetic---and we suggest that the plasma enters this region in H-mode as a consequence of the bootstrap current and Shafranov shift altering the magnetic field, which may occur if the normalised pressure gradient is $α_{\rm MHD} \simgt 1$ and collisionality is low. By performing simulations in more realistic magnetic geometries, we demonstrate a large reduction in collisionless, electrostatic turbulent transport when going from density and temperature profiles typical of L- and H-mode, respectively. This reduction is shown to be a consequence of both the bootstrap current lowering the global magnetic shear, and the pressure gradient altering the local magnetic shear, pushing the plasma towards the second-stability region. A path connecting the L- and H-mode equilibria is constructed, along which the energy and particle fluxes exhibit non-monotonic behaviour as a function of the pressure gradient.

items.title: Galerkin reduced order model for two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection
items.summary: In this work, Galerkin projection is used to build reduced-order models (ROM) for two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard (RB) convection with no-slip walls. We compare an uncoupled projection approach that uses separate orthonormal bases for velocity and temperature with a coupled formalism where the equations are projected onto a single basis combining velocity and temperature components. Orthonormal bases for modal projection are obtained as the eigenfunctions of the controllability Gramian of the linearized RB equations, eliminating the need for DNS snapshot databases required by traditional POD-based approaches. Various coupled and uncoupled ROMs with different numbers of modes are generated and validated against direct numerical simulations (DNS) over a wide range of Rayleigh numbers. One of the objectives is to determine their domain of validity as a function of the system dimension and the Rayleigh number. DNS and ROM results are compared in terms of mean vertical profiles, heat flux, flow structures, dynamical regimes and energy spectra. Crucially, unlike previous POD-based Galerkin models for thermal convection, these ROMs do not require closure models and remain numerically stable. The coupled approach shows better agreement with DNS in terms of mean vertical profiles and Nusselt number scaling. The capabilities of these models are exploited to conduct a detailed bifurcation analysis at $Pr = 10$ using Poincaré sections and Lyapunov exponents, precisely identifying the transitions between periodic, quasiperiodic, and chaotic states with significant reductions of computational cost.

items.title: Detecting space objects with Earth-observation radar satellites
items.summary: Millimetre-to-centimetre orbital debris poses a hazard to spacecraft, but its abundance remains difficult to measure. Spaceborne radars offer a substantial sensitivity advantage at close range: received echo power decreases with the fourth power of distance, so an otherwise identical object ten times closer produces a 10,000 times stronger echo. We investigate this opportunity using openly available Sentinel-1 radar voltages recorded on six calendar days. Catalogue-assisted processing identifies a manually validated sample of 76 objects at ranges of 41.7--492.9 km, including satellites, rocket bodies and debris fragments. A blind search recovers two selected debris transits without using their orbital predictions during detection. A short debris encounter also demonstrates how precise range and Doppler measurements can refine a catalogue orbit. Ground scatter increases the effective background and is the principal sensitivity limitation in Earth-looking observations. An ideal receiver-noise sensitivity comparison predicts detectable conducting-sphere diameters of approximately 3.4 mm for Sentinel-1 and 0.6 mm for EarthCARE at 10 km range, assuming coherent integration limited by beam transit time and a 10 ms cap. These results establish the feasibility of space-object detection using existing Earth-observation radars and motivate statistical debris surveys and targeted orbit refinement following collision warnings. Observations directed away from Earth and receive windows adapted to nearby objects could improve sensitivity to small debris.

items.title: Silicon and silicon nitride photonic ring resonator arrays for photonic trimming metrology
items.summary: Proposed silicon on silicon oxide 4x4 matrix multiplier for use in refractive index measurements, based on the Advanced Micro Foundry deep ultraviolet process. Agreement between simulated spectra and analytic design spectra demonstrate the intended performance of the components given a 1550 nm wavelength spectrum analysis. Intended purpose of the design includes optical damage analysis of the cladding, and photonic chip refractive index analysis following sub-threshold laser ablation. Femtosecond multi-shot tuning of refractive index is not a recommended application, due to round trip-losses causing quality factor and transfer function degradation.

items.title: Spatial effects of Kuramoto modeling on the power-grid frequencies
items.summary: Spatial coupling and heterogeneity can generate complex power-grid frequency dynamics. We investigate the contributions of spatial structure, intrinsic nonlinear dynamics, and external driving using the Kuramoto model (KM), with and without uncorrelated noise, and compare its predictions with real-grid measurements. We analyse one month of 100 ms frequency measurements from 16 Hungarian transmission-grid sites and simulate the KM on a 387-node transmission network and two-dimensional lattices. The measured power spectra exhibit two scaling regimes, with exponents of approximately 1.63 and 2.23. One-second frequency increments decorrelate rapidly, while correlations of their local inverse variance decay slowly, initially as a power law, $τ^{-0.26(2)}$, up to 15 minutes. A superstatistical Gaussian mixture based on measured local variances captures much of the non-Gaussian increment distribution, but not the rare extreme events. We also estimate the non-stationary long-time frequency autocorrelation exponent. KM simulations on low-dimensional networks exhibit algebraically decaying autocorrelations and power spectra, consistent with the measurements and the Wiener-Khinchin relation in the steady state. On the heterogeneous transmission network, partial synchronization and frequency locking produce persistent spatial patterns and multi-peaked frequency distributions. However, neither deterministic KM dynamics nor independent Gaussian driving reproduces the measured spectra and increment statistics simultaneously. Moreover, empirical frequency fluctuations are largely shared across substations, whereas simulated fluctuations mainly reflect relative node motion. These findings suggest that spatially coupled nonlinear dynamics contribute to observed frequency fluctuations alongside external driving, including 15-minute power dispatches.

items.title: Analytical Framework Relating Capacitance-Frequency Measurements and Hysteresis in Perovskite Solar Cells
items.summary: Mobile ion migration strongly influences the electrical response and current-voltage hysteresis of perovskite solar cells. However, quantitative determination of ionic transport parameters typically requires transient measurements, extensive numerical simulations, and/or fitting procedures involving multiple uncertain parameters. Here, we present an analytical model that establishes a direct relationship between capacitance-frequency (C-f) characteristics and ionic transport properties in perovskite solar cells, while accounting for interlayer effects. The model describes the transition from the ion-screened depletion capacitance at low frequencies to the geometric capacitance at high frequencies and demonstrates that the characteristic transition frequency provides a direct measure of the dielectric relaxation time for ions. Furthermore, the model establishes a quantitative connection between C-f characteristics and scan-rate-dependent current-voltage hysteresis, enabling prediction of the scan-rate window in which maximum hysteresis occurs. Drift-diffusion simulations show excellent agreement with the analytical predictions over wide ranges of ion density, ion mobility, transport-layer mobility and doping concentration. Experimental measurements confirm the predicted correlation between capacitance and hysteresis. By providing a direct, physically transparent, and computationally efficient route for extracting ionic transport parameters from routine impedance measurements, this work offers a practical tool for quantifying ion migration and understanding dynamic phenomena in perovskite solar cells.

items.title: Exploring the near-kernel sector of quantum reduced loop gravity
items.summary: We study the near-kernel sector of the Hamiltonian constraint operator in the one-vertex model of quantum reduced loop gravity using exact diagonalisation methods and variational Monte Carlo methods with neural quantum states. The analysis is based on the symmetric Hamiltonian containing both Euclidean and Lorentzian contributions, and on the variational minimization of the positive quadratic operator $\hat{Q}=\hat{C}^2$, where $\hat{C}$ is the symmetric Hamilton constraint, in truncated Hilbert spaces with spin cutoff up to $j_\text{max}=1001$.
