items.title: Evolutionary games on networks with negative edge-based environmental feedback
items.summary: Environmental feedback can fundamentally alter the game payoff structure underlying the evolution of cooperation. How feedback-evolving games interact with population structure under non-weak selection remains incompletely understood. We study an evolutionary game on networks in which each edge has a binary environmental state that determines the payoff matrix used by the two connected individuals. By assumption, cooperation tends to improve the local environment, which in turn favors defection, thereby creating negative feedback between strategies coupled with the environmental condition. We analyze the model under strong selection using a mean-field approximation, a pair approximation that tracks both strategy pairs and edge environments, and agent-based simulations. In well-mixed populations, the feedback can generate bistability between full cooperation and full defection, as well as sustained oscillations arising through a Hopf bifurcation. Sparse networks (i.e., with low nodes' degrees) can eliminate bistability, suppress oscillations, and produce stable intermediate levels of cooperation. The pair approximation captures these effects and generally agrees more closely with simulations on sparse networks than the mean-field approximation. Our results show that edge-based environmental feedback and network structure, such as density of edges, interact to determine whether the fraction of cooperators stabilizes or oscillates over time.

items.title: A Witness for Quantum Correlations Using Nonlinear Spectroscopy
items.summary: The ability to detect and quantify entanglement in molecular systems is essential for understanding their quantum correlations and to evaluating molecules as platforms for quantum technologies. Here we show how signals from existing spectroscopic techniques can provide sufficient information to witness entanglement. The main ingredient is a spectroscopic map from admissible quantum states to a finite-dimensional space of signal coefficients, which are expectation values of state-independent effective observables. The molecular response model and measurement protocol determine the effective observables for a fixed system bipartition, and the spectroscopic map defines sets of joint expectation values compatible with all admissible quantum states and their separable subset. We illustrate the construction of the effective observables and their expectation value sets using rotational invariants and the spectral structure of optical signals. Fluorescence dynamics and photon coincidences provide a complementary example. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for entanglement certification with established spectroscopic techniques.

items.title: Toward universal excited-state machine-learned potentials: a local excitation Hamiltonian for size consistency and transferability
items.summary: Universal machine-learned interatomic potentials could make excited-state simulations across chemical space routine, but excitation energies, unlike ground-state energies, are not sums of atomic contributions. The excited states of noninteracting molecules are the union of their states, which pooled multistate readouts reproduce at best for the lowest state. We introduce LEH-MACE, whose excitation energies are the eigenvalues of a local excitation Hamiltonian assembled from atom-centred blocks, so this union holds exactly. We generated TD-DFT energies and forces for about 300,000 equilibrium, thermal, and excited-state geometries of over 100,000 molecules. LEH-MACE's advantage over direct readouts grew with the distance from the training data and was largest above $S_1$, with about half their $S_2$ and $S_3$ errors for long conjugated oligomers. For molecule pairs, only LEH-MACE kept its single-molecule accuracy, while a softmin readout remained superior for $S_1$ dynamics of larger chromophores. Exact size consistency is thus one step toward such potentials.

items.title: Self-similar structure of non-isothermal variable-density mushy Stefan problems and an improved low-Mach enthalpy method
items.summary: The enthalpy method was introduced in the late 1970s to simulate phase-change problems on fixed grids without explicitly tracking the moving phase-change front. It remains one of the most widely used approaches in academic and commercial software for the simulation of industrial melting and solidification processes. For pure phase-change materials (PCMs) that melt or solidify at a single temperature, the enthalpy method introduces an artificial mushy region bounded by the solidus temperature, $T^{\rm sol}$, and the liquidus temperature, $T^{\rm liq}$. As the numerical parameter $ΔT=T^{\rm liq}- T^{\rm sol}$ approaches zero, the solution obtained with the enthalpy method is generally assumed to converge to that of the classical Stefan problem, in which the phase-change front is infinitesimally thin. This assumption is largely based on benchmark studies performed under the simplifying assumption of equal solid and liquid densities. In this work, we systematically investigate the accuracy and spatio-temporal convergence properties of the enthalpy method for both low- and high-density-ratio phase-change problems. Because the limiting behavior $ΔT\rightarrow0$ is difficult to realize numerically, owing to the diminishing thickness of the mushy region, we formulate and analyze the finite-$ΔT$ mushy Stefan problem solved by the enthalpy method. We show that this problem possesses a self-similar structure that reduces the governing equations to a boundary-value problem involving two unknown parameters. The theoretical analysis also enables improvements to our previously developed low-Mach enthalpy method, enhancing its stability and accuracy as the density ratio between the two phases increases from $\mathcal{O}(1)$ to $\mathcal{O}(3)$.

items.title: Dysfunctional Functionals and their Therapies in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory
items.summary: The exchange-correlation functional in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory (TDDFT) is known to have dependence on past densities and initial states, and yet this memory-dependence is ignored in practical calculations which almost always use an adiabatic approximation. We discuss the dysfunction that arises due to this deficiency and point to therapies that go beyond the adiabatic approximation. Still, adiabatic TDDFT has had success in a wide range of systems for response properties and for fully non-equilibrium dynamics, and why this is so is only partially understood. This, together with the rigorous foundation of the exact theory and its favorable system-size scaling, provides tremendous impetus for continuing to strive towards improved approximations to the exact functionals, and a deeper understanding of the impact of approximations in applications.

items.title: g4chargeit: Geant4-based kinetic Monte Carlo simulations of charging in dielectric materials
items.summary: We present g4chargeit, a kinetic Monte Carlo framework built on Geant4 for self-consistent simulation of time-dependent electrostatic charging in dielectric materials. The model explicitly incorporates stochastic particle transport and scattering processes using validated Geant4 cross-sections, while self-consistently evolving the electric potential and field. As a representative application, we simulate the charging of regolith grains under average dayside conditions on the Moon. The surface of the Moon, in addition to other airless planetary bodies, are regularly exposed to solar ultraviolet photons and solar-wind plasma, creating a radiation environment in which electrostatic interactions among regolith grains become significant. Until now, simulations of regolith charging have often relied on analytical approximations that oversimplify grain geometry and interaction mechanisms. Our Geant4-based simulations reveal charge accumulation within intergrain micro-cavities, leading to repulsive electrostatic forces consistent with experimental observations. The framework establishes a multiscale approach that links microscopic scattering events to the continuity equation of surface charge density and to the formation of macroscopic surface charge patches in complex grain geometries. Although demonstrated here for planetary regolith, the method is general and applicable to a broad range of dielectric charging problems. The code is openly available at https://github.com/kgandhi63/g4chargeit.git.

items.title: Fast Organic Crystal Structure Prediction with Unit Cell Flow Matching
items.summary: Organic crystal structure prediction (CSP) is a requirement for computational modelling of organic solids, but traditionally costs several CPU-years per molecule. Generative models such as OXtal dramatically reduce this cost by sampling stable organic crystal structures directly. However, OXtal forgoes explicit lattice parametrization in favour of modelling large crops of the bulk material with expensive triangle layers, which can incur a computational cost of minutes per molecule. In this paper, we reduce this to seconds with Clari, a large-scale flow matching model that generates redundancy-free unit cells and replaces triangle layers with pair-bias attention. Clari requires only atom types and bonds as input and does not need an RDKit-sanitizable input molecule, which expands its applicability to challenging chemistries such as fullerenes, metal complexes, and atom clusters. We further ablate key design choices such as auxiliary losses, timestep distributions, noise priors, and self-conditioning. On OXtal's test sets, we surpass OXtal's solve rate while obtaining a speedup of 15-30$\times$. Because Clari also models explicit hydrogens, it supports inference-time scaling via direct energy ranking, without any decoration or relaxation step. When generating 150 crystals and selecting the top-30 by energy, we further improve solve rate while maintaining a speedup of 5-8$\times$. We also introduce the CSD Teaching Subset as a new test split of diverse and complex molecules for future benchmarking. Our contributions enable CSP within seconds, making large-scale virtual screening of organic solids practical. Code is available at https://github.com/the-matter-lab/clari.

items.title: A versatile beamline for attosecond photoelectron and photon spectroscopy
items.summary: We report on the development of a versatile attosecond beamline for ultrafast spectroscopy of atoms and molecules, as well as for the metrology of infrared laser pulses. Using a few-cycle pulse (approximately 5 fs) for driving the high-order harmonic generation process, we show that the modulation of the harmonic flux in the cut-off spectral region, induced by a weak perturbing field, enables complete electric-field characterization of the perturbing pulse. Phase-sensitive detection with a lock-in amplifier further reveals polarization-dependent effects, observed as modulations at twice the fundamental optical frequency, emphasizing the sub-laser-cycle electronic control inherent to the measurement technique. In addition, the beamline supports the implementation of two-color (extreme ultraviolet and infrared) phase-sensitive experiments using approximately 30 fs pulses and a velocity map imaging spectrometer (VMI). This configuration will enable the study of photoemission time delays in atomic and molecular systems. Together, these results establish the beamline as a robust and adaptable platform for probing attosecond dynamics across diverse experimental approaches.

items.title: Linear Generator Networks for Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations
items.summary: Most physical systems are governed by nonlinear partial differential equations, yet the analytical tools that make linear systems transparent, such as eigenspectra, dispersion relations and modal decomposition, remain unavailable in nonlinear settings. We introduce Linear Generator Network-Koopman (LGN-KM), a neural operator that learns a nonlinear lift and a continuous-time linear generator for the lifted dynamics through the decomposition $L_k = S - D_k$, where $S$ is skew-symmetric (conservative coupling) and $D_k$ is positive-definite diagonal (mode-selective dissipation). The decomposition guarantees stability by construction and exposes the eigenstructure directly, making linear-systems analysis available on a nonlinear PDE. On 2D Navier-Stokes turbulence, the generator yields a complete multi-branch dispersion relation and models trained independently at viscosities $100\times$ apart learn the same coupling spectrum ($R^2 = 0.87$). The same architecture shows the corresponding diffusive damping on FitzHugh-Nagumo reaction-diffusion, and for pulse propagation in optical fibers, the oscillation frequencies of the learned generator match the fiber's dispersion relation, giving the group-velocity dispersion to within $3.1\%$ with no fitted constant. The architecture additionally enables long-horizon stability, $O(1)$ continuous-time evaluation, and physics-informed cross-regime model transfer.

items.title: Molecular Photoionization Spectra from Signed Dyson Orbitals and Anharmonic Nuclear Motion
items.summary: Molecular photoelectron bands couple changes in nuclear structure to the energy-dependent scattering of the departing electron. Band intensities require both nuclear transition moments and electronic continuum amplitudes. We present SPARKS (Scattering and Photoionization: Amplitudes, Response Kernels and Spectra), a molecular photoionization approach that connects signed Dyson orbitals to complex molecular dipole amplitudes and harmonic or anharmonic nuclear transition moments. Compact B-spline and finite-element discrete-variable representations support spectral and sparse outgoing-boundary solvers. Independent molecular checks reproduce a reference H$_2^+$ spectrum and CO continuum amplitudes, while analytic hydrogen photoionization tests establish the continuum normalization. For H$_2$O/H$_2$O$^+$, electronic derivatives activate a Franck--Condon-dark fundamental and enter the same nuclear operator used in harmonic, perturbative and internal-coordinate variational calculations. Furan extends the nuclear treatment to all 21 vibrational coordinates in a selected configuration-interaction window, including low-lying out-of-plane states. Four epichlorohydrin ionization channels show how orbital mixing reshapes cross sections and angular distributions at similar Dyson norms. Energy conservation is imposed separately for every vibronic transition at fixed photon energy. The resulting spectra retain vibrational assignments and electronic interference, connecting weak-band activation, anharmonic spacings and photoelectron angular distributions within one physical description.

items.title: Lifting mechanical zero modes without dispersion
items.summary: Floppy frameworks carry flat bands of zero-frequency mechanisms with no finite-frequency resonance, and couplings that lift them usually spread them. We show that an on-site tensor lifts a mechanism band without first-order dispersion exactly when, projected onto the mechanisms, it acts as wavevector-independent scalars on orthogonal pieces. Three structures achieve this: local normal modes, invariant symmetry sectors, and a balance law. A mechanism moves both ends of every bond between two vertex classes equally along it, and where the inter-class bond tensors are class scalars this balance law fixes its norm shares and hence the flat value from geometry alone. For the fluorite net the band lies outside the tensor spectrum, at 14/9 of the contact stiffness to first order, and stays flat to all orders in a fixed cage. A placement inside a tiling dual that keeps the common symmetry supplies such tensors, because each contact star inherits its site symmetry. Ten catalogued dual pairs lift flat; half are eigenvalue cases a resolved count matches, and the balance law explains flat bands in random cages too. Duality makes the rigid cage common. In a printable beam-frame lattice, contacts that lock joint rotation remove first-order bending dispersion whenever bonded mechanisms are orthogonal local normals.

items.title: On deep squeezing or cooling a parametric resonator using feedback
items.summary: Here we analyze ways to achieve deep subthreshold squeezing or cooling of fluctuations in a parametric resonator enhanced by a lock-in amplifier feedback loop. The main advance and novelty of this paper is that we analyzed the full impact of this feedback on the response of the parametric resonator to an ac drive or to additive noise. Due to this feedback, the dynamics of the parametric resonator becomes more complex and, in addition to a saddle-node bifurcation (SNB), a Hopf bifurcation (HB) at the instability threshold can also occur. We calculate the phase-dependent amplification gain in the response of the resonator to an added ac signal with three independent techniques: approximately using the averaging method (AM) or the harmonic balance method (HBM), and more precisely using Floquet theory (FT) and Green's functions. The HB was predicted by the AM, FT, and a modified version of the HBM that takes into account quasi-periodicity. In our analysis of fluctuations, we were able to calculate the noise spectral density and the squeezing or cooling of fluctuations using Fourier techniques and FT. Deamplification and cooling occur near the HB, whereas deep squeezing and heating occur near a SNB. Furthermore, we show that there is an optimal amount of parametric pumping and feedback to reach the strongest cooling. The theoretical framework presented here is general and could be applied to a wide range of physical implementations.

items.title: A Heuristic Mirror-Bulk Model of Schwarzschild Black Hole Interiors
items.summary: Schwarzschild -- non-rotating and chargeless -- black holes (BHs) are classically understood to be voids of extreme gravitation, with modern and contemporary apporaches having involved string-theoretical black branes and superfluid analogs. In this study, we reconsider Schwarzschild BHs by letting its black brane be a closed spherical surface, within which a mirror-bulk fluid is contained, mirrored by surface-dwelling Hawking radiation quanta. By employing a once-used variational method of solving the Einstein field equations, the eneregtic output is approximated by the metric Ansatz input. Here, we consider a Tangherlini-like black 2-brane metric Ansatz in 3+1 spacetime, and via $G_{μν}=8πGT_{μν}$ the geometric information of the time-time component $G_{00}$ determines the corresponding (effective) energy density $T_{00}$ and the respective energy profile $E:=T_{00}V$. These are found to be functions of the radial coordinate, which also applies to the BH interior $r\in[0,~r_S]$. We explore and discuss the mirror-bulk energy content, internal pressure, and the mass- and pressure-gradients of a mirror-bulk BH.

items.title: Guiding future global temperature distributions with simulations and observations
items.summary: Assessing climate risks requires projections of daily temperature distributions, including rare and spatially widespread extremes. Climate simulations are costly and biased, while correcting them toward observations risks suppressing inter-model differences. We train a single machine-learning emulator, a conditional diffusion model, on seventeen CMIP6 models and ERA5 reanalysis to generate spatially coherent daily temperature fields conditioned on model identity, date, and CO2-equivalent concentration. At sampling time, diffusion guidance reduces model biases by steering each emulated climate-model distribution toward observations, with its strength selected through perfect-model experiments using withheld simulated futures. Observational influence decreases with projection horizon and forcing. Across seventeen synthetic targets, guidance more than halves median biases in the 1st and 99th percentiles of daily temperature, improves probabilistic scores and reliability, and reduces median annual global-mean temperature RMSE by 32-57% across three emission scenarios. In a detailed benchmark, guidance also outperforms established bias corrections on daily-field probabilistic scores. Efficient sampling generates large ensembles without further climate simulations. For example, our framework corrects CMIP6's roughly threefold historical overestimate of extreme-heat coverage, yet projects that concurrent extremes will affect nearly half of global land on a typical day in the 2080s under SSP3-7.0.

items.title: Online Imitation Learning for Stabilizing Vlasov--Poisson Plasmas
items.summary: We study the problem of controlling instability in the Vlasov--Poisson plasma systems, a fundamental challenge for nuclear fusion control. Motivated by the partial observability of plasma states in practice, we investigate imitation learning algorithms that learn from a fully-observable expert controller, but operate under macroscopic measurements. We theoretically establish a separation between online and offline imitation learning --- even a small behavior cloning error leads to error compounding that exponentially amplifies instability over time. By way of contrast, the online imitation learning loss can polynomially control the stability of rollout trajectories. We then propose a DAgger-style algorithm that learns the stabilizing controller under partial observability. Simulation results on a 1D Vlasov--Poisson system demonstrate that our algorithm can effectively stabilize plasma instabilities over longer time horizons than behavior cloning.

items.title: Low-Rank Tensor Manifolds for Turbulent Field Reconstruction from Sparse Data
items.summary: Reconstructing turbulent flow fields from sparse and irregular measurements remains challenging because the underlying inverse problem is severely underdetermined. Here we present MANTRA, a manifold-based tensor framework that represents each velocity component in a continuous tensor-product space while constraining its coefficient tensor to a low-rank Tucker manifold. This structure provides a compact, data-adaptive representation without requiring gridded observations or governing equations. Riemannian optimization and adaptive selection of rank and basis complexity enable the model to exploit coordinate-wise spatiotemporal correlations. In simulations of forced isotropic turbulence and flow over a cylinder, MANTRA recovers multiscale structures at sampling densities orders of magnitude below the underlying grids and remains accurate under Gaussian noise up to 20% of the peak velocity. It also recovers leading coordinate-wise correlation structures from sparse observations. Applied to experimental particle-tracking velocimetry of an oscillating impinging jet, MANTRA reveals time-evolving structures that are not apparent from the scattered measurements alone.

items.title: Fluctuations in Aharonov-Bohm Electrodynamics
items.summary: We consider the application of the Fluctuation Dissipation Theorem (FDT) to the electrodynamics of Aharonov-Bohm (ABE), which differs from Maxwell's in that it allows for local non-conservation of charge. For the case of a system of non-conserved charges at thermal equilibrium we obtain the same spectral distribution of energy of the electromagnetic field as in Maxwell electrodynamics. However, the electric field contribution to that energy doubles that in Maxwell case, while the magnetic contribution is the same as in Maxwell theory, the electric excess energy is compensated by a negative contribution arising form the Aharonov-Bohm (AB) scalar field. For a conductor with local non-conservation of charge described by the $γ$ model, we derive the spectrum of current correlation at first order in $γ$, which results in a violet noise contribution added to the classical Johnson-Nyquist white noise result for the voltage fluctuations in a conductor.

items.title: SWXAI: A Unified Multimodal Explainability Library for Space Weather Forecasting and Heliophysics
items.summary: Space weather forecasting and heliophysics increasingly rely on machine learning models that process heterogeneous inputs such as multi-viewpoint multi-wavelength solar images and rasters, multivariate time series, spatial annotations, and tabular event-level data. However, explainability workflows remain fragmented across libraries, model interfaces, and output formats, limiting reuse and reproducibility. We present SWXAI, an open-source library that unifies explainable AI (XAI) workflows for image, time-series, and tabular data in space weather forecasting and heliophysics. SWXAI provides a common, extensible interface across commonly used vision, time-series, and tabular learning models, with validation, adaptation, and persistent explanation objects. It also includes domain-grounded examples, reproducible notebooks, tests, and documentation, enabling users to inspect outputs, swap models or explainers, and extend workflows to new heliophysics datasets. SWXAI reduces modality-specific engineering overhead and supports comparable, reusable explanations across heterogeneous scientific machine learning pipelines. A benchmark against direct backend implementations shows that SWXAI substantially reduces the code users write to produce an explanation, with no practical runtime cost.

items.title: How the elastic axis folds the transonic flutter boundary: shock energy transfer and conformally calibrated active learning
items.summary: Isogai's case A, a pitch-plunge aerofoil whose elastic axis lies half a chord ahead of the leading edge, has a folded transonic flutter boundary in inviscid flow, with several flutter speeds at one Mach number. We map this boundary and its elastic-axis family with coupled Euler simulations, a Gaussian-process surrogate of the damping trained by batch active learning, and distribution-free split conformal prediction, which bounds the marginal error rate of stability calls. Three failure modes of damping labels are invisible in the residuals, and the half-degree mean incidence left by an impulsive start at $1^\circ$ freestream incidence raises the flutter speed at the dip by 2.8%, more than any numerical setting. With 80 simulations the learned case A boundary labels 63 of 64 independent runs correctly, and at most 1.8% of calibrated calls on held-out runs are wrong. Over Mach number, elastic axis and flutter speed index, 193 simulations show that, for the case A structure about the axis, the inviscid fold exists only for axes more than about 0.4 chord ahead of the leading edge, on two meshes. Chordwise energy budgets, closed three ways, explain both branches. On the lower branch the falling reduced frequency, at unchanged shock phase, raises the shock input and lowers the upstream damping similarly. On the upper branch the shock is pinned at the trailing edge; moving the axis aft brings the flutter-mode pivot towards the section, so the upstream damping falls faster than the residual shock input and the fold closes.

items.title: Joos-Weinberg covariant field with mass and spin $\frac{3}{2}$
items.summary: We present the explicit theory of the Joos-Weinberg covariant field with spin $\frac{3}{2}$ which is a eight-dimensional massive covariant field transforming according to the representation $(\frac{3}{2},0)\oplus(0, \frac{3}{2})$ of the group $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$. As the transformation matrices of this representation are still unknown, we apply a new method for deriving them using exclusively maximally reducible representations, e. g. $(1,0)\otimes(\frac{1}{2},0)$ instead of the irreducible one $(1,\frac{1}{2})=(1,0)\otimes(0,\frac{1}{2})$ we meet in usual frameworks. After applying this method, we obtain a $12$-component covariant field transforming according to the representation $[(1,0)\otimes(\frac{1}{2},0)]\oplus [(0,1)\otimes(0, \frac{1}{2})]$ which is maximally reducible, up to subspaces of irreducible representations of the $SU(2)$ group. Consequently, after developing the theory in the direct product basis of the representation $(1,0)\otimes(\frac{1}{2},0)$, we can separate the sector of spin half revealing thus the genuine Joos-Weinberg covariant massive field of spin $\frac{3}{2}$. The theory of this field is build naturally deriving the field equation and associated matrices, Lagrangian formalism, inner product and the closed expressions of the orthonormal mode spinors.

items.title: Natural Lithopanspermia to Earth: Transport, Shielding, and Survival Limits for Solar-System and Extrasolar Donor Classes
items.summary: Natural panspermia is a transport-and-establishment hypothesis, not a theory of abiogenesis. The Earth-specific question is whether any nonterrestrial donor remains competitive with terrestrial origin once launch, planetary-system escape, transit, Earth interception, atmospheric entry, terminal loading, and post-delivery establishment are imposed. We formulate this problem as a donor-class dependent Earth-directed transport-survival kernel, supplemented by a minimum protected-depth envelope d_{min}(t_{flight}) and a survival-weighted buried-volume fraction F_{bur} for the low-shock spall population. The resulting hierarchy is strongly ordered under current transport and survival constraints. Hard panspermia is physically credible only on Solar-System scales: early Mars combines demonstrated lithic exchange with Earth, low escape speed, early aqueous habitability, and a rare 10^2-10^4 yr transfer tail, whereas the more common 10^5-10^7 yr martian transfer regime requires lightly shocked meter-class carriers. Beyond the Solar System, low-v_{inf} capture and long-duration survival fail simultaneously; even the Solar birth-cluster channel yields only ~3 x 10^{-5} f_{seed} expected Earth-seeding events, where f_{seed} is the conditional probability that a viable arrival establishes life on Earth. Indigenous terrestrial origin therefore remains the default inference, early Mars is the only quantitatively serious external hard-panspermia alternative, and extrasolar or intergalactic hard panspermia is not competitive for Earth's actual origin history. Soft panspermia is much more plausible as chemical enrichment of early terrestrial abiogenesis.

items.title: Navier-Stokes characteristic boundary conditions for the Spectral Difference method on simplex elements
items.summary: Unsteady compressible simulations with high-order methods on unstructured meshes require boundaries that let acoustic, entropy and vorticity waves leave the domain without spurious reflection. For the spectral difference (SD) method, the Navier-Stokes characteristic boundary conditions (NSCBC) have only been formulated on quadrilaterals and hexahedra. Their strong-form formalism relies on a line of flux points normal to the boundary face, which does not exist on triangles and tetrahedra. This paper extends the NSCBC to the SD method on simplex elements, including multi-species reacting gases. The characteristic analysis is performed in the physical frame of each flux point of the boundary face, and the normal derivative of the normal flux is evaluated using the Raviart-Thomas divergence operator. The boundary fluxes are recovered from a linear system local to each boundary element, whose matrix depends on the geometry only. The treatment is compared with the tensor-product formulation at a comparable number of degrees of freedom on a series of test cases covering acoustic, vortical, viscous and reacting flows on triangles and tetrahedra. In all cases, the results are in close agreement with those obtained on quadrilaterals and hexahedra, so that the NSCBC become available for the SD method on simplex meshes, which are well suited to complex geometries.

items.title: Status of Accelerator Automation in the Community: Classification, Survey Results, and the Role of AI and Machine Learning
items.summary: The increasing complexity of particle accelerators and the growing demand for operational efficiency have intensified the focus on automation in accelerator control systems. However, there is still a lack of a common language to describe and compare the level of automation across different facilities. This article presents a generic classification scheme for accelerator automation, defining five distinct levels ranging from basic operational assistance to full autonomy. To assess the current state of automation in the accelerator community, a structured survey was conducted during the 14th Workshop on Accelerator Operations (WAO 2025). Responses from major laboratories indicate that more than one third of accelerators currently operate at the lowest level 1 (operational assistance), and no facility has yet reached full automation. However, projections show a clear trend toward higher levels within the next decade. Key drivers include optimization algorithms for autotuning, finite-state machines, and closed-loop feedback systems. This study provides both a conceptual framework and a snapshot of current implementation practices, supporting a shared understanding of accelerator automation across the community.

items.title: Distributed Acoustic Fiber Sensing for Research Campuses and Large Scientific Infrastructures -- The Hamburg WAVE proto-network
items.summary: Here, we demonstrate and investigate how Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) can be utilized on research campuses and in large scientific infrastructures to study environmental vibrations and reduce their impact on high-precision experiments. We first discuss the potential of DAS in the context of particle accelerators, gravitational wave detection experiments and research campuses. Next, we present the results of our seismic measurement campaign conducted with our proto-network, which involved the probing of over 12 km of fiber, in May 2021. This campaign was conducted by the Hamburg WAVE initiative in Science City Hamburg Bahrenfeld and included DESY, the European XFEL, PETRA III and the University of Hamburg. Our proto-network confirms the ability to observe natural, anthropogenic, and infrastructural vibrations and how and where these couple into different parts of the heterogeneously set up fiber network. We also present results on a study of noise and motion coupling aspects of DAS probing double-redundant fiber loops in a unique environment, the European XFEL. Our results show that DAS can greatly benefit research campuses and large scientific infrastructures and they highlight the opportunities and challenges of implementing and operating such seismic networks.

items.title: From populations to absolute binding affinities in molecular simulations: exact volumetric terms and practical estimators
items.summary: Biomolecular simulations of binding commonly confine the unbound ligand with volumetric restraints to accelerate convergence. However, a general account of how such restraints enter the volumetric term of the standard binding free energy, and of how this term should be evaluated from histogram data, is currently lacking. We take as our starting point the established relation, in the dilute limit, between the binding constant $K$ and the relative populations of the bound and unbound states, which we re-derive from the canonical partition function of molecular solutes in explicit solvent. Building on this relation, we show that a restraint that leaves the bound state unaffected and confines a homogeneous unbound region modifies the volumetric term in a single way, by replacing the system volume with the volume of the region over which the unbound population is evaluated. This yields closed-form estimators for restrained simulations, computable from histograms of any suitably defined reaction coordinate, with the volumetric term kept explicit. Previous expressions based on the potential of mean force are recovered as a special case. The analysis also exposes two distinct errors in current practice: single-bin estimators, which reduce the bound state to one histogram bin and are not valid estimators of $K$, and working formulas that omit the bin width entering the volumetric term, which make the result depend on the unit of length. We apply the estimators to a Lennard-Jones dimer, the cucurbit[7]uril/1-adamantanol host--guest complex, and the galactonate--DgoT ligand--protein complex.

items.title: Spectroscopic method for determining the onset of clustering in supersonic gas jets
items.summary: This article presents an original spectroscopic method for determining the parameters of the initial stage of clustering in supersonic jets. The method was tested on supersonic jets of argon and nitrogen, excited by electrons at a distance of 30 millimetres from the nozzle exit, where the influence of secondary processes on the intensity of the observed radiation is significantly suppressed. For argon, the continuum emission from neutral excited clusters was used as an indicator of cluster formation in the supersonic argon jet. In the case of nitrogen, for which no emissions attributable exclusively to clusters have been recorded, a study was carried out on the effect of clustering on the redistribution of the intensities of atomic lines and molecular bands in the Lyman Birge Hopfield system.

items.title: Exact analytic anisotropic three-dimensional equilibria with nested magnetic surfaces, confined drift orbits and without spatial symmetry
items.summary: Exact toroidal fluid and kinetic equilibria with nested magnetic surfaces and no continuous symmetry are of great interest in laboratory, astrophysical and space plasmas. Their existence and stability have been open in physics and mathematics for decades. We construct such anisotropic-pressure equilibria by applying the Clemente transformation to exact vacuum fields. They connect smoothly to these fields on a fixed regular domain and preserve a regular magnetic axis, perfectly nested surfaces and spatially varying rotational transform. To our knowledge, the sheared configurations are the first exact anisotropic equilibria combining these properties with positive pressures and a positive firehose margin. The fixed-boundary Chew--Goldberger--Low (CGL) quadratic energy splits into a nonnegative vacuum-field term and a local pressure term, nonnegative for p_perp/p_parallel <= (3+\sqrt{21})/2 ~ 3.79. For p_parallel >= p_perp each configuration minimizes the finite-amplitude CGL energy over smooth boundary-fixed ideal material deformations. For the current-free configurations, physical guiding-center distributions produce these pressures within the same bound, with no free energy for magnetic-moment-conserving electrostatic perturbations. Trapped particles inherit the vacuum field's second adiabatic invariant at a rescaled magnetic moment, so local closed action contours carry over. The equilibrium code DESC reproduces them from the exact solution. Kinetic stability for surface-dependent rescalings and against general nonlinear electromagnetic perturbations remains open.

items.title: A new approach to measuring both the steady flow curve and the planar extensional viscosity of complex fluids using exponential shear
items.summary: We revisit the protocol known as Exponential Shear (ES), first proposed by Doshi and Dealy in 1986. This is a transient strong flow that can be readily imposed in the laboratory using commercial strain-controlled (separate motor and transducer) rheometers which accurately measure both the (exponentially) time-varying torque and normal force exerted by the sample. Numerous studies over the years have proposed competing definitions of an appropriate material function for reporting data obtained from the exponentially time-varying imposed deformation. We revisit this unresolved challenge and carefully reconsider the exponential material kinematics involved and the proper definition of the corresponding material functions. We show that by understanding the time-varying eigenvalues and eigenvectors of both the shearing kinematics and the evolving state of stress in the sample it is, in fact, possible to use an exponential shear test to quantitatively map out \textit{both} the full flow curve (of shear viscosity vs. shear rate) and the steady planar extensional viscosity curve as a function of deformation rate. These findings are supported by numerical simulations of a number of nonlinear viscoelastic constitutive models, asymptotic analysis, as well as experiments with several polymeric liquids.

items.title: Universal Approximation by Equivariant Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks with a Bilinear Readout
items.summary: We prove universal approximation for the bilinear-readout equivariant message-passing network (BREMP), a reference architecture for equivariant graph neural network interatomic potentials. Its layers combine equivariant convolutions with affine maps, and its readout forms invariants from products of the equivariant features. We construct a one-layer feature that determines the local environment up to permutations of atoms of the same type. The construction uses spherical harmonic filters of degree no larger than the largest number of neighbors at a common distance from the center. Iterating the construction recovers the environment reachable in as many hops as there are layers, using the same bound on filter degrees at the layer cutoff. The readout approximates every continuous invariant function of the features uniformly on compact sets. Together these give universal approximation of atomic energies at a prescribed physical range using a shorter layer cutoff. We assume that, throughout the admissible class, message passing reaches all neighbors in each physical environment within a common number of layers. Finally, DPA4, an interatomic potential architecture in production use, inherits this result by approximating the BREMP layers constructed in the proof and realizing the bilinear readout.

items.title: Simultaneous 3D acoustic modulation and imaging of proton-induced nanodroplet vaporization for proton therapy monitoring
items.summary: Superheated nanodroplets exposed to ionizing radiation vaporize into echogenic microbubbles, enabling ultrasound-based radiation therapy monitoring and proton range verification. However, at body temperature, decafluorobutane nanodroplets are insensitive to primary protons, and vaporize only when traversed by rare heavy secondary particles, limiting the in vivo applicability of this concept. We previously demonstrated that acoustic modulation at pressures well below the Acoustic Droplet Vaporization threshold can transiently increase nanodroplet sensitivity to radiation, enabling vaporization by primary protons. However, as acoustic modulation was applied by a focused single-element transducer, sensitization was restricted to a small region of the irradiated volume, and monitoring required an additional imaging probe. Here, we introduce a compact implementation that combines wide-field acoustic modulation and volumetric imaging on the same large-element matrix array, enabling simultaneous nanodroplet sensitization to protons and vaporization monitoring across the entire irradiated volume. The resulting 3D vaporization maps were fitted to the proton stopping distribution to estimate beam position and width parameters. At body temperature and starting from acoustic pressures as low as 122 kPa, we observed a transition from a response dominated by secondary particles to a response dominated by primary protons. The resulting vaporization peak at the proton range enabled sub-millimeter range estimation and detection of a 1.05 mm range shift with both accuracy and precision below 0.2 mm. These results demonstrate proton range verification and 3D treatment monitoring with acoustically-modulated decafluorobutane nanodroplets and represent an important step towards the envisioned clinical application.

items.title: Detuning-Controlled Vibrational Autler--Townes Passage toward Single-Sublevel Orientation of Nonpolar Molecules
items.summary: Single-sublevel preparation would give collision and surface-scattering experiments access to oriented molecules, yet established orientation methods either require a permanent dipole moment or select only partially. We introduce all-optical Autler--Townes state-selective adiabatic passage (ASAP), in which a detuned infrared field dresses a rovibrational transition, and the selected dressed branch is mapped adiabatically onto one magnetic sublevel as the field vanishes. We resolve the magnetic-sublevel-selected rovibrational Autler--Townes doublet of the R(0) transition of $^{13}$CO$_2$ and show that the coupling strength and detuning set both its separation and the partition of the bare-state composition between its two components. The spectral selectivity of the target dressed branch reaches 97\% at a coupling detuning of $-1.2$~MHz. A density-matrix model calibrated against these spectra returns, for the dressed molecules, a target-sublevel population approaching 0.9 over a broad range of coupling powers and detunings.

items.title: 2D polaritons for Squeezing and Shrinking Light
items.summary: Two-dimensional (2D) materials have emerged as an extraordinary platform for polaritonics, given their remarkable ability to confine light to deep sub-wavelength scales. However, as material thicknesses reach the nanometer limit, macroscopic electrodynamic models become inadequate for the description of light-matter coupling in 2D materials, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of 2D polaritons. In this work, we develop a comprehensive quantum microscopic framework that describes 2D polaritons through a general, scale-less Hamiltonian. Starting from the quantum properties of a polarizable 2D surface, we derive collective excitations and we identify both transverse electric magnetic modes existing outside the light cone. Our results demonstrate that these 2D systems facilitate a powerful synergy between extreme wavelength shrinking and intrinsic quantum squeezing of electric field quadratures. By establishing this theoretical roadmap, our work provides the essential architecture for controlling non-classical states of light at the nanoscale, opening new avenues for high-precision quantum sensing and the development of next-generation optoelectronic devices

items.title: Effect of Turbulence and Inhomogeneities on the Propagation of Kinetic Scale Waves
items.summary: Context. Electromagnetic ion-scale waves are well known to occur in the solar wind. Eikonal (WKB) like effects may play an important role in the interplay between the propagation and local kinetic plasma dynamics of ion cyclotron waves. Aims. This Letter aims to explore the interplay of ICW propagation with turbulence and local kinetic plasmas using ray tracing equations for ICWs in a moving medium, in which turbulent gradients are present. Methods. Parker Solar Probe observations of ICWs in the solar wind are studied using ray equations in a moving medium. Gradients in the dispersion relation responsible for WKB evolution of ICW are constrained and compared with a Parker spiral model. Results. The empirical gradients, which contain turbulent motions, greatly enhance the efficiency of WKB effects. However, the typical refraction rates are significantly slower than expected quasilinear evolution of the observed wave populations, which suggests that local kinetic physics dominates over nonlinear expansion effects. Conclusions. Turbulence can effectively increase WKB effects due to gradients caused by nonlinear interactions. In the solar wind these gradients are not sufficient to substantially change an individual ion-scale ICW over its lifetime. Incorporating kinetic effects of expansion may help advance the understanding of generation and absorption of ICW and their role in heating in the solar wind.

items.title: Stochastic Acceleration Downstream of Astrophysical Shocks
items.summary: Generation and evolution of turbulence at shock fronts are crucial aspects of the process of particle acceleration in different classes of sources. Here we aim at describing the fate of non-thermal particles and turbulence in the downstream region of an astrophysical shock, both in the case in which turbulence is solely produced upstream and advected through the shock and in the case in which additional turbulence is injected downstream. In particular we will provide an estimate of the effect of stochastic acceleration on particles accelerated at the shock and then advected behind it. The calculations will be specialized to supernova remnant shocks. The temporal evolution of the particle distribution function downstream of the shock and the power spectrum of the turbulent perturbations are both followed by solving numerically the transport equations for the two quantities, accounting for the damping of waves due to the particles that resonantly interact with them, which makes the problem non-linear. Our calculations show that, if waves are only self-generated upstream via Bell instability, they are not able to significantly modify the particle spectrum in the downstream region. Additionally, turbulent cascading in $k$-space quickly drains their energy, further limiting the stochastic acceleration of particles. If, on the other hand, there are additional sources of turbulence downstream, then these waves can contribute meaningfully to second order Fermi acceleration and alter the spectrum of particles. This may reflect in the spectrum of gamma radiation produced through $pp$ scattering downstream. Although second order Fermi acceleration is typically slower than diffusive shock acceleration, particles are expected to stay downstream of shocks for much longer times during which stochastic acceleration can modify their spectrum and affect the spectra of multi-messenger emissions.

items.title: Improving the convergence of coupled quasinormal-mode theory for optical resonators
items.summary: Quasinormal modes (QNMs) provide a rigorous framework for describing resonances in open optical systems, including radiative and material losses. Recent coupled-QNM theories use the modes of individual resonators to predict the resonances and optical responses of coupled systems, without relying on phenomenological coupling parameters. However, their accuracy can deteriorate when the resonators confine light weakly and radiate strongly, often requiring many modes to obtain reliable predictions. Here, we introduce a reformulation of coupled-QNM theory that substantially improves its accuracy when only a small number of modes of the individual resonators are retained. The approach builds on the same underlying QNM framework but treats the fields mediating the interaction between resonators differently, leading to a new expression for the coupling coefficients. Numerical comparisons show that this extended-domain formulation is particularly advantageous for resonators with strong ra-diative losses, enabling more efficient modeling of a broader range of coupled photonic sys-tems.

items.title: Bifurcation-based phononic frequency combs in a forced van der Pol-Duffing oscillator
items.summary: Here, we analyze the dynamics of a forced Van der Pol-Duffing oscillator in search of phononic frequency comb (PFC) generation. When the drive amplitude is small, quasi-periodic self-oscillations are dominant, and we obtain a PFC spectrum response of the oscillator. When the drive amplitude is sufficiently large, we obtain frequency locking. We observe that near the transition to frequency locking the PFC spectrum is strongest and has more peaks. With increasing drive amplitude, the peaks coalesce, and the PFC spectrum disappears at an infinite-period saddle-node or homoclinic bifurcation. We also study the stability of the frequency-locked responses and find that a PFC spectrum can also occur near a subcritical Hopf bifurcation. We find that the first-order averaged equations of our nonlinear dynamical system are identical to the equations of motion of the Stuart-Landau oscillator. We use averaging techniques up to second order to characterize the quasi-periodic solutions. Very good agreement with numerical integration results are obtained. We complement our analysis by proposing a phenomenological model of nonlinear dissipative coupling between two modes that accounts for the negative dissipation term in the van der Pol-Duffing equation of motion.

items.title: Origins of suppressed self-diffusion of nanoscale constituents of a complex liquid
items.summary: Understanding and ultimately controlling the transformations and properties of nanoscale systems, from proteins to synthetic nanomaterial assemblies, is limited by the inability to uncover their dynamics on their characteristic length and time scales. Here, we nevertheless demonstrate this ability using MHz X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) -- directly elucidating the characteristic microsecond-dynamics of density fluctuations of semiconductor nanocrystals (NCs), not only in a colloidal dispersion but, more importantly, in a liquid phase consisting of densely packed, yet mobile, NCs with no long-range order. We find the wavevector-dependent fluctuation rates in the liquid phase are suppressed relative to those in the colloidal phase and relative to observations of densely packed repulsive particles. We show that the suppressed rates are due to a substantial decrease in the self-diffusion of NCs, which we attribute to explicit attractive interactions. Using coarse-grained simulations, we find that the extracted shape and strength of the interparticle potential explains the stability of the liquid phase, in contrast to the gelation observed via XPCS in many other charged colloidal systems. This work opens the door to elucidating fast, condensed phase dynamics in complex fluids and other nanoscale soft matter, such as densely packed proteins and non-equilibrium self-assembly processes, in addition to designing microscopic strategies to avert gelation.

items.title: Discovery of the Solution to the "Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen Paradox"
items.summary: In 1935, Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen (EPR) published a thought experiment that is entirely correct, has been demonstrated in real experiments, and is now the most famous in quantum physics. Their pioneering work described, for the first time, quantum correlations and can be regarded as a very early glimpse into today's `deep' quantum technologies, by which I mean those that enhance functionality by making use of quantum correlations. However, their work also produces a paradox that Erwin Schrödinger had already recognised as such in 1935 and which has since been cemented by the so-called Bell experiments. Here, I can now pinpoint the cause of the paradox in the EPR line of reasoning. It boils down to a single assumption by EPR, which I prove to be false. I show that this resolves the paradox.

items.title: Entropy-Driven Initiation and Cytoskeletal Viscoelasticity in Endocytosis: An Onsager Variational Framework
items.summary: Receptor-mediated endocytosis requires a particle to approach the cell membrane to within a few nanometers before ligand--receptor binding can occur. Existing continuum models often start from an already established contact and do not explicitly describe how crowding particles on the extracellular side influence the distribution of the particle near the membrane. We examine entropic depletion forces as one possible nonspecific contribution to this initial approach. For ideal depletants, the Asakura--Oosawa excluded-volume construction gives an exact depletion potential for the planar geometry before contact. The potential and force vanish continuously at the onset of excluded-volume overlap. This interaction provides a possible contribution to membrane proximity before specific binding, while its extension to curved wrapping geometries requires additional approximation. Within a reduced continuum model, we combine depletion attraction, ligand--receptor binding, membrane deformation, and cytoskeletal viscoelastic dissipation. The viscoelastic contact is formulated through a hereditary integral and a standard linear solid. The kinetic model gives a conditional minimum ligand density for complete engulfment, a finite particle-size window, and a stiffness-dependent upper limit. When the stationary radius lies inside the domain of finite positive wrapping times, the estimated wrapping time has a minimum at a radius that decreases with increasing binding energy density. At fixed viscosity and other independent parameters, the same time approximation predicts slower wrapping as cell stiffness increases. The two positive roots defining the size window merge at a limiting parameter value, which characterizes closure of the admissible size interval. Depletion attraction is interpreted as one possible contribution to particle-membrane association, alongside electrostatic interactions

items.title: Dynamics of fluid-fluid displacements in a model rough fracture beyond the quasistatic limit: A spectral approach
items.summary: In fluid-fluid displacements in porous and fractured materials, viscous friction in microscale interfacial (Haines) jumps is intimately linked to macroscale energy dissipation and the associated pressure-saturation (retention) hysteresis. The mode of control (flow rate vs. pressure) and the driving rate (from quasistatic to finite) can substantially affect hysteresis. Despite the significance of hysteresis and dissipation in various technological and natural processes, a quantitative understanding of the link between the micro- and macro-scales, and of the impact of the inherent heterogeneity of porous media, remains elusive. An ``imperfect'' Hele-Shaw cell of variable aperture is a simple model system which allows to study all these in details. However, simulating fluid-fluid interface evolution in heterogeneous media, even in such a simple system, is computationally prohibitive, as multiple length and time scales need to be resolved simultaneously. We develop here a spectral computational approach for interface evolution and energy dissipation and validate it via comparison to computational fluid dynamics simulations and experiments. Computational efficiency is demonstrated by following interface evolution in a cell with a single ``defect'', as well as with random roughness; in both, disparate length scales lead to nontrivial dynamics over many orders of magnitude in time. We also show theoretically that, in the quasi-static limit, while viscous forces during Haines jumps fully account for the energy dissipated between consecutive metastable equilibria, viscosity does not change the total dissipated amount, merely the relaxation time. Our approach provides a stepping stone towards upscaling of fluid-fluid flows in porous media.

items.title: GLOBE: Accurate Surrogates for Boundary-Driven PDEs via Domain-Inspired Architectures and Equivariance
items.summary: We introduce GLOBE, a nonlinear neural surrogate for boundary-driven, homogeneous, weakly nonlinear PDEs that draws inductive bias from boundary-element methods and equivariant ML, representing solutions as superpositions of learnable Green's-function-like kernels evaluated from boundary faces to targets. The architecture is translation-, rotation-, and parity-equivariant; discretization-invariant; and units-invariant via rigorous nondimensionalization. On AirFRANS (steady incompressible RANS over NACA airfoils), a compact ~117k-parameter GLOBE model has lower mean-squared error than published values for the strongest reported ML surrogates on both the interpolation and low-data splits, in single-run comparisons under the released AirFRANS normalization. The model evaluates fields at arbitrary points, handles non-watertight meshes, and generalizes under Reynolds number and angle-of-attack distribution shifts. We further introduce a hierarchical Barnes-Hut acceleration that exploits the kernel's far-field decay to reduce evaluation cost from quadratic to near-linear in the number of boundary elements, with a tunable opening angle that recovers exact dense evaluation in the zero-angle limit. Quantitative validation focuses on 2D AirFRANS; on 3D DrivAerML cars, GLOBE predicts surface and volume fields on the full meshes, and we compare it with a matched Transolver baseline. Together, these results show that boundary-element-inspired inductive biases can substantially improve the accuracy of ML surrogates for boundary-driven PDEs while scaling to large 3D meshes.

items.title: Nonlinear Optical Properties of MXenes for Photonic Applications
items.summary: MXenes - a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition-metal carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides - have emerged as powerful nonlinear photonic materials owing to their metallic conductivity, ultrafast carrier dynamics, broadband optical response, and highly tunable surface chemistry. This Review provides the first comprehensive overview of the nonlinear optical (NLO) properties of MXenes and their growing impact on advanced photonic technologies. We discuss state-of-the-art synthesis strategies, from fluoride-based etching to molten-salt, electrochemical, and CVD-enabled routes, highlighting how structural quality and surface terminations govern optical behaviour. A detailed analysis of third-order nonlinearities including Kerr effects, two- and multi-photon absorption, saturable and reverse-saturable absorption, and harmonic generation is presented, supported by quantitative comparisons across MXene families. We further examine modelling approaches linking band structure to nonlinear response and survey application frontiers such as gas sensing, ultrafast lasers, all-optical limiters, and emerging photonic neural networks. Finally, we outline future research directions spanning material engineering, device integration, and quantum/nonlinear metasurface platforms. Together, these insights position MXenes as a transformative materials platform for next-generation nonlinear photonics and ultrafast all-optical information processing.

items.title: Significant heat transfer enhancement via polymer additives in two-dimensional sheared convection
items.summary: Heat dissipation is critical in modern engineering and polymer additives offer a potential route to improve fluid-based cooling. We study elasticity-enhanced heat transfer in two-dimensional, thermally stratified Poiseuille flow. At Reynolds numbers $Re \lesssim 1000$, we observe two linearly unstable modes: the recently identified elasticity-induced centre mode (Khalid \textit{et al.}, \textit{J. Fluid Mech.}\@\ \textbf{915}, 2021) and the classical buoyancy-driven convective mode (Kelly, \textit{Adv. Appl. Mech.}\@\nobreakspace\textbf{31}, 35--112, 1994). Direct numerical simulations show that the centre mode develops into a nonlinear `arrowhead' state but yields negligible heat transfer enhancement (typically $\approx 0.03\%$ above the conductive state). By contrast, polymers can enhance the heat flux associated with the convective mode by up to $1100\%$. The nonlinear convective-mode states are periodic orbits or travelling waves, dominated by hook-like polymer-stress structures that can attach to channel walls. Both unattached and attached hooks act as `polymer walls', steering flow along rather than across them. Unattached hooks deflect fluid vertically around them in the channel interior and reduce flow rate, whereas wall-attached hooks travel more slowly, reorganising the flow into strong counter-rotating rolls and triggering extreme enhancement. The elasto-buoyant nature of these states is confirmed by perturbation kinetic energy budgets, showing that polymer and buoyancy sustain the states synergistically. Wall-attached hooks enable rapid thermal equilibration but impose a large hydraulic penalty, making them suitable for process streams requiring fast temperature adjustment. Unattached hooks provide a more thermally efficient regime for heat transport. These results highlight the potential of elastic fluids for future heat transfer enhancement technologies.

items.title: Parameterized Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Efficient Simulation of Embedded Microfluidic Chip Cooling
items.summary: Embedded microfluidic cooling is a promising technology for dissipating the intense heat generated by high-performance electronic chips. However, the design and optimization of such coolers impose prohibitive computational costs when using conventional numerical solvers. Here, we present a parameterized physics-informed neural network (PINN) as a deep learning framework for rapidly and accurately predicting the thermohydraulic performance of embedded manifold microchannels. By incorporating four geometric dimensions along with three spatial coordinates as the network inputs, the proposed model enables multiphysics prediction across a continuous design space. Remarkably, our predicted velocity and temperature fields differ from finite-element simulations by relative errors of only 8.1% and 5.6%, respectively, while reducing the computational time and cost by over four orders of magnitude. Key to this framework is a composite strategy combining geometric ansatz embedding, the SOAP optimizer, and a thermal-conductivity-based curriculum learning scheme, which helps overcome the convergence challenges inherent in training PINNs for complex three-dimensional flows. Notably, by leveraging a highly optimized JAX backend, the network achieves convergence on a single consumer-grade GPU in less than four hours. Our approach offers a physics-consistent, real-time surrogate model that can substantially accelerate innovations in advanced microfluidic cooling of future electronics.

items.title: Hyperbolic dynamic friction models for viscoelastic sliding and rolling contact
items.summary: This paper considers the sliding and rolling contact between viscoelastic bodies. Combining linear viscoelastic rheologies for bristle-like elements with nonlinear dynamic friction models, and under the assumption of small deformations and displacement gradients, it derives a class of viscoelasto-kinematic equations, formulated as a system of semilinear partial differential equations (PDEs) governing the evolution of the frictional force, bristle deformations, and internal state variables at the interface between the contacting bodies. The resulting system is analysed mathematically, demonstrating that linear viscoelasticity preserves the hyperbolic character of the PDE systems typically encountered in rolling contact. The proposed theory is illustrated through representative examples of both sliding and rolling contact, highlighting that these two processes, whilst often treated as distinct, may in fact exhibit closely related underlying dynamics. Overall, the framework provides a general theoretical setting applicable to a broad class of viscoelastic frictional systems.

items.title: Precision-informed Fourier compression of refractive index tomograms with voxel-wise error control
items.summary: Significance: Holotomography (HT) generates large refractive index (RI) volumes and time series, creating a need for compact storage with controlled numerical fidelity. Aim: We sought to reduce storage by directly encoding reconstructed three-dimensional RI volumes in Fourier space with voxelwise validation against an assigned error budget. Approach: Quantized Fourier coefficients represent volumetric structure, while spatial residual quantization uses a 1% safety margin without storing separate corrections for individual voxels. We evaluated cellular and organoid data, concurrent processing, and extensions to dielectric-tensor and absorption tomography. Results: At a budget of 0.0001 RI units, complete packets achieved compression ratios of 7.89-9.50 relative to float32 arrays and were 28-30% smaller than BitRound-Pcodec packets satisfying the same error limit. Concurrent processing reduced encoding and decoding wall times by factors of 5.14 and 4.81 without changing packets. The fixed margin passed all primary-budget tests but failed at one smaller budget in both precision-sweep inputs. Conclusions: Precision-informed volumetric Fourier coding reduces storage of holotomograms with verified voxel-wise fidelity at the primary budget, at additional computational cost.

items.title: Vibe-FDTR: An agent-oriented framework for reproducible frequency-domain thermoreflectance data analysis
items.summary: Frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) is a laser pump-probe technique widely used to measure thermal properties at the micro- and nanoscale; however, it relies on a complex data analysis procedure that demands substantial domain expertise and is susceptible to subtle human errors. Here, we present Vibe-FDTR, an agent-oriented framework that enables large language model (LLM) agents to perform reliable and reproducible FDTR analyses directly from natural language requests. This framework couples a configuration-driven FDTR code package, which enforces physical and parametric consistency, with procedural agent skills that translate user intentions into organized and verifiable analysis steps. We evaluate Vibe-FDTR using a controlled benchmark with two levels: synthetic single-step tasks and real-data multi-step tasks based on measurements of gold-coated graphite samples. Across the two levels, agents using Vibe-FDTR achieve success rates of 100% and 98.9%, respectively. In sharp contrast, ablating skills (Code-agent) reduces performance to 91.4% and 36.7%, which drops further to 38.6% and 0% when the domain package is also omitted (Agent-only). Beyond success rate, Vibe-FDTR also reduces computational cost by 87.7% relative to the Code-agent variant and cuts execution time by more than 60%. Finally, an optional expert mode supports experimental planning via autonomous sensitivity and uncertainty evaluations, and formulates physically grounded recommendations for underspecified tasks. These results demonstrate that encapsulating domain code and expert knowledge into agent skills offers a promising route toward low-barrier, autonomous, and trustworthy thermal metrology.

items.title: Cavitation near the oscillating piezoelectric plate in water
items.summary: Gas and vapor bubbles at a wall can reduce the skin friction of a liquid flow. We estimate whether an oscillating piezoelectric plate mounted flush with the wall can create such a near-wall bubble layer by acoustic cavitation. Once the cavitation threshold is reached, the liquid can no longer follow the receding plate, and the excess plate displacement is accommodated by cavitation bubbles forming at the wall; this kinematic argument gives the bubble volume generated per stroke and its energy cost. Homogeneous cavitation in pure water (about -30 MPa) requires pressure amplitudes far beyond those of flat piezoelectric plates and produces submicron bubbles that collapse within nanoseconds. Heterogeneous cavitation on wall and gas nuclei (-0.1 to -1 MPa) is within reach of piezoceramics and concentrates the void on fewer, larger wal-attached bubbles, which survive between strokes if they exceed a few micrometres at 5 MHz. The acoustic power needed to sustain a bubble layer in a turbulent boundary layer at 10 m/s is about 20 kW/m2 for heterogeneous and about 0.4 MW/m2 for homogeneous cavitation.

items.title: The Physics of Interstellar Travel
items.summary: How can we send an uncrewed spacecraft to the nearest stars within a human lifetime? What propulsion methods are available? Will it survive impacts in the interstellar medium? What science will it do at its destination? How can it send back data over enormous distances? In this short semi-popular article, I examine various aspects of the physics of interstellar travel, its challenges and possible solutions. I focus on nuclear rockets, laser sails, dust impacts, and communication. These, as well as other issues such as navigation and onboard power, are explored in more detail in my book, The Physics of Interstellar Travel (2026).

items.title: Same Contacts, Different Rooms:Meeting Format Shapes LLM Group Influence Beyond Pairwise Contact Counts
items.summary: Simulations of LLM agent collectives usually summarise interaction as a pairwise contact network. We test that summary with a contact-matched intervention: the members, their initial stances and every pairwise contact count stay fixed while the meetings are reorganised, and each member gives a one-step support readout after reading the arguments of everyone present. Across six open-weight LLMs and 14 debate topics, merging triads into five-person meetings (resize) moves group support more than reshuffling who meets in triads (regroup), although both move the same 60 dyadic exposures. The root-mean-square change is 4.36 versus 2.59 percentage points (pp), larger for resize in all six models and in 81 of 84 model-topic cells. Resizing also has a consistent direction: it amplifies the initial majority of the merged members by 1.72 pp, in every model, whereas regrouping has no direction (<= 0.03 pp). A contact network cannot represent regrouping at all, yet pairwise rules applied meeting by meeting explain up to 76% of its effect, and with identical weights they raise resize R^2 by 0.51-0.58 for two models. We show that the gap between the two placements is an exact Jensen gap of the sigmoid readout, bounded by how much a member's predicted logits vary across meetings; this dispersion tracks the gap with log-log r=0.97 and tells a modeller when contact counts are a safe summary. Meeting format is a first-class variable for LLM social simulation.

items.title: High-quality electron beam generation from laser wakefield accelerators for driving compact free electron lasers
items.summary: Despite the successful demonstration of compact free electron lasers (FELs) driven by laser wakefield accelerators (LWFAs), the pursuit of further enhancements in high-gain compact FELs presents a challenge due to the limitations in electron beam quality. In this work, we pinpoint the pivotal physics and optimization strategies for high-quality single-stage LWFAs that are crucial for high-gain FELs. We have delved into the synergistic injection mechanism, where the self-evolution injection threshold is far from reached at the injection position, with both the shock front and self-evolution of the laser playing a role in the injection process. A thorough discussion has been provided on the beam-quality degradation and optimization strategies, in terms of global (slice) energy spread and projected (slice) emittance. With the goal of achieving high-gain FELs driven by LWFAs, we have also explored the synthesis quality of the electron beam to determine an optimized power gain length. A comprehensive start-to-end simulation has been conducted, demonstrating the effectiveness of compact FELs powered by these high-quality electron beams. The resulting radiation reaches the saturation regime after a 4.5-meter-long undulator, with an energy of 17.4 μJ and a power of 6.0 GW at a wavelength of 23.9 nm. This proposed scheme offers not only a framework for optimizing beam quality in LWFAs, but also a promising path for future compact LWFA-driven FELs to achieve saturated regimes, opening up new possibilities for widespread applications.

items.title: Counterexample-driven autonomous research with application to excess radiated energy in a Z-pinch
items.summary: Recent breakthroughs in artificial-intelligence-assisted mathematics show that open-ended machine search can outperform human mathematicians, yet transferring this paradigm to physics requires refactoring the research workflow. We introduce Simjecture, an open-source framework in which language-model agents pursue human-defined physical conjectures. The framework tackles two central challenges in this transfer: first, because physics is empirical and no model is final, it structures inquiry around counterexample-driven falsification and prospective hypothesis repair; second, because physical theories must interact with the real world, it uses computational physics as an executable testbed while separating the qualification of numerical instruments from scientific claim review so solvers and diagnostics can be adapted within a recorded investigation. We apply the framework in a 136.3 h investigation to tackle the long-standing problem of radiated energy exceeding the imploding-shell kinetic energy in a Z-pinch. The investigation reveals competing effects of energy conversion, retention, and release timing. Stronger coherent helical deformation increases resistive conversion while reducing radiation and increasing retained energy. In a matched fine-grid test, broadening the trailing-plasma profile delays the later radiation maximum by 1.80 ns and recovers an early 153 J bolometric deficit to within 0.08% by 44 ns, with a spectral response that shifts during the pulse. These results provide new insight into energy conversion in high-energy-density plasma physics and demonstrate a new paradigm for physics research.

items.title: Neural Modal Decomposition: Architectural Priors from Observables
items.summary: Many engineering building blocks behave as multi-port linear time-invariant systems. RF cavities, photonic devices, and superconducting quantum chips, despite their different underlying physics, all share a common mathematical structure for their port-level response. Each entry of the response matrix is a sum of contributions from a small number of intrinsic resonant modes, the pole-residue form. A model capable of predicting such responses for arbitrary geometries and arbitrary port configurations, while simultaneously extracting the underlying eigenmode structure, could therefore offer a design principle potentially applicable across all these domains. We propose a neural framework that learns this modal decomposition end-to-end, supervised only by system-level observables and without supervising the modal parameters themselves. The architecture decomposes into a port-independent pole predictor and two port-dependent coupling predictors whose outputs are combined entry-wise, separating intrinsic from port-dependent features. This factorization yields a single trained model that generalizes to port counts unseen during training, whereas direct regression needs a separate model for each port count, with an output size that grows as $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$. Although the modal parameters are never supervised, the freely parameterized poles converge to the physical resonances, in agreement with poles extracted by the AAA rational approximation algorithm. We instantiate the framework in radio-frequency electromagnetic surrogate modeling. A model trained only on 2-port data accurately predicts $N$-port responses unseen during training.

items.title: A Multidimensional Evaluation Framework for Artificial Intelligence-Based Ocean State Forecasts
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) based ocean state forecasts now approach or surpass those produced by operational ocean forecasting systems as measured by conventional pointwise metrics. However, these metrics may favor spatially smoothed forecasts and cannot determine whether forecast variables remain physically coherent. Forecast evaluation should therefore move beyond overall pointwise accuracy toward assessing forecast trustworthiness. We propose a multidimensional framework comprising overall pointwise accuracy, physical consistency, and distributional consistency.
