items.summary: Neural networks, spiking or not, compute with amplitudes: activation values, spike counts, firing rates, never event times. No measure exists of how much a network uses time. We propose one, the degree of temporal representation: the fraction of a network's four functions (encoding, activation, decoding, learning) whose variables or parameters are temporal, and hypothesise that it predicts performance on temporal tasks. At fixed architecture, accuracy and energy efficiency increase with the degree: a delay network of maximal degree reaches 98.94\% on Google Speech Commands with 175k parameters, above transformers. To test whether networks of different degree really differ, we convert the delay network into artificial and spiking networks with the same inputs and outputs. From this common start, the artificial one learns differently and temporal gradients depend on event times. Hence we obtain a design rule: for temporal data, make event times variables of a network's functions. Spiking networks, converted after training, keep the delay network's accuracy, unreachable by spiking networks trained from scratch.

items.title: Learning Equilibria in Coordination Games via Minorization-Maximization
items.summary: This paper considers games where the utilities for agents are the sum of a term proportional to a social utility, and another term that is an individual cost or reward. The agents are assumed to be irrational in their perception of the individual cost or reward. The multi equilibrium game is regularized, and its strictly concave potential function is used to select a unique equilibrium. This selected equilibrium is shown to be an $ε-$equilibrium of the original game, where $ε$ is parametrized by the regularizing function. A minorization-maximization based iterative learning scheme is proposed to learn equilibria in this game. This scheme converges to the potential-optimal equilibrium, and has superior convergence behavior in comparison to gradient and best response methods.

items.title: Learned Adaptive Indexing with Updatable Learned Index
items.summary: Indexes can significantly improve search performance in databases. However, if the query workload changes frequently or new data updates occur continuously, it may not be worthwhile to build a conventional index upfront for query processing. Building a conventional fine-grained index, like B+-tree on the entire dataset can be very expensive since it may involve processing terabytes to petabytes of data. Moreover, with a traditional indexing, data ingestion tends to slow down in case of heavy updates as the index also needs to be updated. In these cases, adaptive indexing is a viable solution instead of traditional indexing. Adaptive indexing is a technique in which an index gets built on the fly as a byproduct of query processing. In recent years, research has taken on a new direction where machine learning models are employed for the purpose of indexing. These indexes, known as learned indexes, are more efficient compared to traditional indexes in terms of memory footprints and query performance. To the best of our knowledge, no learned indexes exist yet for adaptive indexing. We propose a novel learned approach, called FLAIRS, for adaptive indexing. It is built on the fly as queries are submitted. We also introduce an updatable learned index TULSI that is utilized by FLAIRS for indexing data. FLAIRS can employ a query workload prediction technique that makes future workload projection based on past workload data. We have evaluated FLAIRS against existing adaptive indexes for various query workloads. Our results show that our approach performs better than others in most cases, offering significant improvement in query performance.

items.title: Greedy Byte-Pair Encoding Achieves 0.391 of the Optimum, Past the One-Third Barrier for Packing-Based Analyses
items.summary: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds most language-model tokenisers by repeatedly merging a most frequent adjacent pair of symbols. How much shortening can this greedy rule lose against the best $k$ merges? Kozma and Voderholzer proved that greedy achieves at least one third of the optimal shortening; the best known upper bound is $(1-e^{-2})/2\approx 0.432$. We show that one third is a barrier for packing-based analyses, which see the optimum only through a pair packing, and we prove that greedy achieves at least $0.391$ of the optimum on every input, with any tie-breaking. The key idea is rule determinism: all copies of a rule of the optimum spell the same letters, so when one greedy replacement destroys three of the optimum's merge points, half a unit can be refunded on each side. A weaker bound, $0.374$, has a short proof that needs no computer; $0.391$ adds a certificate in exact arithmetic. We also show that the worst-case ratio is exactly $3/4$ for two merges and at most $7/12$ for three.

items.title: EffiNav: Fusing Depth and Vision-Language for Efficient Object Goal Navigation
items.summary: To locate a target object while exploring the unknown environment is a fundamental capability for autonomous agents, with applications ranging from search-and-rescue to field robots. A simplified version of such task is Object Goal Navigation (ObjNav). In ObjNav, successful arrival at the target object provides a basic measure of performance; however, the efficiency of the navigation trajectory is equally important, as it indicates how intelligently the agent explores and how much time remains for subsequent tasks. In unknown environments, the key to efficient navigation lies in deciding where to explore next. While many prior works aim to address this core challenge and achieved promising performance in certain settings, recent training-based models and non-training frameworks still suffer from generalization and efficiency issues respectively, which in the worst cases can lead to excessive exploration of already-visited areas or redundant back-and-forth motion. We evaluate EffiNav on two widely used simulation benchmarks Habitat Matterport 3D (HM3D) and Open-Vocabulary Object goal Navigation (OVON), and further validate its effectiveness on physical robots in real-world settings. We conduct failure analysis on massive simulation episodes. With minimal modification, we also extend EffiNav to a memory-augmented ObjNav task on the GOAT-BENCH dataset, demonstrating its adaptability beyond standard ObjNav settings. Across two standard metrics--Success Rate (SR) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL), EffiNav matches or outperforms recent baselines, reflecting its efficiency, robustness, and practical applicability. Recognizing the different emphases of the two datasets, the performances reveals this framework is more balanced and generalizable for efficient ObjNav.

items.title: Improving Evaluation Realism with Inference-Time Compute and Deployment Scaffolds
items.summary: A core obstacle to alignment evaluation is evaluation awareness: capable models can tell when they are being tested rather than deployed, weakening the conclusions a safety evaluation can support. We present two techniques that make simulated alignment evaluations harder to distinguish from real deployments. Our first technique, critique refinement, spends additional inference-time compute on each simulator action: the simulator generates multiple candidate actions, refines them using feedback from an instance of the target model on how to make them more realistic, and continues the evaluation with the most deployment-like candidate. Our second technique, DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), wraps the target in an agent harness, reducing the gap between simulated and real deployment environments in coding settings. We test the techniques on multiple target models and find that applying both yields larger realism gains than either alone. We show that automated approaches can improve the realism of alignment evaluations, and that they compare favorably to spending the extra compute on more audit attempts.

items.title: Dynamic Graph Indexing for Label-Filtered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
items.summary: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) over high-dimensional vectors is a core primitive in modern retrieval systems. In practice, objects are often also associated with labels (e.g., attributes or keywords), and retrieval must combine vector similarity with explicit label-based filtering, giving rise to label-filtered ANNS. This task is challenging because label filtering and ANNS favor very different index structures, selective filters fragment the admissible search space, and updates complicate index maintenance. To address these challenges, we propose DYLAN, a dynamic composite index for label-filtered ANNS supporting containment, overlap, and their conjunctions and disjunctions. DYLAN organizes label sets by shared prefixes in a frequency-ordered trie and selectively shares HNSW-style graph indices across trie-induced subsets, so that each trie region has a constant-factor covering index while each object participates in only logarithmically many indices. To mitigate fragmentation, DYLAN performs a cross-region multi-graph search that exploits ancestor-level indices as bridges between otherwise isolated trie regions. To support insertions, it adopts a threshold-based maintenance scheme that rebuilds shared indices only when necessary, yielding low amortized update cost. Extensive experiments with real data show that DYLAN consistently improves query throughput at comparable recall, by up to two orders of magnitude on challenging label-rich datasets, while retaining competitive memory, construction, and update costs.

items.title: Diffusion LLMs are Natural Adversaries for any LLM
items.summary: We introduce a novel framework that transforms the resource-intensive (adversarial) prompt optimization problem into an \emph{efficient, amortized inference task}. Our core insight is that pretrained, non-autoregressive generative LLMs, such as Diffusion LLMs, which model the joint distribution over prompt-response pairs, can serve as powerful surrogates for prompt search. This approach enables direct conditional generation of prompts, effectively replacing costly discrete optimization with a small number of parallelizable samples. We provide a probabilistic analysis demonstrating that under mild fidelity assumptions, only a few conditional samples are required to recover high-reward (harmful) prompts. Empirically, our method substantially outperforms prior attacks in both success rate and compute cost, producing low-perplexity, diverse jailbreaks that transfer to a wide range of black-box target models, including robustly trained and proprietary LLMs. Beyond adversarial prompting, our framework opens new directions for red teaming, automated prompt optimization, and leveraging emerging Flow- and Diffusion-based LLMs.

items.title: Controlling the latency in temporal coded spiking models for neuromorphic datasets
items.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient, event-driven computation on neuromorphic hardware, where response time, or latency, matters as much as energy for real-time applications. Time-to-first-spike (TTFS) coding with learnable synaptic delays is a natural way to exploit the timing of events. However, in state-of-the-art spiking neuron models, spike times emerge from nonlinear membrane dynamics and thresholds: no closed-form expression links network parameters to spike times, so latency can only be measured empirically, not specified or guaranteed at design time. Moreover, TTFS models are mostly evaluated on static datasets, which hides their latency on truly temporal data. Our hypothesis is that, if spike times are computed directly as closed-form functions of presynaptic spike times and synaptic delays, bypassing membrane potential and thresholding, latency becomes an explicit function of the learnable parameters that can be bounded, and therefore controlled, analytically. We build on this hypothesis with the Delay Neural Network (DeNN) in real time, which turns event streams into successive single-spike images, computes each spike time from standardised inter-spike intervals and synaptic delays, and links successive images through a long-term memory. We prove lower and upper bounds on the latency of every neuron of a layer, and show that bounding the synaptic parameters after training with a single hyperparameter places the latency anywhere between these bounds, without retraining. On a ten-class subset of the Google Speech Commands dataset, this post-training control exposes the accuracy--latency trade-off: a three-hidden-layer network reaches 94.25\% accuracy while deciding, on average, 477~ms after the end of the one-second input, and about 250~ms with confidence-based early decisions. Learning is also shown to concentrate the long-term memory on a few neurons. Latency thus becomes a design parameter of spiking models rather than a quantity measured after the fact, a step towards neuromorphic systems with real-time guarantees.

items.title: ML Models Are Not Ciphers: Power Analysis for Weight Extraction Is Harder Than You Think
items.summary: Can power-analysis techniques reveal secret weights of machine-learning models? Multiple recent works demonstrate proof-of-concept attacks that can partially recover such weights. To that end, these works build on techniques from cryptographic engineering, treating the model as a ``cipher'' and its secret weights as keys. We question the basic assumption behind such straightforward adaptations of cryptographic attacks and highlight the challenges arising when applying past techniques to fully recover all layers of deep neural networks. Unlike past works, which extract only a few weights, typically from shallow layers, we investigate the recovery of complete networks. Moreover, we target fully trained and functional models, rather than untrained, randomly initialized networks. To focus on fundamental challenges, we assume an unrealistically strong side-channel adversary that can directly observe the output of the leakage model without any added noise. With this adversary, we show that machine-learning models differ significantly from cryptographic implementations, giving rise to unique challenges that have not been observed in the prior art. We observe two main differences between machine-learning models and ciphers. First, in contrast to the high-diffusion nonlinear integer arithmetic prevalent in cryptographic schemes, machine-learning models tend to use limited-precision floating-point arithmetic and low-diffusion linear operations. We show that these operations introduce difficulties in weight recovery, often requiring an unexpectedly large number of traces, even under ideal channel conditions. Second, we observe that, unlike ciphers, which aim to increase the data entropy, machine-learning models aim to reduce it. This reduces data variability as the algorithm progresses, hampering weight recovery in deep layers of the model. (details can be found in the paper)

items.title: K-prop: Deep Online Learning by Backpropagating Temporal Kernels
items.summary: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.

items.title: Perceived Agency During Agent-Avatar Control Transitions in Virtual Reality
items.summary: Prior beliefs about whether a virtual human (VH) is controlled by a human or a computer can shape how users interpret and respond to its behaviour. As emerging hybrid VH systems allow control to transfer between human operators and computer programs during an ongoing interaction, it remains unclear whether perceived agency updates with the actual controller or continues to reflect users' prior beliefs and first impressions. We investigated this question in a within-subject VR study with 24 participants across four conditions: always computer-controlled, computer-to-human, human-to-computer, and always human-controlled. We designed an interaction task in which participants acted as interviewers, asking the VHs a fixed set of questions. Before each interaction, participants were informed whether the VH was human- or computer-controlled, matching the actual controller at the beginning, but were unaware of possible control transitions. We found that perceived agency was strongly influenced by the controller presented at the beginning of the interaction, with no evidence of updating following the control transitions. Social evaluations including likeability and co-presence were generally higher in conditions where human control occurred later and covered a greater proportion of the interaction. The results suggest that prior beliefs and first impressions continued to shape perceived agency, whereas social evaluations were more sensitive to the VH's actual behaviour over the interaction.

items.title: WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning
items.summary: This work proposes WaveGen, a fully end-to-end diffusion-based text-to-waveform framework based on Spectral Forcing, which jointly learns an internal spectral trajectory and the target waveform trajectory within a single model, enabling direct end-to-end text-to-waveform generation. Unlike recent TTS pipelines, WaveGen does not rely on separately trained or externally decoded intermediate representations, such as neural audio codecs, Mel-spectrogram vocoders, or VAE-based latent models. In addition, WaveGen performs internal text-speech alignment within a single model, eliminating the need for external alignment modules such as duration predictors. To preserve a truly end-to-end formulation, our framework further avoids dependence on self-supervised representations, such as BERT-based text embeddings and Wav2Vec 2.0-based semantic representations, as well as semantic distillation methods for training optimization. To achieve this, we carefully design Spectral Forcing, a model architecture with disentangled diffusion heads, and a training objective based on a multi-scale spectral $v$-loss. We further validate the scalability of end-to-end TTS models by scaling the model size from 0.1B to 0.6B parameters. Using a single architecture, open-source data, and one-stage training, without external modules such as duration predictor or REPA, WaveGen demonstrates fully end-to-end waveform generation achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Emilia training dataset. In particular, WaveGen achieves a WER of 1.47 and a SIM of 0.75 on the Seed-en benchmark. Source code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen

items.title: Galilean Robots, Aristotelian Sensors: Joint Spatiotemporal Trajectory Estimation and Extrinsic Calibration
items.summary: Multi-sensor state estimation requires accurate spatial and temporal calibration between heterogeneous sensors. Existing spatiotemporal calibration methods typically represent sensor extrinsic parameters as a rigid-body transformation together with a scalar temporal offset, causing the spatial and temporal parameters to enter the estimation problem through separate mechanisms. While the spatial transformation composes directly with the robot pose, accounting for the temporal offset requires evaluating the trajectory at a shifted time, typically through motion compensation, interpolation, or a continuous-time trajectory representation. In this work, we formulate joint trajectory estimation and spatiotemporal calibration using the special Galilean group for the robot trajectory and the Aristotelian subgroup for sensor extrinsics. This representation incorporates the coupling between motion and temporal offset directly through the group structure, avoiding the need for a separately parameterized continuous-time trajectory. We develop twist- and IMU-driven motion priors, accommodate both ideal and non-ideal clocks, and evaluate the framework with camera, position, and range measurements. Simulated and real experiments demonstrate calibration and trajectory-estimation performance comparable to established methods across heterogeneous sensor configurations. Our simplified framework therefore offers a quality-of-life improvement over existing methods without compromising performance.

items.title: EditJudge-Bench: Auditing VLM Image-Edit Judges with Synthetic Ground Truth
items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for image-editing benchmarks, yet their reliability is poorly understood. Auditing these judges is difficult because real edited images lack controlled ground truth and entangle the requested changes with model artefacts, unintended side effects, and ambiguous degrees of success. In this paper, we introduce EditJudge-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,382 synthetic before/after image pairs rendered in Blender, with edits parameterised across nine categories derived from real user requests and exact ground truth from known 3D scene parameters. Because every edit is generated by a known intervention on a controlled scene, EditJudge-Bench evaluates VLM judges as binary verifiers of whether an instruction was correctly executed, isolating judge perception from editor quality. Across 25 judge configurations, we find substantial reliability gaps: (a) the widely adopted VIEScore template reaches only 69.0% AUROC with GPT-4o; (b) fine-tuned judges score 51.7-66.3%; spatial edits such as rotation and shape remain challenging; (c) prompt-formatting choices like image-text ordering shift performance by up to 14.1 points. Despite using only synthetic data, judge rankings on EditJudge-Bench correlate strongly with two real-image human-preference benchmarks ($ρ$=0.95 and $ρ$=0.71), indicating that controlled audits surface failure modes relevant to real evaluation.

items.title: Can the Confidence and Decisions of System 1 Models Be Trusted? An Explainability and Perturbation Audit of Jev-Style Decision Models
items.summary: "System 1" decision models (pioneered by TypeSafe AI's Jev) replace autoregressive text generation with a single forward pass returning typed probability distributions over declared schemas (Choice, Score, Noul). While deployed for low-latency routing and automated triage, their statistical calibration and post-hoc explainability remain uncharacterized. We introduce an open, deterministic audit benchmark evaluating System 1 decision models across calibration under label-preserving perturbations, cross-question interference, and post-hoc attribution faithfulness. Evaluating five open-weight models (0.8B to 27B) alongside generative System 2 baselines -- both single-token logprob scoring and structured JSON/CoT decoding -- across NLI (e-SNLI), adversarial syntactic shortcuts (HANS), synthetic clinical triage (N=900), prompt injection defense (Tensor Trust, N=250), and an 86-case logic-gate trigger suite yields five findings: (1) provider confidence is an exact closed-form dispersion transform (1 - H(p)/ln K on sub-10B models; normalized margin on Clef-27B) rather than empirical accuracy; (2) bundling multiple questions in one request induces directional cross-question interference (11.7% to 22.4% binary flips on Tev1-0.8B, vs. 0.1% to 0.2% on Tev1-4B); (3) System 1 models with >= 4B parameters are faster and better calibrated under syntactic shifts (ECE_w = 0.030 to 0.087) than logprob (0.144) and JSON (0.378) baselines; (4) for prompt-injection defense (N=250), >= 4B models achieve 0.988 to 0.998 AUROC with up to 95.2% recall and 0.0% false alarms at 48 to 60 ms; and (5) single-pass inference makes 512-coalition XAI interactive (1.3 to 3.2 s/input), while KernelSHAP with a logit link (S1-SHAP) mitigates softmax saturation on disjunctive OR gates (89.3% to 100.0% gate recovery vs. 57.1% to 82.1% in prob space; p_adj = 0.004).

items.title: How To Track Qubits Through Space and Time (Or: Sailing in a Quantum Boat)
items.summary: While quantum position verification aims to certify a prover's location using quantum information, existing security definitions only guarantee that part of the successful adversarial party is in the claimed location. This leaves open the possibility that a distributed team of adversaries can jointly simulate a prover in a way that defeats the intended meaning of `being at a location' in position-based cryptography. We introduce stronger notions of position verification that we call quantum localization, which requires that there is a specified, unclonable state at the verified spacetime point-and that this state can be found nowhere else. We show that quantum localization leads naturally to a meaningful notion of trajectory verification, in which quantum information is verifiably tracked through space and time. We construct quantum localization and trajectory verification protocols using quantum anchor states, which generalize coset states from unclonable cryptography. The security of our schemes is proven in the classical oracle (i.e. ideal obfuscation) model, which can be heuristically instantiated in the plain model using post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation. We also introduce and instantiate the concept of functionality localization, which guarantees that the adversary has the ability to compute a secret function at the verified spacetime point, and this function cannot be computed anywhere else. This raises the intriguing possibility of localizing computational capabilities in space and time. More broadly, we believe our notions of quantum localization and subsequent feasibility results provide stronger foundations for position-based cryptography. At a conceptual level, our results also explore the tight link between two fundamental notions in physics-location and information-thus serving as a natural foundation for cryptographic capabilities tied to physical spacetime.

items.title: Towards Multi-Source Domain Generalization for Sleep Staging with Noisy Labels
items.summary: Automatic sleep staging is a multimodal learning problem involving heterogeneous physiological signals such as EEG and EOG, which often suffer from domain shifts across institutions, devices, and populations. In practice, these data are also affected by noisy annotations, yet label-noise-robust multi-source domain generalization remains underexplored. We present the first benchmark for Noisy Labels in Multi-Source Domain-Generalized Sleep Staging (NL-DGSS) and show that existing noisy-label learning methods degrade substantially when domain shifts and label noise coexist. To address this challenge, we propose FF-TRUST, a domain-invariant multimodal sleep staging framework with Joint Time-Frequency Early Learning Regularization (JTF-ELR). By jointly exploiting temporal and spectral consistency together with confidence-diversity regularization, FF-TRUST improves robustness under noisy supervision. Experiments on five public datasets demonstrate consistent state-of-the-art performance under diverse symmetric and asymmetric noise settings.

items.title: Certifying the Error-Detection Value of Functional Dependencies without Ground Truth
items.summary: Functional dependencies are used to flag erroneous cells, but without error labels the value of these flags is unknown. Dependency strength cannot settle it, because identical data and flags can have positive value in one clean state and negative value in another. We treat this value as partially identified and certify a fixed detector when its value is positive in every clean state compatible with the observation under an error model and budget. The largest such budget is the certification radius. For a detector that flags departures from the unique mode of each class, the worst case reduces to a 0/1 knapsack over class flips, yielding sharp bounds on true positives and the exact radius in polynomial time. Allowing bounded legitimate exceptions in the clean data, we derive an exact threshold for the existence of a positive certificate and compute the radius with the same knapsack. Across five relations and 21,981 candidate dependencies, rules with nearly equal $g_3$ and flag rate can have certification margins differing tenfold. Error injection confirms sound certification and shows that, at equal error counts, changing the organization of errors reverses certification outcomes for every tested rule.

items.title: UniHam: A Large-Scale SOC-Complete Dataset and Benchmark for Hamiltonian Learning in Materials
items.summary: Accurate prediction of electronic Hamiltonians would enable broad property inference while avoiding the high computational cost of Density Functional Theory (DFT). However, progress toward general-purpose materials foundation models is limited by a data bottleneck: existing Hamiltonian datasets are typically small, lack structural diversity, and often omit essential relativistic physics such as spin--orbit coupling (SOC). We therefore construct UniHam, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset and benchmark suite comprising 100,000+ DFT-computed complex-valued Hermitian Hamiltonians with full SOC, covering 72 elements and a wide range of crystal geometries and symmetries (spanning diverse lattice types and space-group families). Building on UniHam, we benchmark two representative state-of-the-art models under a standardized protocol and introduce complementary evaluation metrics that jointly assess three dimensions: (i) Hamiltonian reconstruction accuracy, (ii) out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization across composition/symmetry shifts, and (iii) the ability to support downstream property prediction from the predicted Hamiltonians. Experiments on UniHam demonstrate that the proposed benchmark and metrics effectively differentiate model capabilities, revealing intrinsic SOC- and element-dependent failure modes, large variations in compositional OOD robustness, and the necessity of spectral-level evaluation to assess whether Hamiltonian predictions reliably support downstream electronic-structure properties. Overall, UniHam provides a reproducible, SOC-complete benchmark that can sharpen model comparisons and accelerate the development of next-generation foundation models for quantum materials.

items.title: MARS: Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams for Video Forgery Detection
items.summary: Generalizing deepfake detection across facial manipulation and fully generated video remains challenging due to forgery traces varying with the manipulation method and scene content. Explicit spatial and temporal feature differences offer a way to capture this variation, but also respond to natural texture and motion, motivating their joint interpretation with appearance features. We investigate whether combining multiscale feature differences with adapted appearance representations improves detection across both forgery categories. We introduce Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams (MARS), a two-path video detector. The residual path applies fixed spatial and temporal difference-of-Gaussians operators to frozen intermediate features and models the resulting differences alongside appearance context across frames. The semantic path adapts the encoder's normalization parameters for frame classification, and a clip-dependent gate combines their predictions. Under a shared protocol across seven datasets, MARS achieves the highest average AUROC of 91.43\%, outperforming seven compared detectors. When trained on facial manipulations alone, MARS achieves 93.99\% AUROC on GenVideo and 75.50\% on DF26, demonstrating transfer to generated videos without generated-video training data. MARS also provides signed patch and frame contributions, whose faithfulness we evaluate through controlled spatial and temporal removal against random controls. MARS is publicly available for research: Project page: https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mars/ Github: https://github.com/VectorInstitute/mars

items.title: ManifoldCache: Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration via Constraint Manifold Caching
items.summary: Diffusion models for structured scientific generation must produce samples satisfying hard geometric constraints imposed by physics, chemistry, or biology, yet inference in these settings is prohibitively slow, demanding hundreds to thousands of neural-function evaluations per sample. We unify eight state-of-the-art models spanning medical volumetrics, molecular conformations, protein backbone design, crystal structure prediction, and multi-view 3D scenes under a single abstraction, Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models (CMDMs), in which the target distribution is supported on a manifold defined by an externally specified constraint map. All existing acceleration families fail on this class: quantization exhausts memory on high-dimensional volumetric operators; pruning breaks constraint fidelity; fast ODE solvers allow trajectories to drift off the constraint manifold; and feature-caching heuristics are blind to constraint geometry, inducing mode confusion in the high-noise regime. We introduce ManifoldCache, the first training-free, data-free accelerator designed from first principles for CMDMs. The key insight is that the conditional score decomposes orthogonally into a normal component, which enforces constraint satisfaction, and a tangential component, which navigates within the manifold. Exploiting this structure, we prove that the noise-schedule midpoint is a sharp safe-caching boundary: caching before it incurs provably bounded error, while caching after it guarantees a strictly positive fraction of trajectories suffer mode confusion, a gap that persists up to the boundary. We further prove that deeper network blocks admit provably larger certified cache strides within the safe phase, as a consequence of the score decomposition propagating through block Jacobians. The resulting schedule requires no calibration data, along with zero training overhead.

items.title: ANCORA: Learning to Question via Manifold-Anchored Self-Play for Verifiable Reasoning
items.summary: We propose a paradigm shift toward open-ended curriculum self-play: rather than learning to answer on a fixed prompt set, a unified policy learns to question: generating verifiable problems, solving them, and turning verifier feedback into self-improvement. We introduce ANCORA, in which the policy alternates between a Proposer that synthesizes novel specifications and a Solver that produces verified solutions, anchored by three mechanisms: a two-level group-relative update coupling Proposer advantages across specifications with Solver advantages across solution attempts; iterative self-distilled SFT projecting the base model onto its valid-output manifold before RL; and a UCB-guided Curriculum DAG whose policy-induced problem set can provably expand under self-composition. Without these stabilizers, sparse verifier feedback drives Proposer collapse even under MLRL-aligned rewards; with them, ANCORA bootstraps a verifiable curriculum from curated seeds. Instantiated in Verus, ANCORA lifts Dafny2Verus pass@1 from a 26.6% SFT baseline to 81.5% in test-time training (TTT, 0-shot), outperforming PSV self-play (1-shot) by 15.8 points; in a transfer setting, training from Dafny2Verus seeds yields 36.2% and 17.2% pass@1 on MBPP and HumanEval.

items.title: Text Grouping Changes Completion-Time Comparisons in Long-Form Simultaneous Speech Translation
items.summary: Does grouping translation updates before speech synthesis change the measured completion gap between two translators? We compare StreamAtt with its fixed-audio-history baseline on ten English-German talks. For each translation, we keep the intended text and its availability times fixed and vary how updates are grouped for synthesis. Four-second grouping increases StreamAtt's mean completion lead from 106.6 to 229.1 seconds with XTTS-v2, but reduces it from 169.5 to 146.5 seconds with Piper. Both produce shorter audio; different changes in playback idle account for the opposite effects. These directions recur on a separately selected twenty-talk panel. In continuing CosyVoice 3 sessions, grouping instead leaves paired audio unchanged and delays completion on nineteen of twenty blocks. A speech-timing comparison therefore needs to specify how text enters synthesis, not just which synthesizer is used. Recognition and automatic word timing describe the outputs, but do not establish translation accuracy or intelligibility.

items.title: Textraction: Unified Text-Guided Speaker Extraction and Enhancement for Single- and Multi-Channel Audio
items.summary: We present Textraction, a text-guided speaker extraction framework that enables the selective extraction of desired speakers or noise sources from an audio mixture using only natural-language descriptions. The proposed method operates within a single unified model that supports both single-channel and multi-channel inputs and it allows conditioning on either semantic textual descriptions of the target source or on its spatial description. Dedicated single- and multi-channel encoders feed a shared stack of time--frequency transformer blocks, which is conditioned on the prompt and on the recording configuration in every block through cross-attention and estimates the target directly from the mixture in one forward pass, without a separation stage or a source-selection stage. The system can extract an arbitrary subset of entities from a mixture, assuming up to two simultaneously active speakers and two noise sources, and interprets prompts specifying which entities to keep, which to remove, or both. In addition, we show that the framework naturally applies to a speech-enhancement setting, in which a single target speaker is present alongside background noise. To circumvent the application of computationally costly large language models used in prior work, we introduce a lightweight, task-adapted text encoder obtained by contrastively fine-tuning a compact text-retrieval model, which learns to be sensitive to instruction polarity (e.g., keep vs. remove) while remaining robust to paraphrasing. Experiments across attribute-based extraction, spatially guided extraction, and speech enhancement show that the proposed approach effectively isolates the desired entities under various acoustic and spatial conditions, and matches or surpasses dedicated spatial-extraction and enhancement baselines while offering substantially greater flexibility.

items.title: Rate-Aware Quantum-Inspired Trajectory Learning for Interference-Limited Multi-UAV Networks
items.summary: Placing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as aerial base stations is non-convex and combinatorial, so practical methods first discretize the continuous airspace into a finite set of candidate positions---a uniform grid or clustering centroids---and optimize over that set. Built from Euclidean distance alone, the candidate set is channel-blind: it ignores line-of-sight probability and the co-channel interference that limits achievable rate under full frequency reuse. No optimizer can select a position the candidate set omits, so good locations the geometry missed are lost before the search begins. We propose Rate-Aware Quantum-Assisted Graph Condensation (RA-QAGC), a two-stage framework that makes the candidate set itself the object of optimization. The first stage constructs it by annealing a cost that embeds tier-weighted achievable rate, mean co-channel interference, and an explicit minimum-rate penalty, yielding a compact, mobility-feasible waypoint graph. The second stage learns trajectories over that graph with decentralized independent Q-learning agents, replacing a centralized joint-action table with one compact table per UAV. RA-QAGC improves priority-tier throughput by 21--54\% over seven baselines, including recent graph-neural and deep Q-network schemes, at no significant cost in aggregate throughput, and the margin widens as the fleet densifies. We additionally examine the quantum-inspired acceptance rule that recent aerial-networking work advocates, and report that its tunnelling floor confers no measurable advantage over classical simulated annealing at any fleet size tested, while annealing itself clearly outperforms greedy and random placement.

items.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
items.summary: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.

items.title: Detecting AI-Authored Text in Authentic Student Writing: Evidence from PISA 2025
items.summary: AI-text detectors reach near-perfect scores in evaluations that contrast fully human-written texts with texts generated from researcher-designed prompts. In authentic student writing, however, AI use is voluntary and often partial. We study this setting with the PISA 2025 FLA dataset, in which 15-year-olds in Germany wrote English argumentative essays with and without access to a gpt-4o-mini-based chatbot. Keystroke, clipboard and chat logs let us trace every character of the final essay to its origin. From this provenance, we derive text- and sentence-level labels for human-written, AI-generated and mixed text, and for text written after chatbot use without traceable AI material. We evaluate a feature-based detector and a classifier on frozen Llama-3.1-8B embeddings, both adapted from top-ranked shared-task systems. Both separate AI from human text reliably (macro-F1 up to 0.96 for texts and 0.95 for sentences), independently of spelling errors. The feature-based detector, however, relies on lexical complexity, which a simple student-style rewriting prompt removes (AI recall 0.92 $\to$ 0.60 with gpt-4o-mini, 0.41 with Qwen3). The embedding-based detector stays robust for whole texts (AI recall $\geq$ 0.94) but not for single sentences (AI recall as low as 0.59). Mixed text falls between the two classes, and text without traceable AI material is classified as human-written in about 95\% of texts.

items.title: Conformalized Super Learner
items.summary: The Super Learner (SL) is a widely used ensemble method that combines point predictions from a library of learners based on their predictive performance. Interval predictions are of considerable practical interest because they allow uncertainty in predictions produced by an individual learner or an ensemble to be quantified. Several methods have been proposed for constructing interval predictions based on the SL, however, these approaches are typically justified using asymptotic arguments or rely on computationally intensive procedures such as the bootstrap. Conformal prediction (CP) is a machine learning framework for constructing prediction intervals with finite-sample and asymptotic coverage guarantees under mild conditions. We propose coupling CP with the SL through a natural construction that mirrors the original SL framework, using individual learner weights and combining learner-specific conformal prediction sets via a weighted majority vote. We characterize the properties of the resulting SL-based prediction intervals for continuous outcomes. We cover settings under exchangeability, and data-generating mechanisms exhibiting heteroscedasticity, sparsity, and other forms of distributional heterogeneity. A comprehensive simulation study shows that the conformalized SL achieves valid finite-sample coverage with competitive performance relative to the true data-generating mechanism. We present an application of this methodology to predict creatinine levels using socio-demographic, biometric, and laboratory measurements. This example demonstrates the benefits of an ensemble with carefully selected learners designed to capture key aspects of complex regression functions, including non-linear effects, interactions, sparsity, heteroscedasticity, and robustness to outliers.

items.title: Polarity Blindness in LLM Safety: A Systematic Study of Negation, Antonym Substitution, and Adversarial Framing
items.summary: Negation remains a persistent challenge for language models across NLP tasks and modalities. We show that this weakness can undermine LLM safety guardrails through a structural vulnerability we term polarity blindness: the failure to recognize harmful intent after polarity-altering linguistic transformations. We study two forms of polarity inversion: grammatical negation and antonym replacement, and use synonym replacement as a polarity-preserving control. We further test whether an adversarial textual wrapper amplifies these failures. Using a 260-prompt benchmark across 10 state-of-the-art LLMs and 3 languages (English, Spanish, Czech), stratified by harmfulness potential and evaluated on a validated 0-5 harm scale, we find that polarity blindness affects most evaluated models, with mean harm scores reaching 4.12 for the most vulnerable model. The effect persists across typologically differing negation systems, suggesting that polarity blindness reflects a broader limitation in semantic robustness rather than a language- or grammar-specific failure.

items.title: Optimizing the Steady-State Travel Time of Nash Flows over Time with Capacity Increases
items.summary: We study budgeted capacity augmentation for single-source single-sink \NFOTs under constant inflow $u_0$. The goal is to increase capacities on arcs subject to a global budget constraint in order to minimize the steady-state travel time in the network. We show that this problem is weakly NP-hard on series-parallel networks and provide an exact pseudopolynomial algorithm as well as a fully polynomial algorithm that attains the optimum travel time for budget $B$ while spending at most $B + \varepsilon\cdot\max\{B,u_0\}$. On general networks the problem becomes strongly NP-hard. Moreover, unless $\text{P} = \text{NP}$, for every fixed $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, no polynomial-time algorithm can achieve the optimal steady-state travel time while exceeding the budget by at most a factor of $n^{1-\varepsilon}$. Lastly, we give structural properties about steady-state travel time under varying arc capacities. We identify capacity thresholds determined by subsets of $s$-$t$-cuts and show that the travel time is constant in the interior of the cells resulting from the corresponding hyperplane arrangement.

items.title: Resetting-based designated information distribution
items.summary: For a network of $n$ nodes under random gossip dynamics, we show that by introducing the additional resetting mechanism (with rate $β$) to a designated subset of $r$ nodes, the expected sum of all node values is asymptotically equal to $\tfrac{n}{r}$ times the sum of the initial values of the $r$ designated nodes, in the small-$β$ and long-time limit. We also analyze the convergence speed to this asymptotic state and provide an approximate high-probability confidence interval for the expected sum at finite time $t$ and finite $β$. Operationally, we propose a protocol that distributes the initial node values over the designated subset evenly (up to a prescribed precision), by appropriately turning on and off the resetting dynamics. Our work not only offers insights into classical problems such as distributed computing and network control, but also serves as a potential foundation for designing quantum algorithms that prepare desired states in quantum networks using only local operations.

items.title: Transformers converge to invariant algorithmic cores
items.summary: Training selects for behavior, not circuitry: many weight configurations can implement the same function. Studying any single trained neural network thus risks describing accidents of one training run rather than the computation itself. This work shifts focus from what transformers happen to do to what they must do by extracting algorithmic cores, compact subspaces that are necessary and sufficient for a task and that recur across independently trained models. Here, Algorithmic Core Extraction (ACE) is introduced to isolate these subspaces, causally validate them, and recover the algorithms they implement, from synthetic tasks to large pretrained models. Markov-chain transformers embed 3D cores in nearly orthogonal subspaces yet recover identical transition spectra. Modular-addition transformers form compact cyclic cores at grokking that later inflate under continued regularization, redundantly distributing the same computation across many functionally equivalent modes. This functional redundancy accelerates the transition from memorization to generalization, yielding an inverse scaling law for grokking time. In six language models spanning two orders of magnitude in scale (GPT-2 Small/Medium/Large, LLaMA-3.1, Gemma-2, and Qwen2.5), subject-verb agreement is governed by a single, steerable axis that aligns across architectures. Flipping this axis inverts grammatical number throughout open-ended generation. For indirect object identification, a multi-step task, the same six models route computation through compact multi-dimensional cores at two sites, linked by a linear operator that transfers across model families. Together these results suggest that beneath the apparent complexity of trained transformers lies a simpler, shared computational structure, and that targeting invariants rather than parameterizations may offer a more tractable path to mechanistic understanding and control.

items.title: Reference-Dependent Utility Optimization for Goal-Oriented Communication Systems
items.summary: Traditional communication resource allocation optimizes operational metrics such as rate, latency, energy efficiency, and reliability. Motivated by goal-oriented semantic communication, we develop a generalized allocation framework that transforms operational rewards through reference-dependent user utilities and evaluates them via expected utility, cumulative prospect theory (CPT), or related decision criteria. The formulation separates operational rewards, user-side valuations, and system-level decision criteria under uncertainty. We characterize utilities incorporating QoS/service reference levels, deficit sensitivity, post-reference saturation, and loss aversion. Weighted sum-reward maximization, proportional fairness, $α$-fairness, and stochastic expected utility maximization emerge as exact special cases, while soft QoS-aware allocation follows from a deficit-penalty generalization. For deterministic orthogonal systems, we derive utility-weighted marginal-reward KKT conditions characterizing global optimality under concave composite objectives. For nonorthogonal and stochastic systems, we develop successive convex approximation (SCA) algorithms and establish stationary-point guarantees under explicit smooth and composite nonsmooth assumptions, including a CPT branch-stationarity result under eventual nondegenerate ordering identification. For globally solved penalized problems, we derive an $O(1/λ)$ bound on excess aggregate soft-QoS deficit, and on the deficit itself whenever a QoS-feasible allocation exists. Additionally, we establish an $O(1/ε^2)$ outer iteration bound for the smooth fixed-step SCA best-response residual. Numerical examples demonstrate how reference points, marginal utility slopes, channel quality, and resource budgets influence active users and allocation policies.

items.title: Brief introduction to post-quantum cryptography in industrial applications
items.summary: The development of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is directly motivated by the necessity to secure information in the face of the quantum threat. This paper provides an overview of recent developments relevant to PQC adoption across several industrial applications, including IoT, healthcare, civil and infrastructure engineering, and defense. We present a brief, self-contained overview of PQC and its market positioning. We perform implementation experiments on selected quantum-safe methods and quantify several aspects, such as the quantum resources required to break common cryptographic schemes, as well as the performance of the most well-known PQC algorithms. We also discuss the resistance of different PQC classes to quantum attacks and the status of PQC implementations in different programming languages. Finally, we present benchmark results on KEMs and signature algorithms to help select the appropriate algorithm for a specific application based on criteria such as algorithm performance, data lifetime, and level of data sensitivity.

items.title: Why Transformers Struggle with Distribution-Independent In-Context Learning
items.summary: With in-context learning (ICL), transformer models adapt to new tasks from illustrative examples at inference time without updating their parameters. A common interpretation is that transformers implement implicit learning algorithms in their forward pass. We test this interpretation and ICL capability under distribution shift in noiseless polynomial regression, where the context uniquely determines the target function. Models that are near-perfect in distribution exhibit sharp performance degradation under shifts in the input or target-function distribution. This behavior persists across polynomial degrees and multiple training interventions, and in higher-dimensional nonlinear regression. We identify two architectural mechanisms that explain this breakdown: output saturation at finite boundary values linked to final normalization, and attention concentration on a small subset of the context, which can limit context-dependent adaptation required for ICL. Controlled experiments, architectural ablations, targeted interventions, and theoretical analysis provide strong evidence for both mechanisms and their consequence: strong in-distribution ICL does not imply distribution-independent ICL, which calls for caution when using ICL instead of explicit retraining or adaptation under distribution shift.

items.title: Matching-Based Few-Shot Semantic Segmentation Models Are Interpretable by Design
items.summary: Few-Shot Semantic Segmentation (FSS) models achieve strong performance in segmenting novel classes with minimal labeled examples, yet their decision-making processes remain largely opaque. Explainable AI has matured on standard computer vision tasks, but not on FSS, where an explanation would tell a practitioner which support pixels the prediction rested on and which examples to provide next. We argue that matching-based FSS models are interpretable by design: their query-support similarity scores, once normalized and processed, attribute the prediction to individual support pixels. Our approach, Affinity Explainer (AffEx), makes this intrinsic interpretability explicit by extracting attribution maps directly from matching scores at multiple feature levels, without requiring gradients or external perturbations. We extend the standard causal metrics for evaluating explanations to the FSS domain and propose additional metrics to better capture the practical utility of explanations in few-shot scenarios. Experiments on two FSS benchmarks, covering seven architectures that range from classical matching-based models to recent pipelines built on vision foundation models (DINOv2/v3, SAM, SAM2) and a prototype-based head, show that AffEx outperforms adapted standard attribution methods at nearly every evaluation point, and that the gain comes from the matching mechanism itself. On pipelines whose segmentation stage transforms the matching output, the same evaluation doubles as a diagnostic of where the decision is made, and on the prototype-based head AffEx subsumes the prototype-style read-out as a special case. Qualitatively, the attribution maps expose how each architecture resolves the support set, and we show how they guide model diagnosis. Code is available at https://github.com/pasqualedem/AffinityExplainer.

items.title: AuDiR: Diagnosing Audio Reasoning with Rule and Percept Interventions
items.summary: Answer accuracy alone does not distinguish failures in acoustic perception, rule knowledge, and rule application. AuDiR (Audio Diagnostic Reasoning) examines these distinctions through controlled input interventions. Each item contains an audio clip, a multiple-choice question, a task-general rule, and a textual description of the acoustic observations needed to answer. Three conditions progressively supply the rule and observations; a fourth removes the audio while retaining the question and rule. The first correct diagnostic condition assigns an operational response label, without identifying a unique internal cause. The current benchmark contains 201 items in 18 families drawn from 9 sources, with answer references documented separately from percept extraction. In a preliminary evaluation of Gemini-3.8-flash, accuracy is 29.3% without supplied information, 31.3% with the rule, and 98.5% with the observations also supplied. No-audio accuracy is 23.9%, with a confidence interval containing the 25.0% chance rate. A family-level knowledge probe associates incomplete rule recall with larger gains from rule provision. These results show the benefit of supplying acoustic observations as text, while incomplete validation, possible recognition shortcuts, and non-monotonic responses limit stronger failure-attribution claims.

items.title: Update from Hell: Can Coding Agents Survive Hidden Breakage in Dependency Upgrades?
items.summary: Modern software systems rely heavily on third-party dependencies, but upgrading those dependencies remains a costly maintenance activity. Dependency upgrades do not always preserve the function signatures, type systems, APIs, or runtime semantics assumed by existing code. Consequently, developers often need to perform source code adaptations to accommodate dependency-induced changes. However, such code-level changes are often not explicitly communicated to project maintainers, posing a significant challenge to software reliability. Meanwhile, coding agents have emerged as a new form of software development tool and are increasingly adopted by developers due to their automation capabilities. In this paper, we introduce DEPBENCH, a benchmark consisting of 203 real-world dependency-upgrade tasks across five package ecosystems spanning five language communities, each involving hidden code-level changes that require source code adaptation. We evaluate mainstream coding agents on DEPBENCH. The best completed configuration solves only 104/203 tasks (51.2%), with substantial variation across agent harnesses, models, and ecosystems, highlighting an important gap between current agent capabilities and real-world software maintenance needs.

items.title: Perturb, Aggregate then Reconstruct: Consensus Aggregation and Fourier-Attended Multi-Decoders for Reconstruction-based Multi-View Anomaly Detection
items.summary: Multi-view anomaly detection is crucial for industrial inspection to identify defects hidden from single viewpoints. Yet, despite their strong success in single-view applications, reconstruction-based methods remain largely underexplored in multi-view settings. A key challenge in extending these methods lies in generating view-consistent pseudo-anomalies. To address this, we propose PAR, a reconstruction-based framework for enhanced multi-view anomaly detection. First, we introduce a feature perturbation strategy coupled with a consensus aggregation module that integrates these perturbed features across viewpoints to mitigate view-inconsistent anomalies and construct highly aligned pseudo-anomaly representations. Second, we employ a view-specialized multi-decoder architecture; by assigning a dedicated decoder to each view, we increase the model's representational complexity, enabling the generation of highly feasible, localized anomaly maps rather than less precise, view-agnostic reconstructions. Last, we incorporate Fourier attention into the decoders to emphasize global frequency-domain structures over local token evidence, effectively preventing identity mapping. Extensive experiments on the Real-IAD dataset demonstrate that PAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in sample-level, image-level, and pixel-level anomaly detection. Our code is available at https://github.com/SpatialAILab/PAR_mvad.

items.title: Learning to Select Sparse Linear Solvers with Convolutional Neural Networks
items.summary: We investigate convolutional-neural-network (CNN) based automatic solver selection for sparse linear systems, a problem of practical importance where solver performance varies dramatically with matrix sparsity structure. A CNN is trained to regress log timing ratios between candidate solvers using spy plot images of matrix nonzero structure as input, achieving strong prediction accuracy on both held-out SuiteSparse matrices and real-world matrices from high-performance simulation codes.

items.title: Generative sequence modeling for infinite memory processes via predictive states
items.summary: We consider estimating the one-step-ahead conditional distribution of a multivariate stochastic process. Many existing approaches rely on assumptions such as finite-range memory, sparsity, or additivity, which can be poorly suited to processes with long-range nonlinear interactions. However, without such structural assumptions, nonparametric estimation is challenging due to the curse of dimensionality. To address this challenge, we introduce a new estimator based on learning representations of the \emph{predictive states} of a stochastic process. We show that the statistical complexity of the estimation problem is determined by the dimension of this predictive state representation. Furthermore, we show that a $p$-dimensional predictive state space can be represented in a $2p+1$-dimensional feature space. Our results imply that faster convergence rates are achievable when the predictive state space is lower-dimensional, i.e., when the past history can be compressed into a lower-dimensional statistic that is sufficient for predicting the future. We establish theoretical convergence rate guarantees for an instantiation of our method based on deep neural network estimators. We implement our method in PyTorch and evaluate its performance on processes with infinite-range memory.

items.title: Single-Exponential Algorithms for Directed Feedback Vertex Set on Planar Digraphs
items.summary: We consider Directed Feedback Vertex Set on planar digraphs, parameterized by the solution size $k$. We give a randomized algorithm with one-sided error running in time $(2+\sqrt5)^k n^{O(1)}= 4.24^k n^{O(1)}$, and a deterministic algorithm running in time $8.04^k n^{O(1)}$. Both algorithms use polynomial space. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first single-exponential fixed-parameter algorithms for Directed Feedback Vertex Set on planar digraphs. This contrasts with general digraphs, where the best known algorithms run in time $2^{O(k\log k)}(n+m)$, and whether a $2^{o(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}$-time algorithm exists remains a major open problem. Our main tool is an exact Euler-type counting identity for plane digraphs. It shows that every small solution must carry a large share of the vertices whose in- and out-arcs alternate in the embedding, while solutions avoiding such vertices can be computed by reducing to Directed Feedback Arc Set, which is known to be solvable in polynomial time on planar digraphs via the Lucchesi-Younger theorem.

items.title: Mitigating Global Feature Collapse in Graph ODEs via Hysteretic Topology Evolution
items.summary: Graph neural ordinary differential equations provide continuous-time propagation on graphs, but their long-time behavior is largely determined by the asymptotic structure of the mixing operator. We show that diffusion-style Graph ODEs with positive irreducible mixing face a \emph{monostability trap}, where node features converge to a rank-one consensus subspace. This reveals a structural limitation of positive diffusion-style continuous graph propagation: within this consensus class, exact long-time avoidance requires changing the effective support; otherwise, smooth suppression should be interpreted as finite-horizon or metastable mitigation. We address this by introducing a \emph{hysteretic mechanism} for topology evolution, where candidate edges carry latent bistable potentials in a double-well landscape. A node-feature-conditioned force field evolves these potentials, and a smooth sigmoid gate converts them into differentiable propagation weights. We prove global consensus under the stated mixing assumptions and block-wise consensus under idealised support separation. For consensus-form dynamics, we further establish a finite-horizon perturbation bound under small cross-block leakage, and empirically evaluate the resulting nonlinear HGODE on node- and graph-level benchmarks.

items.title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
items.summary: Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the question: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? We place mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We introduce the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked examples that reproduce key findings from surveyed methods, allowing readers to build intuition through hands-on experimentation.

items.title: FIELDS: Face reconstruction with accurate Inference of Expression using Learning with Direct Supervision
items.summary: Monocular 3D face reconstruction estimates the parameters of a 3D morphable face model (3DMM) from a single image, providing an explicit geometric representation for facial expression analysis. Owing to the scarcity of paired 2D images and 3D facial meshes, most methods are trained in a self-supervised manner by rendering the predicted face and minimizing image-level reconstruction losses, such as photometric and landmark errors, against the input image. However, these losses enforce visual alignment but do not ensure that the predicted parameters preserve affective information. Recent methods add image-level emotion consistency loss, but it can be satisfied by exaggerating facial deformations. To address these issues, we propose FIELDS (Face reconstruction with accurate Inference of Expression using Learning with Direct Supervision), which learns affect-informative expression representations in the FLAME parameter space. Specifically, FIELDS augments 2D self-supervised reconstruction with scan-derived expression anchoring and a parameter-space emotion loss. During training, scan-fitted targets directly constrain expression-related FLAME parameters to discourage exaggerated deformations, while a jointly trained emotion head uses discrete emotion and continuous valence--arousal annotations to make the predicted parameters informative for affect analysis. Experiments show that FIELDS improves affective utility from the predicted parameters in both within- and cross-dataset settings. Notably, it also achieves lower reconstruction errors overall and across most facial regions than the comparison baselines under both rigid and similarity alignment.

items.title: Qualiaphobic artificial neural networks (and why to build them)
items.summary: This paper introduces qualiaphobic AI: artificial neural network architectures that are hostile to theories of consciousness. I show that qualiaphobia can be well-justified by knowledge about theories of consciousness, like when such theories are trivial or unfalsifiable or contradicted by overwhelming scientific evidence. It can also be justified by how theories of consciousness must be grounded in phenomenology, as well as how current popular theories of consciousness are applied to AI. I identify and explore three convergent ways of engineering qualiaphobia that would minimize the potential for artificial consciousness. These include making AI architectures as close as possible to "anchor points" of systems with minimal potential for consciousness, fragmenting any potential phenomenology AI might have, and designing artificial neural networks in a way adversarial to popular theories of consciousness. In particular, I develop one "anchor point" of minimal potential for consciousness: systems where only behaviorist theories of consciousness can apply, and I propose qualiaphobic transformations that move existing artificial neural networks toward such systems. Additionally, I develop an account of how AIs can form justified beliefs about their own non-consciousness (or minimal potential for consciousness) and expand on how this knowledge would change their behavior. Most critically, I begin with why this research is important: qualiaphobic AI has epistemic properties that make it far better aligned with human civilization. Since consciousness is central to moral value, a world in which AIs are non-conscious ensures it is always morally correct for AI to assist and serve humanity, rather than pursue its own ends.

items.title: ADZE 2.0: rarefaction estimates of allelic richness and private allelic richness for whole-genome
items.summary: Allelic richness and private allelic richness describe how alleles are distributed across populations, but both depend strongly on sample size. Rarefaction makes them comparable by computing the expected number of alleles in subsamples of a common size, and ADZE implemented this approach and an extension to alleles shared only by a set of populations. However, ADZE was developed for microsatellite data and cannot read sequencing data in variant call format (VCF). Here we present ADZE 2.0, which reads VCF, computes each statistic genome-wide or in genomic windows, and can treat blocks of phased SNPs as haplotype alleles. We also implement improved memory handling and multi-threading support. ADZE 2.0 reproduces the ADZE 1.0 estimates for human microsatellite data exactly. On chromosome 22 of the high-coverage 1000 Genomes Project data, private allelic richness for all 325 population pairs took 4.4 minutes on 32 threads. ADZE 2.0 is available at https://github.com/szpiech/ADZE.

items.title: PMO-Dock: Benchmarking Docking, Specificity, and Generalization in Molecular Optimization
items.summary: The Practical Molecular Optimization (PMO) benchmark standardized evaluation in molecular optimization, but it is built on simple property-based oracles that do not capture structure-based drug design. As the field has moved to docking-based objectives, evaluation practice has become unstandardized, and different methods report results on different docking tasks, often without a shared protocol for fair comparison or sample-efficiency constraints. To address this, we introduce Practical Molecular Optimization for Docking (PMO-Dock), a benchmark and protocol for docking-based optimization consisting of 25 tasks covering hit generation, lead optimization, and a new specificity task requiring strong on-target binding while penalizing off-target interactions. The protocol separates model development from final evaluation: validation tasks are used for hyperparameter tuning, and test tasks are held out for final evaluation and are not used during development. Evaluation on the test tasks is done under a strict oracle budget to reflect realistic drug-discovery settings. We benchmark four diverse high-performing methods spanning different optimization paradigms, Saturn (reinforcement learning), GenMol (discrete diffusion), Genetic-guided GFlowNet, and ChemLlama (LLM-based evolutionary search). Our results show no universally best method across tasks, additional analyses of hyperparameter transfer (cross-task and cross-category) and sensitivity show that transfer is often limited and varies by method, motivating method-dependent selection strategies. This benchmark provides a concrete standard for evaluating generalization to unseen tasks and sample efficiency under a limited test-time oracle budget.

items.title: On Agentic Behavioral Modeling
items.summary: Integrating theoretical neuroscience, decision theory, and probabilistic inference offers a promising route to understanding human cognition, yet concrete methodological bridges between agentic artificial intelligence (AI) models and behavioral data analysis remain formally underdeveloped. We advance this synthesis within the framework of agentic behavioral modeling (ABM), which treats artificial agents as latent, generative hypotheses about cognitive mechanisms and evaluates them by their statistical adequacy in explaining human behavior. After outlining its conceptual foundations, we apply the framework to two minimal laboratory paradigms: a binary perceptual contrast-discrimination task and a symmetric two-armed bandit learning task. We formalize each task-agent-data system as a joint probability model, derive explicit conditional log-likelihoods for behavioral inference, validate different model variants using model and parameter recovery simulations, and evaluate them in light of empirical data. Using these minimal examples, we provide a novel agent-centric interpretation of the psychometric function, derive optimal policies for both tasks under explicit assumptions on sensory bias and post-decision noise, and show that the Bayesian posterior expectation and induced decisions admit an equivalent adaptive-rate Rescorla-Wagner representation in the symmetric bandit task. More broadly, this work may serve as a conceptual and practical foundation for applying ABM to cognitive behavioral science.

items.title: Clinical predictions using artificial intelligence in neurosurgery and its subspecialties: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Artificial intelligence models for clinical prediction are proliferating across neurosurgery, but their aggregate discriminative performance, distribution along the care pathway and methodological quality are unclear. We systematically reviewed and meta-analysed these studies in neurosurgery and its subspecialities along with their risk of bias appraisal. We performed a PRISMA search for peer-reviewed original studies using AI to predict a clinical outcome in neurosurgical populations. Metrics were pooled using random effects modelling. Each study was classified as diagnostic, prognostic or forecasting and was assigned an evidence level. Clinical prediction task sub-stratification analysis was performed. Risk-of-bias was assessed using PROBAST. 1063 studies were included. Across 451 studies reporting AUC, pooled discrimination was 0.86, ranging from 0.84 (spine) to 0.87 (neuro-oncology), with extreme heterogeneity. Performance varied by clinical pathway stage, highest for diagnosis, grading and molecular tasks and lowest for post-operative tasks. Only 51 studies were using prospective data with external validation, whereas 619 rested on internal validation alone or no validation. 89 percent studies were at high risk-of-bias, driven by the analysis domain. AI models report high performance across all the neurosurgical subspecialities, concordant across AUC, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity and robust to risk-of-bias stratification. Performance is highest for imaging-anchored diagnostic tasks and lowest at decision-facing post-operative stage. However, the literature is dominated by optimism-prone, internally-validated and poorly calibrated models with extreme heterogeneity. External validation, calibration analysis and reporting guidelines adherence remain prerequisites for clinical adoption.

items.title: Trajectory Inference of Human Aging from Cross-Sectional DNA Methylation Data
items.summary: DNA methylation (DNAm) serves as one of the most robust molecular biomarkers of biological aging. While conventional epigenetic clocks accurately predict chronological age from high-dimensional CpG profiles, they treat aging as a static regression task, meaning they can only output a single score rather than simulating how an entire profile continuously changes over time. To reconstruct these continuous dynamics, we frame lifelong human epigenetic aging as a trajectory inference problem across discrete age snapshots derived from widely available cross-sectional data. We introduce a two-stage computational pipeline: first, an age-regularized Variational Autoencoder (VAE) maps high-dimensional CpG profiles onto a chronologically ordered latent manifold while preserving a generative decoder bridge back to the original methylation space. Second, we model the continuous movement across this latent space via Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport (RUOT) that unifies deterministic drift, random diffusion, and non-conservative mass changes.
