By using low-cost screening to shrink the search space, constructing edge-specific candidate conditioning sets from local graph structure, and invoking FMCIT only in a budget-controlled refinement stage, GPC-FMCIT reduces both the deployment cost of individual nonlinear CI queries and the overall query complexity. On synthetic nonlinear structural equation models, GPC-FMCIT improves CPDAG recovery over PC-stable baselines and requires far fewer FMCIT queries than direct FMCIT-based PC search, and on hESC gene-expression data it yields smaller graphs than PC/FisherZ in a descriptive comparison. Overall, our results suggest that, through the joint design of reusable conditional resampling and controlled graph search, generative nonlinear CI testing can become a practical component of PC-style causal discovery.

items.title: When the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers (and the Same Answer Isn't Always Right): A Taxonomy of Failure Mechanisms, Testing, and Mitigation Strategies for LLM-Assisted Evidence Synthesis Read-and-Evaluate Tasks
items.summary: LLM read-and-evaluate tasks include study screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and critical appraisal in the evidence synthesis field. These task differ in the amount of LLM interpretation they require. Some tasks involve retrieving relatively simple information, such as an author name, sample size, or publication year. Others require the LLM to read source material, interpret it against predefined criteria, and make a judgement. Researchers should assess whether LLM judgements are accurate, supported by appropriate source evidence, and reproducible under specified conditions. A correct judgement does not necessarily indicate that the underlying evaluation process is reliable. We developed a taxonomy for identifying mechanisms that may compromise these properties and for informing the selection and reporting of appropriate evaluation methods. The taxonomy outlines potential ways that LLM judgments from read-and-evaluate tasks can fail, called TRAILS (Taxonomy of Reliability And Instability in LLM-assisted evidence Synthesis). The TRAILS taxonomy addresses two complementary questions. First, what mechanisms can cause the same read-and-evaluate task to produce different judgements across repeated LLM runs? Second, what mechanisms can systematically affect the judgement or required output in a way that is not apparent from the judgement itself? This study presents 38 mechanisms and identifies the deployment settings in which each can operate, approaches for testing them, and mitigation strategies. We also show why repeatability or accuracy does not rule out a hidden judgement failure and why human evaluation should assess whether a judgement is grounded in the supplied evidence, independent of inappropriate external influence, and produced through a process that can be examined and verified.

items.title: Private Sparse Sketches for Linear Regression
items.summary: Sketching compresses a large dataset into a smaller summary, allowing regression on the sketch to approximate the full-data objective. A sketch released under differential privacy can be reused with any non-private regression solver, any number of times, without further privacy loss. We study private sparse sketches for $\ell_2$ and $\ell_1$ regression. We first prove lower bounds on the noise required by common sparse sketches for both problems when the sketching matrix is public. Since regression on a sketch can be solved without revealing the sketching matrix, we construct sketches whose randomness is kept secret. Hiding how individual records enter the sketch provides an additional source of privacy, allowing less noise for the same privacy guarantee. We prove differential privacy guarantees for both constructions, and experiments on real datasets show improved utility over public-sketch baselines.

items.title: Statopia: A Prover--Library Ecosystem for Automated Formalization and Proof Discovery in Statistics
items.summary: Theoretical results in statistics and machine learning rest on long, technically delicate proofs, and fluent arguments generated by large language models are not necessarily correct. Automated formalization makes such arguments mechanically checkable, and automated proving goes further by discovering machine-checked proofs for statements whose proofs are incomplete or missing altogether. Both require reconstructing assumptions from source materials, accessing specialized mathematical infrastructure and managing long proof developments. We present Statopia, an ecosystem that jointly develops Statopia Prover, an independent agent specialized for formalizing and proving results in statistics and machine learning, and Statlib, a Lean~4 library built with the prover and organized for automated use. The prover controls its own execution without relying on external coding agents. It is built for formal proof discovery and checking existing proofs. A natural-language proof, when available, guides its search but is not required: from a statement alone, the prover develops the argument itself and constructs a Lean proof. Its workflow integrates source preparation, statement review, library supported planning and proof construction. Dynamic proof dependency graphs and task groups support parallel, resumable proof development. Statlib's shared definitions and theorem interfaces are organized for retrieval and composition by agents, and its coverage of statistics keeps expanding. Verified results and usage feedback from the prover inform reviewed library updates, so that proof development drives this expansion. A cross-platform application provides an interactive workspace for uploading source files and running tasks locally or in the cloud.

items.title: Compute-Optimal Pretrain--Fine-tune in Ridge Gradient Descent
items.summary: Pretraining followed by fine-tuning introduces a compute-allocation problem: under a fixed training budget, compute spent improving the upstream objective reduces the compute available for downstream adaptation. Despite its practical importance, this trade-off is not yet well understood theoretically, even in simple models. In this paper, we cast this allocation as a compute-split problem under a two-stage pretrain--fine-tune procedure with fixed total optimisation budget, using regularised least squares trained by gradient descent as a tractable setting. We characterise the optimal split under data-dependent evaluation geometries induced by the fine-tuning problem. Our results show that the allocation depends on how pretraining directions affect fine-tuning predictions and how fine-tuning shifts are seen through downstream data geometry. In particular, the relevant quantities are determined by prediction-relevant spectral components of the pretraining and fine-tuning empirical covariances. Technically, the analysis relies on a basis-invariant, eigenspace-level spectral decomposition, together with perturbative control of the non-commuting pretraining and fine-tuning dynamics.

items.title: Minimax Optimal Early-Stopped Gradient Descent for Gaussian Mixture Classification
items.summary: In overparameterised classification, training data can be linearly separable even when the underlying distribution is not. In this setting, gradient descent (GD) on the logistic loss diverges in norm while converging in direction to a max-margin interpolating classifier, whose implicit bias can be statistically suboptimal. In this work, we show that early stopping can overcome this suboptimality: in a Gaussian mixture model with label-flipping noise, GD stopped at an appropriate oracle time achieves minimax-optimal excess zero-one risk for covariance spectra with fast and continuous decay, including polynomial and exponential spectral decays. Our analysis combines a sharp upper bound for the early-stopped iterate with a matching statistical lower bound over arbitrary classifiers, yielding optimal rates that are validated by experiments. A central technical contribution is a new calibration result that converts excess logistic risk into excess zero-one risk; it handles the model misspecification induced by the label-flipping noise, and removes the square-root rate in standard bounds. We also establish a lower bound for linear interpolators, showing that interpolation can require exponentially more samples than early stopping to achieve the same excess risk.

items.title: From matrix inversion to constraints: provably tighter confidence regions for importance weights in label shift
items.summary: Importance weights are essential in domain adaptation under label shift, yet their utility is often undermined by the finite sample uncertainty associated with their estimation. Existing methods typically analyze this uncertainty through Gaussian elimination on interval-valued linear systems, which leads to overly conservative confidence regions and inefficient downstream applications. We propose a paradigm shift from inversion-based inference to a direct matrix constraint framework. We use this framework to define a joint confidence region and extract marginal intervals via linear programming, deriving provably tighter bounds for importance weights while maintaining exact finite-sample validity. Furthermore, we analyze the confidence region's geometry and provide the theoretical results for its diameter bounds. Evaluated across text, image, multimodal benchmarks, including AGNews, MNIST, CIFAR-10, N24News, and a real-world autonomous driving dataset, nuImages, our approach consistently yields shorter confidence intervals and smaller prediction sets than inversion-based methods.

items.title: Guaranteed Noisy CP Tensor Recovery via Riemannian Optimization on the Segre Manifold
items.summary: Recovering a low-CP-rank tensor from noisy linear measurements is a central challenge in high-dimensional data analysis, with applications spanning tensor PCA, scalar-on-tensor regression, tensor-on-tensor regression, and beyond. We exploit the intrinsic geometry of rank-one tensors by casting the recovery task as an optimization problem over the Segre manifold, the smooth Riemannian manifold of rank-one tensors. This geometric viewpoint yields two powerful algorithms: Riemannian Gradient Descent (RGD) and Riemannian Gauss-Newton (RGN), each of which preserves feasibility at every iteration. Under mild noise assumptions, we prove that RGD converges at a local linear rate, while RGN exhibits an initial local quadratic phase followed by linear refinement to the statistical error. Extensive synthetic experiments validate these convergence guarantees and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our methods.

items.title: Covariate-Adjusted Deep Causal Learning for Heterogeneous Panel Data Models
items.summary: This paper studies the task of estimating heterogeneous treatment effects in causal panel data models with covariate effects. We propose a novel Covariate-Adjusted Deep Causal Learning (CoDEAL) framework that cohesively deals with the underlying heterogeneity and nonlinearity of both panel units and covariate effects. CoDEAL integrates nonlinear covariate effect components (parameterized by a feed-forward neural network) with nonlinear factor structures (modeled by a multi-output autoencoder) to form a heterogeneous causal panel model. The nonlinear covariate component flexibly captures complex covariate influences on outcomes, and the nonlinear factor decomposition enables CoDEAL to effectively capture both cross-sectional and temporal dependencies inherent in the data panel. This latent structural information is subsequently integrated into a customized matrix completion algorithm, thereby facilitating more accurate counterfactual imputation. Moreover, the use of a multi-output autoencoder explicitly accounts for heterogeneity across units and enhances the model interpretability of the latent factors. We establish theoretical guarantees on the convergence of the estimated counterfactuals and demonstrate the compelling performance of the proposed method using extensive simulation studies and real-world data applications.

items.title: Cause-specific structural nested cumulative survival time models for competing risks, with application to the Antibody Mediated Prevention trials
items.summary: The Antibody Mediated Prevention (AMP) trials randomized participants to VRC01, a broadly neutralizing antibody, or placebo; the primary analysis estimated prevention efficacy against overall HIV-1 acquisition and against acquisition of VRC01-sensitive strains. All participants were offered daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and PrEP uptake in a trial may differ substantially from uptake in other settings. It is therefore of interest to estimate the effect of oral PrEP on acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive strains, as well as the counterfactual cumulative incidence of such acquisition under no or limited PrEP uptake. To address these questions, we extend the structural nested cumulative survival time model (SNCSTM), a causal survival model for time-varying treatments, to a cause-specific version. We show that the cause-specific SNCSTM is closely related to the Fine--Gray subdistribution hazard model, and we study identification under two frameworks. The first, based on sequential ignorability, applies when the time-varying treatment is distinct from the randomized assignment, as with oral PrEP use in AMP. The second, based on an instrumental variable, applies when the time-varying treatment represents compliance with the randomized assignment, and it accommodates unmeasured confounding between the time-varying treatment and event time. Under both frameworks, we propose consistent and asymptotically normal estimators of the structural parameters. We apply the methods to HVTN 704/HPTN 085, one of the two AMP trials, to estimate the effects of oral PrEP use and of VRC01 infusions administered every 8 weeks on acquisition of VRC01-sensitive and VRC01-insensitive HIV-1 strains. We also estimate the counterfactual strain-specific cumulative incidence curves under no oral PrEP use and under full adherence to the scheduled VRC01 infusions.

items.title: A weighted edge-count two-sample test for multivariate and object data
items.summary: Two-sample tests for multivariate data and non-Euclidean data are widely used in many fields. Parametric tests are mostly restrained to certain types of data that meets the assumptions of the parametric models. In this paper, we study a nonparametric testing procedure that utilizes graphs representing the similarity among observations. It can be applied to any data types as long as an informative similarity measure on the sample space can be defined. The classic test based on a similarity graph has a problem when the two sample sizes are different. We solve the problem by applying appropriate weights to different components of the classic test statistic. The new test exhibits substantial power gains in simulation studies. Its asymptotic permutation null distribution is derived and shown to work well under finite samples, facilitating its application to large datasets. The new test is illustrated through an analysis on a real dataset of network data.

items.title: Choosing the basis to compare multivariate distributions: bases, copulas and optimal transport
items.summary: We study the choice of an orthonormal basis for comparing two probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ through their one-dimensional projections. We show that two distributions have a common copula in a given basis if and only if their optimal transport can be performed componentwise along the directions of that basis. This motivates the notion of componentwise related distributions and leads to a structural analysis of the bases in which such a representation is possible. In particular, we establish an essential uniqueness result for the corresponding orthogonal decomposition and characterize elliptical families through equality in Gelbrich's bound within location-scatter families. For general distributions, we consider the maximum, over all orthonormal bases, of the sum of the squared quadratic Wasserstein distances between the corresponding one-dimensional projections. We prove that the resulting quantity is a metric, induces the same topology as the quadratic Wasserstein distance, and lies between the Gelbrich and Wasserstein distances, with equality in the upper bound precisely for component-wise related distributions. We also derive first-order conditions for an optimal basis and establish stability and almost-sure consistency of empirical optimal bases. Simulations and examples illustrate the computational feasibility and competitive performance of the proposed procedures and suggest new applications of copulas to multivariate distributional comparisons.

items.title: Transformers Provably Implement In-Context Reinforcement Learning with Policy Improvement
items.summary: We investigate the ability of transformers to perform in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL), where a model must infer and execute learning algorithms from trajectory data without parameter updates. We show that a linear self-attention transformer block can provably implement policy-improvement methods, including semi-gradient SARSA and actor-critic, via explicit parameter constructions. Beyond existence, we design a teacher-mimicking training procedure, analyze its gradient-flow dynamics, and establish the first convergence guarantee in the ICRL literature: under suitable richness conditions on the training MDP distribution, gradient flow converges locally and exponentially to an optimal parameter manifold corresponding to the desired RL update. Empirically, training transformers on randomly generated tabular MDPs confirms these predictions: the learned models recover the parameter structure of our explicit constructions and, when deployed on unseen MDPs, deliver strong in-context control performance. Together, these results illuminate how transformer architectures internalize and execute classical reinforcement learning algorithms in context, bridging mechanistic understanding and training dynamics in ICRL.

items.title: Toward a theory of Evaluability
items.summary: Machine learning models, particularly large foundation models, are increasingly evaluated along multiple axes that are relevant for their usage. In addition to accuracy measures appropriate for the specific task of interest, measures capturing safety, calibration and fairness properties are often of interest. The classical approach to these problems assumes that the test set has been held out from the training process, an assumption that is increasingly harder to justify for large foundation models. In this work, we formalize a notion of evaluability without this assumption, and ask if it is feasible to evaluate black-box models in settings where our test samples may have been used during training. We study this problem under different settings, capturing different levels of access to the model. We first study the natural setting, where the evaluator only looks at the output of the model on the test set. We fully characterize the class of distributions where accurate evaluation is possible, and show tight upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity of evaluation. Our results show that black-box evaluation in this setup is feasible if and only if the distribution is close to being small support. We then consider evaluation algorithms that can query the model on additional inputs and demonstrate connections to self-correctors studied in program testing. Using these, we show that a small amount of query access can increase the power of the evaluator for natural distributions and concept classes.

items.title: Towards Reliable LLM Evaluation: Correcting the Winner's Curse in Adaptive Benchmarking
items.summary: Adaptive prompt and program search makes LLM evaluation selection-sensitive. Once benchmark items are reused inside tuning, the observed winner's score need not estimate the fresh-data performance of the full tune-then-deploy procedure. We study inference for this procedure-level target under explicit tuning budgets. We propose SIREN, a selection-aware repeated-split reporting protocol that freezes the post-search shortlist, separates splitwise selection from held-out evaluation, and uses an item-level Gaussian multiplier bootstrap for uncertainty quantification. In a fixed-shortlist regime with smooth stabilized selection, the estimator admits a first-order item-level representation, and the bootstrap yields valid simultaneous inference on a finite budget grid. This supports confidence intervals for procedure-performance curves and pre-specified equal-budget and cross-budget comparisons. Controlled simulations and MMLU-Pro tuning experiments show that winner-based reporting can be optimistic and can change deployment conclusions, while SIREN remains close to the finite-sample reporting target.

items.title: Deep Gaussian Processes on Directed Acyclic Graphs
items.summary: Many real-world processes can be represented as compositions of functions along a directed acyclic graph (DAG). In causal modelling, these correspond to the underlying mechanisms; in engineering, to multiple fidelity levels; and in gene-regulatory networks, to transcription factors. These functions are partially observed across the DAG, with noisy and heterogeneously sampled measurements, posing significant challenges for reconstruction, uncertainty propagation, and inference. To tackle these challenges, we place priors over functions and naturally arrive at Deep Gaussian Processes over DAGs. We theoretically study their prior-collapse behaviour and the effect of graph topology and intermediate observations on the preservation of information. We obtain almost-sure lower bounds on the asymptotic frequency of depths at which the distinction between inputs is preserved, identify broad kernel classes for which these hold, and prove an observation by \citep{dunlop2018} on the role of input connections. We offer a structured variational approximation that retains graph dependencies, preserves compositional uncertainty, and captures the explaining-away behaviour of colliders. Finally, we empirically validate our theory and methodology at scale and under DAG misspecification. We then model a latent-collider DAG, a protein signalling network, and a multi-fidelity \mbox{heavy-ion} collision emulation task, attaining state-of-the-art performance while recovering low-fidelity contributions and yielding interpretability over the simulator hierarchy.

items.title: Persistent-Transient Policy Evaluation for Markov Chains via Minimal Peripheral Quotients
items.summary: We study fixed-policy evaluation for finite Markov chains that may be reducible and periodic. Classical evaluation methods with gain and bias decomposition are not always diagnostic: the gain records only invariant Cesàro averages, while persistent phase-dependent behavior is absorbed into the bias together with genuinely transient effects. We identify the real peripheral invariant subspace $\mathcal{K}(P)$ of the transition matrix $P$ as the source of this ambiguity. Quotienting by $\mathcal{K}(P)$ is the minimal exact quotient that removes all non-decaying modes and makes the remaining dynamics strictly stable. After choosing a gauge projection $Π$ with kernel $\mathcal{K}(P)$, the reward admits a unique decomposition $r = g_Π^\star + (I-P)v_Π^\star$, where $g_Π^\star$ is a persistent regime profile and $v_Π^\star$ is a gauge-fixed transient component. An exact comparison with classical normalized gain and bias shows that the new pair reallocates the same information into a persistent profile and a gauge-fixed representative of the transient quotient. This decomposition reconstructs finite-horizon returns, recovers statewise average reward, admits a transient-cost interpretation, and yields a stable estimator under a generative model.

items.title: Inference for Non-Probability Samples Using Error-Prone Auxiliary Information
items.summary: Non-probability samples are a potential source of rich information for making statistical inferences. However, these datasets often suffer from quality issues, in particular selection bias. The data from a non-probability sample may be combined with auxiliary information from the population or from a reference probability sample to address this bias. The auxiliary information present on these other sources is generally considered to be error-free, however this is not always the case. In this paper, we present a novel semiparametric approach to estimate the participation probabilities of units on a non-probability sample while accounting for error-prone auxiliary information in the reference data source. The approach combines a logistic regression model for the participation probabilities with a nonparametric kernel regression model for the error-prone auxiliary variables. Through a simulation study and real-world data analysis we show that our proposed approach effectively mitigates selection bias and accounts for measurement error, while estimates from methods which ignore the measurement error still exhibit some bias. The consistency of the Inverse Probability Weighted estimator produced using the participation probabilities derived from our approach is demonstrated, and a bootstrap variance approach for the estimator is described.

items.title: Estimation and Inference for Causal Explainability
items.summary: Understanding how much each variable contributes to an outcome is a central question across disciplines. A causal view of explainability is favorable for its ability in uncovering underlying mechanisms and generalizing to new contexts. Based on a family of causal explainability quantities, we develop methods for their estimation and inference. In particular, we construct a one-step correction estimator using semi-parametric efficiency theory, which explicitly leverages the independence structure of variables to reduce the asymptotic variance. For a null hypothesis on the boundary, i.e., zero explainability, we show its equivalence to Fisher's sharp null, which motivates a randomization-based inference procedure. Finally, we illustrate the empirical efficacy of our approach through simulations as well as an immigration experiment dataset, where we investigate how features and their interactions shape public opinion toward admitting immigrants.

items.title: JUBILEE: A Benchmark Environment for Off-Policy Evaluation in Debt Collections
items.summary: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value a candidate decision policy would achieve, using only data logged by the policy already in production. In debt collections, unrecorded factors can influence both actions and outcomes. This paper presents JUBILEE, a benchmark environment built around a debt-collections simulator that generates million-loan panels with competing risks, rare recovery events, and hidden factors driving both outcomes and assignment. The evaluation includes an 80-run comparison of tabular and gradient-boosted estimators under two synthetic outcome mechanisms and a 190-run parameter grid. Independent policy simulations provide reference values with estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty for a synthetic reward score and for simulated cash. With hidden factors influencing action assignment, several tabular methods agree closely while underestimating the field-visit policy's score, an error that also appears with boosted models. Intervals from tabular doubly robust estimation usually contain the reference without hidden assignment dependence but mostly miss it when that dependence is present. Estimates from randomized decisions do not show the same large error, although their limited precision leaves policy choice uncertain. The decision consequences depend on how policy value is defined. The field-visit policy ranks last under the score and first under simulated cash, which excludes channel costs. Under cash, log-based estimators miss this best candidate in nearly every run with hidden assignment dependence in the paired study. JUBILEE supports reproducible study of these failure modes under specified collections mechanisms.

items.title: High-Dimensional Markov-Switching Ordinary Differential Processes
items.summary: Complex systems often evolve in continuous time but are observed only at discrete time points with measurement noise. When the interactions can change across unobserved states, recovering both the state transitions and the differential equations is important for mechanistic insight and for identifying time-varying directed graphs. However, this recovery is challenging in high dimensions. In this paper, we study estimation and graph recovery for high-dimensional Markov-switching ordinary differential equation models from noisy discrete observations. We model the switching between states by a latent continuous-time Markov chain, and within each state the drift is a sparse additive function with unknown nonlinear components. We approximate each component by a finite basis expansion and estimate the parameters under group sparsity. Our procedure estimates the latent trajectories by wavelet smoothing and then runs a penalized surrogate expectation-maximization algorithm. Under stationarity and geometric $β$-mixing, given a sufficiently accurate estimated trajectory and other local regularity conditions, we show that the algorithm converges geometrically to a neighborhood of the true parameters. Finally, in an application to resting-state fMRI data, the procedure identifies multiple connectivity states, whose occupation times we compare descriptively between the children with combined-type ADHD and the typically developing children used in the fit.

items.title: Bayesian transfer for offline Q-learning with multi-task Gaussian processes
items.summary: Offline reinforcement learning can benefit from data collected in related tasks, yet indiscriminate knowledge transfer may lead to negative transfer under task mismatch and limited target-data coverage. We propose a target-aware Bayesian transfer framework for offline Q-learning based on multi-task Gaussian processes that jointly model task-specific Q-functions. Source tasks are assessed using target predictive evidence and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), while posterior uncertainty and behavior-supported action sets guide conservative Bellman updates and policy extraction. To account for the dependence induced by Bellman bootstrapping, we distinguish Bellman innovations from bootstrap errors and establish stability and predictive source-selection results under explicit regularity conditions. We further derive selection-adaptive posterior contraction and offline policy-performance bounds, identifying the structural conditions under which source information can be pooled to achieve minimax-optimal rates in a shared-function Gaussian sequence experiment. Simulation studies with heterogeneous source tasks demonstrate improved target Q-function estimation and reduced material negative transfer compared with indiscriminate source pooling. An application to human decision-making data further shows higher average expected immediate payoff than both target-only learning and matched-size random source selection. These results highlight the benefits of combining target-aware source selection with uncertainty-aware conservative learning for reliable and sample-efficient offline reinforcement learning.

items.title: Overlap-Excluded Estimation of Participation Probabilities for Non-Probability Samples
items.summary: Correction of selection bias is crucial for making valid statistical inferences about a finite population using non-probability datasets. Various approaches have been proposed to correct this bias and obtain estimates of finite population quantities such as means and totals. The quasi-randomisation approaches, in particular, aim to estimate a `participation probability' for units in the non-probability dataset. These probabilities are then applied in an inverse probability weighting scheme to produce population estimates. In this paper, we propose to estimate the participation probabilities for the non-probability sample by combining the non-probability sample with an available probability sample, while excluding the overlapping units in the probability sample. When the true overlap cannot be determined, we show how the Expectation-Maximization method can be used to simultaneously estimate the overlap and the participation probabilities. We compare the performance of our approach against several alternative methods theoretically and in an empirical context, and demonstrate the efficiency gains that are possible when the overlapping probability sample is excluded.

items.title: Structure-Adaptive Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Kernel Methods
items.summary: We study conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimation from observational data in regimes with potentially weak overlap, when the nuisance response functions lie in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), but the contrast function is structurally simpler. We consider three forms of such simplicity: (i) membership in a lower-complexity RKHS with faster eigenvalue decay, (ii) a source condition relative to the nuisance kernel, or (iii) dependence on a known low-dimensional covariate representation. We develop a unified two-stage kernel ridge regression procedure that remains valid under weak overlap and attains minimax rates determined by the complexity of the contrast function. The procedure avoids propensity-score estimation and separate nuisance convergence-rate assumptions. We also show that a simple model-selection step over candidate contrast spaces and regularization levels satisfies an oracle inequality, enabling adaptation to unknown CATE regularity.

items.title: A Unified Framework for Robust Blinded Sample Size Re-estimation Based on Nuisance Parameters
items.summary: Blinded sample size re-estimation aims to mitigate uncertainty in nuisance parameters at the design stage while preserving the integrity of the trial. It allows the required sample size to be updated without revealing treatment assignments and thereby reduces the risk of an inappropriate sample size. Although numerous procedures have been proposed for different outcome types, a unified framework is still lacking. We therefore develop a general framework for blinded sample size re-estimation based on nuisance parameters. Within this general framework, we develop robust methods to reduce the influence of extreme observations. The proposed framework combines asymptotically linear estimators for the parameter of interest with robust Z-estimators for nuisance parameters, thereby unifying a broad class of existing procedures through different choices of estimating functions. We also propose a general principle for constructing nuisance parameters that can be estimated from blinded data. The proposed framework is supported by asymptotic theory showing that the type I error rate converges to the nominal level under regularity conditions. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method maintains reliable type I error control across a range of settings, including contaminated data and small pilot sample sizes. Compared with existing blinded and unblinded methods, the proposed framework is more flexible and less sensitive to outliers. A clinical trial application illustrates its practical utility.

items.title: Causal Inference for All: Marginal Estimands for Outcomes Truncated by Death
items.summary: In longitudinal studies, outcomes of interest are often truncated by death, meaning that they are only observed or well-defined conditional on intercurrent events such as survival. Existing strategies face a trade-off: causally interpretable estimands, such as survivor average causal effects, target a latent subgroup, whereas while-alive and composite summaries apply to the full population but are difficult to interpret as causal effects on the non-mortality outcome. We address these challenges by introducing methodology for a new set of estimands that (i) concern the entire population, (ii) remain causally interpretable, and (iii) leverage the longitudinal data commonly available in studies with outcomes truncated by death. The set of estimands includes single-world marginal separable effects that generalize conditional separable effects to full-population summaries. We develop identification and estimation results for these estimands and apply the methodology in a reanalysis of a prostate cancer trial, highlighting how different estimands can yield different treatment conclusions.

items.title: Forecasting Replication Study Results from Meta-Analyses
items.summary: Multisite replication projects often rely on published meta-analyses to plan their sample sizes, but meta-analyses tend to overestimate population effects because of publication bias and differences in study characteristics. We developed methods to forecast site-level estimates of a not-yet-conducted replication from a meta-analysis. Extending calibrated estimates from meta-regression, we constructed nonparametric prediction intervals that condition on each site's moderator levels and correct for publication bias through inverse-probability-of-publication weighting under an assumed severity. These intervals achieve nominal coverage asymptotically when population effects are normally distributed, with a bounded coverage error otherwise. We compared four forecasting models (intercept-only meta-analysis or meta-regression, each with and without publication bias correction) in simulation study (81 scenarios and blinded retrospective forecasts of two multisite replications in infant cognition: ManyBabies 1 (104 sites) and ManyBabies 4 (33 sites). Correcting for publication bias improved interval calibration, with gains that increased with bias severity. Meta-regression improved forecasts only when measured moderators explained effect variation and replication sites differed meaningfully on them. In practice, publication bias correction should be the default when forecasting replications from meta-analyses, and replication projects that deliberately vary measured moderators across sites would enable more informative forecasts.

items.title: Adaptive Inference for Functionals of M-Estimands
items.summary: Reinforcement learning and contextual bandit algorithms have become increasingly common in sequential decision-making applications. When these methods are deployed in high-stakes domains, there is growing interest not only in learning effective policies, but also in conducting statistical inference for quantities learned under adaptive data collection. However, classical procedures applied naively in these settings can fail: even when estimators are unbiased, their variance becomes path-dependent and as a result may not be asymptotically normal. A growing literature has emerged to ameliorate this problem, but solutions tend to be problem specific and often rely on correct specification of a working model. In this work, we develop a unified framework for constructing asymptotically valid confidence intervals to cover smooth functionals of nonparametric M-estimands under adaptive sampling. Under Neyman orthogonality, we provide two novel methods for performing inference: (1) a self-normalized statistic based on the realized quadratic variation of the influence function and (2) a statistic using a plug-in estimate of the conditional variance based on reweighted influence function increments. Our results allow for flexible nonparametric estimation of nuisance parameters and remain valid under model misspecification. Our theory is supported by a simulation study for a dynamic pricing application which demonstrates that this method can produce asymptotically valid confidence intervals where standard methods fail.

items.title: Metropolis-Adjusted Diffusion Models
items.summary: Sampling from score-based diffusion models incurs bias due to both time discretisation and the approximation of the score function. A common strategy for reducing this bias is to apply corrector steps based on the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) at each noise level within a predictor-corrector framework. However, ULA is itself a \emph{biased} sampler, as it discretises a continuous diffusion process. In this work, we consider \emph{adjusted} Langevin correctors that employ Metropolis--Hastings (MH) or Barker's accept-reject steps to correct for this bias. Since the target density ratio typically required by MH-based algorithms is unavailable, we propose methods that instead utilise the score function to compute the correct acceptance probability. We introduce the first exact method for adjusting Langevin corrections in diffusion models, based on a two-coin Bernoulli factory algorithm. We also propose an efficient approximation based on Simpson's rule that achieves accuracy of order $5/2$ in the step size at near-zero marginal cost. We demonstrate that these procedures improve sample quality on both synthetic and image datasets, yielding consistent gains in Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) on the latter.

items.title: Gendered Misclassification from Surname-Based Race Imputation
items.summary: Researchers increasingly estimate political behavior based on race and gender from voter files, where race is imputed from surnames and geography. This only works where surnames suggest group membership, an assumption violated where surnames follow norms around marriage. Imputation is therefore biased against women who adopt their husband's surname, especially those who racially inter-marry, an outcome itself endogenous to partisanship. Using six US states recording self-reported race, I show that imputation is less accurate for Asian and Hispanic women, particularly those sharing the surname of a partner of another race, who differ politically from other women of their race. This violates assumptions behind downstream inference approaches, which nearly double the gender gap in partisanship among Asian voters. I derive an expression showing the bias is largest where a group is small. Using maiden rather than marriage-adopted surnames in North Carolina raises accuracy up to fourfold for women married across racial lines. Recovering maiden surnames, or omitting the married surname, removes much of the bias. In a national replication of a study of gender gaps in turnout, the correction more than triples the gap among Asian voters. In Lebanon, where wives register in their husband's locality, the error enters through geography.

items.title: Spectral Graph Sparsification Preserves Representation Geometry in Graph Neural Networks
items.summary: Spectral graph sparsification is a classical tool for reducing graph complexity while preserving Laplacian quadratic forms. In graph neural networks (GNNs), sparsification is often used to accelerate computation while maintaining predictive performance. In this work, we study a complementary representation-level question: does sparsification preserve the geometry of learned embeddings? For polynomial-filter GNNs, we prove that any $ε$-spectral sparsifier induces $O(ε)$ perturbations in polynomial graph filters, multilayer hidden representations, and their Gram matrices. These guarantees imply stability of squared pairwise distances, class means, and covariance structure in embedding space. We further establish finite-time training stability: under smoothness and boundedness assumptions, gradient descent on dense and sparsified graphs produces weight trajectories whose separation grows at most proportionally to the sparsification distortion. Empirically, effective-resistance sparsification validates the predicted perturbation chain on synthetic graphs and preserves hidden representation geometry on real datasets. In our experiments, the gram matrix and training dynamics show low divergence even under substantial sparsification, consistent with the predicted stability under spectral sparsification. Hidden Gram preservation strongly predicts neighborhood preservation and class-centroid stability across FashionMNIST, Cora, and Paul15. Together, these results show that spectral sparsification preserves not only graph operators, but also the representation geometry that supports downstream use of GNN embeddings for interpretability.

items.title: Prescriptive Learning of Linear Policies with Feasibility Guarantees for Binary Decision-Making
items.summary: Binary decision-making under uncertainty arises across a wide range of applications, including energy systems scheduling, transportation, and workforce planning. While machine learning has been increasingly applied to accelerate or replace mixed-integer solvers in such settings, existing approaches rely on predictive learning, training models to reproduce optimal decisions from labeled data, which lacks knowledge of counterfactual outcomes and provides no guarantees that the resulting decisions will be feasible. This limitation is further compounded under distributional shift, where policies trained on historical data may produce systematically infeasible decisions. We propose a prescriptive learning framework for binary decision-making that addresses both limitations. Rather than predicting optimal labels, the framework jointly optimizes over linear decision policies and feasible assignments across all training scenarios, allowing feasible alternatives and their operational performance to be considered directly during training. We further extend the framework to a distributionally robust chance-constrained formulation using a Wasserstein ambiguity set, which enforces feasibility with a prescribed probability under the worst-case distribution in the ambiguity set and enables a tunable trade-off between robustness and solution quality. We demonstrate the framework on two case studies, namely a unit commitment problem and a staff allocation problem. Out-of-sample experiments under test distributions that either match or differ from the training distribution show that the robust model is more conservative when the two distributions coincide, while under distributional shift it substantially reduces unmet demand and lowers total cost by up to 76.5% relative to classical predictive learning.

items.title: Sequential anomaly identification with sampling constraints for composite hypotheses
items.summary: We consider the problem of sequential anomaly identification with sampling constraints, where multiple independent data sources are observed over time, but only a limited subset can be sampled at each instant. The objective is to identify the anomalous sources while controlling the probabilities of at least one false alarm and at least one missed detection below prescribed levels. An identification policy must jointly determine when to stop sampling, which sources to declare anomalous, and how to allocate observations across sources under the sampling constraints. We seek policies that minimize the expected time to decision to a first-order asymptotic approximation as the error probabilities vanish. The observations from each source follow an unknown density belonging to one of two disjoint sets, corresponding to regular and anomalous behavior. Focusing on a nonparametric framework, which allows greater flexibility in modeling regular and anomalous statistical behavior, we establish general conditions for asymptotic optimality and provide a unified characterization of asymptotically optimal policies for composite hypothesis testing under sampling constraints. Simulation results illustrate the performance of the proposed policies, and the robustness of the nonparametric framework.

items.title: Rank-Transformed Dissimilarity Profiles for High-Dimensional Classification
items.summary: Despite advances in representation learning, high-dimensional classification remains challenging in low-sample-size regimes, where the dominant signal may vary across applications and labeled data are often limited. We propose a dissimilarity-profiling classification framework that represents each observation by its class-wise dissimilarity profile, transforming the original feature space into a low-dimensional representation that summarizes how the observation relates to each class. The key idea is to turn an effect of the curse of dimensionality into signal: high-dimensional geometry can induce systematic within-class and between-class dissimilarity patterns under location, scale, or other distributional changes, and these patterns are captured by the class-wise profiles. Building on this representation, we introduce a rank-transformed algorithm that converts dissimilarities into class-wise rank profiles. The proposed method delivers competitive or improved performance relative to commonly used classifiers on two-class, multi-class, network, and real high-dimensional low-sample-size datasets. To clarify the underlying mechanism, we characterize the mean and covariance of a distance-based surrogate, showing how location, scale, and higher-order distributional features enter the profile representation. Contamination experiments show that the rank transformation can improve robustness. The same profile construction applies to non-Euclidean data whenever pairwise dissimilarities can be computed.

items.title: Robust Satisficing Ensemble: Scalable Model Aggregation Under Distribution Shifts
items.summary: Standard ensemble methods can improve robustness by mitigating individual model stochasticity, but they frequently fail to generalize beyond the training distribution, leaving systems vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. We introduce the Robust Satisficing Ensemble (RSE), a scalable probabilistic aggregation framework designed to secure model combinations by minimizing their fragility against distributional changes. By bridging a robust satisficing objective with a quadratic risk surrogate, RSE derives an analytical inner adversary. This fundamental reformulation enables highly efficient weight updates without the computational bottleneck of standard minimax optimization, crucially decoupling optimization complexity from sample size to scale effectively to large datasets. In particular, we prove a geometrically decaying truncation error for the fragility approximation via Lagrange-Burmann expansion and establish stationarity guarantees for RSE. We evaluate RSE across a comprehensive spectrum of distribution shifts, including adversarial label shift (SST-5, TREC), natural subpopulation and temporal shifts (CivilComments, HuffPost). Our results demonstrate that RSE consistently outperforms strong robust baselines, including GroupDRO, IRM, and SRM. These findings establish RSE as a practical, theoretically grounded safeguard for reliable model aggregation in dynamic environments.

items.title: Digital Twins for Clinical Development: A Five-Level Framework from Prognostic Adjustment to In-Silico Trials
items.summary: Digital twins are increasingly discussed in drug development, often narrowly as virtual control arms or synthetic data. We propose a broader framework for data-driven clinical digital twins, organized into five levels according to how much of the trial data matrix of baseline covariates, treatment, and responses is generated by a statistical or machine-learning model trained on historical, external, or real-world data. The levels are: (1) prognostic score adjustment, (2) response trajectory prediction, (3) virtual control, (4) synthetic population, and (5) fully synthetic patients and responses. For each level we describe the estimation workflow, the development decision it can support, and the principal statistical guardrail. As the share of model-generated information increases, the inferential weight placed on the model grows and regulatory maturity generally declines. We argue that credibility requirements should therefore scale with context of use, characterized jointly by model influence and decision consequence, following a risk-based credibility framework. We identify four recurring credibility questions (drift and transportability, estimand alignment, compounding error, and data quality and provenance), summarize the current regulator landscape, and discuss bottlenecks in data, model transferability, collaboration, and lifecycle governance. The central message for statisticians is to start from the decision rather than the model, and to earn trust use by use.

items.title: Bayesian Wombling for Tracking Invasive Species
items.summary: This paper develops Bayesian wombling, or boundary analysis for tracking invasive species. We focus on three invasive species of concern in North America: Lycorma delicatula, Adelges tsugae, and Microstegium vimineum. We aim to demonstrate the applicability of wombling for supporting invasive pest management activities. In spatial science wombling is used widely to track regions of rapid change within the spatial reference domain. We use Gaussian process models for point-referenced spatial data followed by predictive inference on rates of change over curves using line integrals. We extend the wombling model based Bayesian inference framework to feature simple analytic forms that avoid high dimensional quadrature while offering uncertainty quantification over curvilinear spatial boundaries.

items.title: When Are Multimodal Predictions Biologically Supported? A Diagnostic Evaluation Framework
items.summary: Multimodal models in oncology can produce accurate predictions, but accurate prediction does not reveal whether the model has learned biology that is shared across modalities, biology confined to one modality, or spurious correlations that reflect confounders rather than genuine biology. We introduce DECAT, a model-agnostic post-hoc evaluation framework that classifies multimodal representations into four diagnostic scenarios (shared, spurious, modality-specific, or no signal) for a given task and modality, using five null-referenced metrics and a rule-based decision procedure. The framework operates on learned representations, requires no knowledge of which specific confounder is present, and returns indeterminate when the evidence is insufficient. We evaluate multimodal architecture properties using DECAT on synthetic data across four multimodal model classes spanning over 2,500 trained representations, and demonstrate its operational use on 8,979 TCGA patients with both multimodal model embeddings and five pretrained pathology foundation models. Entangled models (e.g., CLIP) detect shared signal near-perfectly on synthetic data but also falsely claim it when it is absent, doing so in the majority of such cases on real foundation model embeddings. This false claim rate increases with signal strength and sample size, so that larger cohorts and stronger representations produce more confident but still incorrect diagnoses. Applied to both multimodal TCGA embeddings and five pathology foundation models without paired RNA, DECAT detects confounding invisible to AUROC without requiring the confounder labels, as confirmed by post-hoc stratification.

items.title: Weak-Instrument Inference and Model Diagnostics in Double Machine Learning for Linear Instrumental Variable Models
items.summary: We study weak-instrument-robust inference in partially linear instrumental-variables models with learned nuisances. Building on an i.i.d. uniform-size baseline, we establish uniform asymptotic validity of clustered cross-fitted Anderson-Rubin inference and cross-fitted score inference under the stated sampling and nuisance-rate conditions. Extensions establish Anderson-Rubin validity for survey-weighted target laws and fold-nested generated instruments. A supporting population benchmark shows that prediction-optimal instrument residualization maximizes concentration when the treatment nuisance is correctly specified. A five-design diagnostic portfolio, a known-truth Monte Carlo, and an exploratory selector examine how nuisance specification and estimation affect realized strength and inference.

items.title: Understanding Randomization in Greedy Model Search
items.summary: We study feature subsampling in greedy model search, a randomization mechanism motivated by random forests and other ensemble methods. Although recent theory draws an analogy between this randomization and ridge regularization, these results largely rely on base learners optimized via ordinary least squares (OLS). We therefore investigate the effects of feature subsampling on greedy forward selection, a tractable abstraction of the adaptive split search used by decision trees. Assuming an orthogonal design, we prove that, under suitable conditions, ensembling with a fixed feature subsampling size can reduce expected training error without increasing degrees of freedom, thereby reducing fixed design prediction error. We also show that both the training error and degrees of freedom need not be monotone in the subsampling rate, breaking the analogy with standard shrinkage methods like the lasso or ridge regression under orthogonality. Furthermore, we characterize the exact asymptotic behavior of the estimator, showing that it adaptively reweights OLS coefficients based on their rank, with weights that are bounded by explicit logistic functions.

items.title: Hadamard Flattening and Gaussian Pooling Sketch for Least Squares with Coordinate-wise Guarantee
items.summary: Randomized sketch-and-solve algorithms accelerate overconstrained $\ell_2$ regression by replacing the input with a much smaller, randomly projected problem. While standard subspace embeddings nearly preserve the regression cost, coordinate-wise accuracy is more delicate: rather than the objective value, we want the solution vector itself to be close to the optimum in $\ell_\infty$ norm. Specifically, we seek $x'\in\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\|x'-x^\star\|_\infty\leq\fracε{\sqrt d}\|Ax^\star-b\|_2\|A^\dagger\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ is the design matrix, $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$ the label vector, $x^\star$ the optimal solution and $A^\dagger$ the pseudo-inverse of $A$. Price, Song and Woodruff introduced this problem and claimed that the subsampled randomized Hadamard transform (SRHT) with $O(ε^{-2}d^{1+Θ(\sqrt{\log\log n/\log d})})$ rows achieves this guarantee; we point out a gap in the proof. Song, Ye, Yin and Zhang later claimed $O(ε^{-2}d\log^3 n)$ rows, but their proof relies on an independence assumption that does not hold in general, and we exhibit an explicit instance on which it fails. To achieve a truly nearly-linear-in-$d$ row count, we introduce a new fast, dense randomized transform combining a randomized Hadamard flattening, a random permutation, and balanced, disjoint Gaussian pooling. Conditioned on the Hadamard-and-permutation stage, the sketched problem becomes an exact Gaussian regression whose noise is independent of the entire sketched design, exactly what Song, Ye, Yin and Zhang's argument was missing. Our sketch yields the $\ell_\infty$ guarantee with $m=O(ε^{-2}d\log d)$ rows, using one Hadamard pass with padded internal dimension $N=\widetilde{O}(n+ε^{-2}d^3)$. It is also efficient to apply: $(SA,Sb)$ can be computed in $O(Nd\log N)=\widetilde{O}(nd+ε^{-2}d^4)$ time.

items.title: Calibrating Scientific Foundation Models with Inference-Time Stochastic Attention
items.summary: Transformer-based scientific foundation models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, but current architectures give deterministic outputs and provide limited support for calibrated predictive uncertainty. We propose Stochastic Attention, a lightweight sample-average inference-time modification that randomizes attention by replacing softmax weights with normalized multinomial samples controlled by a single concentration parameter, and produces predictive ensembles without retraining. To set this parameter, we introduce a calibration objective that matches the stochastic attention output with the target, yielding an efficient univariate post-hoc tuning problem. We evaluate this mechanism on scientific foundation models for weather and time-series forecasting, as well as a regression task. Across benchmarks against baseline methods, Stochastic Attention achieves the strongest native calibration and the sharpest prediction intervals at comparable calibration, with adaptation costs nearly three orders of magnitude lower than the next-best baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/UQUH/StochasticAttention.

items.title: Very fast Bayesian Additive Regression Trees on GPU
items.summary: Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) is a nonparametric Bayesian regression technique based on an ensemble of decision trees. It is part of the toolbox of many statisticians. The overall statistical quality of the regression is typically higher than other generic alternatives, and it requires less manual tuning, making it a good default choice. However, it is a niche method compared to natural competitors such as XGBoost, due to the longer running time, making sample sizes above 10000-100000 a nuisance. We present a GPU implementation of BART, up to 500x faster than the previous state of the art, making BART fast enough to be a viable option on large datasets, and showing that BART parallelizes better than its non-Bayesian counterparts. We also find that, to be as practical as tree boosting on large datasets, BART would need a scalable way to infer the number of trees, which we do not provide. Our implementation is available in the Python package bartz.

items.title: On Generalization in Bilevel Least Squares with Overparameterized Neural Networks
items.summary: Bilevel optimization addresses machine learning problems in which the outer objective is a value function implicitly defined through the solution of an inner problem. While its algorithmic aspects are well developed, its generalization properties remain much less understood. In this paper, we study the generalization of inexact gradient methods when both objectives are least-squares regression problems and when the estimator of the value function's gradient, or hypergradient, is obtained by implicit differentiation in function space. This approach allows us to derive stationarity bounds for these methods in terms of the uniform generalization errors of the two regression functions needed to estimate the hypergradient. When these regression functions are defined as overparameterized two-layer ReLU networks trained by gradient flow with early stopping, we obtain explicit finite-sample bounds on these generalization errors in the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime. Combining these with our general inexact gradient analysis shows the effect of sample size on the overall convergence of the bilevel method. Numerical experiments on synthetic data illustrate our results. Beyond the NTK regime, further experiments reveal an initialization-dependent implicit bias induced by the bilevel structure, which can lead to feature learning at the inner level and overall performance improvements.

items.title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement with Statistical Guarantees
items.summary: Recursive self-improvement offers a promising path toward AI agents that improve through experience by refining their own harnesses without retraining their underlying large language models (LLMs). Making this self-improvement process reliable, however, requires more than generating new updates: agents must decide which changes are worth keeping. A greedy gate that accepts updates based solely on higher validation scores can mistake an observed gain for genuine progress and lead to performance degeneration, whereas overly conservative statistical gates may reject beneficial updates and hinder performance improvement. We introduce Trustworthy Recursive Updates with Statistical Testing (TRUST), a framework that adapts an online multiple hypothesis testing procedure to control the rate of false evolution across rounds, with an LLM analyzing historical context to help determine how much evidence is required to update the incumbent. Under interpretable assumptions, we prove that TRUST limits the proportion of accepted updates that result in unacceptable performance loss. We further derive a lower bound on the final performance gain. Across the benchmarks HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS with the models DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.8-Flash, TRUST reduces the average ratio of accepted inferior updates from the greedy gate's 45.59% to 2.78%, while achieving higher final scores than the state-of-the-art statistical gate baselines for recursive self-improvement. These findings demonstrate that TRUST strikes a balance between statistical reliability and performance gain in recursive self-improvement.

items.title: How reliable is an embedding of the seabed? Repeat-look measurement of frozen encoders on synthetic aperture sonar
items.summary: Pretrained encoders from self-supervised representation learning are increasingly applied to sonar imagery of the seafloor, where they are evaluated with protocols that take one embedding per target. A target patch of seabed, by contrast, is re-imaged from an alternate look on overlapping survey passes, so each embedding is one measurement of that target. Standard protocols cannot say how consistent those measurements are, or how much of their spread belongs to the patch and how much to the acquisition geometry. We treat this as a measurement-reliability problem. Using a synthetic-aperture sonar (SAS) survey, we measure the repeat-look reliability of embeddings from a frozen natural-image encoder (DINOv3 ViT-S/16). Standard single-look metrics, effective rank, clustering and a linear probe for coral, are all stable to the look, and the probe performs well (AUC 0.93). Yet the repeat-look reliability of the same embeddings is poor, with a distance-based intraclass correlation (dbICC) of 0.20 and nearest neighbours and clusters that barely agree across looks. This contradiction resolves as we find the probe learns a stable direction, whose ICC of 0.60 is 3.0 times that of the full embedding. Variance components, calculated from generalizability theory, attribute under a tenth of the within-cell spread to look acquisition geometry. The rest is cell-specific and cannot be separated without repeat passes at matched geometry. A sonar-pretrained encoder (BenthicDINO) and a classical SAS texture descriptor show the same pattern. For this dataset and the tested representations, uses that depend on patch identity fail, such as cross-pass comparison and retrieval, while uses at the level of habitat type (e.g. coral classification) do not. Because the standard metrics did not detect this, we argue that repeat-look reliability should accompany any evaluation of representations of the seafloor.

items.title: Statistical Inference for Rates of Change in Spatial Processes over Riemannian Manifolds
items.summary: Statistical inference for spatial processes from partially realized or scattered data has seen voluminous developments in diverse areas ranging from environmental sciences to business and economics. Inference on the associated rates of change has seen some recent developments. The literature has been restricted to Euclidean domains, where inference is sought on directional derivatives, rates along a chosen direction of interest, at arbitrary locations. Inference for higher order rates, particularly directional curvature has also proved useful in these settings. Modern spatial data often arise from non-Euclidean domains. This manuscript particularly considers spatial processes defined over compact Riemannian manifolds. We develop a comprehensive inferential framework for spatial rates of change for such processes over vector fields. In doing so, we formalize smoothness of process realizations and construct differential processes -- the derivative and curvature processes. We derive conditions for kernels that ensure the existence of these processes and establish validity of the joint multivariate process consisting of the ``parent'' Gaussian process (GP) over the manifold and the associated differential processes. Predictive inference on these rates is devised conditioned on the realized process over the manifold. Manifolds arise as polyhedral meshes in practice. The success of our simulation experiments for assessing derivatives for processes observed over such meshes validate our theoretical findings. By enhancing our understanding of GPs on manifolds, this manuscript unlocks a variety of potential applications in machine learning and statistics where GPs have seen wide usage. We propose a fully model-based approach to inference on the differential processes arising from a spatial process from partially observed or realized data across scattered location on a manifold.

items.title: Lyapunov-Based Sample Complexity Analysis for Weakly-Coupled MDPs
items.summary: We study the sample complexity of learning in average-reward weakly-coupled Markov decision processes (WCMDPs) and Restless Bandits (RBs) under a generative model. Naive reduction to a tabular MDP leads to high complexity bounds as the state-action space is exponentially large in the number of arms $N$. By exploiting the weakly coupled structure, we show that near-optimal policies can be learned with sample and computational complexities that are polynomial in $N$. Specifically, we analyze the plug-in approach, which applies an efficient planning algorithm to an empirical model estimated from data. For fully heterogeneous WCMDPs, we establish the first finite-sample PAC guarantee with polynomial complexity and an $O(1/\sqrt{N})$ optimality gap. For homogeneous RBs, we further prove that a smaller optimality gap is achievable under mild structural assumptions. A primary technical contribution is a novel Lyapunov-based analysis framework. Unlike classical approaches that rely on the difficult-to-control bias function, our framework uses an explicitly constructed Lyapunov function along with a drift transfer technique between the true and empirical models. A key step of independent interest in our framework is a fine-grained perturbation analysis for the underlying linear programming (LP) relaxation, which provides a general tool for analyzing LP-based policies and weakly-coupled systems.

items.title: Calibration of Time-Varying SEIR Models
items.summary: Mechanistic epidemic calibration can be sensitive to short-lived reporting anomalies that give a few observations high leverage under least squares (LSQ). We develop direct forward-solver least absolute deviations (LAD) calibration for time-varying susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed models fitted to reporting-interval incidence, with finite-horizon regularity and large-sample results. A phase-aware Monte Carlo study compares LAD and LSQ across three transmission drivers, four epidemic phases, five reporting mechanisms, and four forecast horizons. All 120,000 primary fits converged. LAD was favored in 56.7% of mean-absolute-error comparisons and 57.9% of weighted-interval-score comparisons overall; under isolated spikes, backlog release, or temporary underreporting, these proportions rose to 73.6% and 72.2%, with strong gains near the epidemic peak. Rolling-origin validation on four synthetic RAPIDD Ebola scenarios also identifies settings where LSQ is preferred, demonstrating the framework's ability to distinguish robustness gains from sustained-trend behavior. Multiple uncertainty and identifiability diagnostics, complete code and data, and an interactive application provide a reproducible computational workflow.

items.title: Matchability-Aware Conformal Prediction for Open-Ended Language Model Generation
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) often do not produce calibrated uncertainty estimates for their answers. We propose CAELUM, a framework that builds semantic prediction sets while separating aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty. CAELUM samples answers using an ensemble of clarification prompts, clusters them by semantic equivalence, and estimates the aleatoric and epistemic components via kernel-based von Neumann entropy before calibrating nonconformity scores with split conformal prediction. We use a weight $w_λ(x)=1+U_{\mathrm{ale}}(x)+λ\,U_{\mathrm{epi}}(x)$ to control for the contribution of the epistemic uncertainty of each instance and fit a coefficient $λ^\star$ to minimize prediction set size. When the objective is nonflat and selection is stable across splits, $λ^\star$ could be a diagnostic, where large values may indicate epistemic dominance (retrieve, abstain) and $λ^\star\to 0$ aleatoric dominance (clarify). For individual queries, a log ratio $R(x)$ compares the weighted epistemic component with the aleatoric component. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the coverage is capped by matchability, the fraction of items whose reference answer appears in any sampled cluster. Empirically, this matchability can be predicted from the original question features using a lightweight classifier. We use those predictions to define a stratum and derive a conformal coverage bound within it. Across 30 LLM and dataset combinations (4-32B), mean coverage is 0.74 in the learned stratum versus 0.65 overall, averaged over the 78 evaluations using the learned classifier. Project page: https://unco3892.github.io/caelum/

items.title: Strongly Adaptive Online Learning with Time-Varying Movement Costs
items.summary: We study online convex optimization (OCO) with time-varying movement costs, where the learner incurs both a loss and a time-dependent penalty for changing its decisions. While previous work has established dynamic regret guarantees for this setting, obtaining strongly adaptive guarantees that hold simultaneously over arbitrary intervals remains an open challenge. We address this by developing a new algorithm which, for every interval $[a,b]\subseteq[T]$ and arbitrary comparator sequence, achieves a data-dependent regret bound of $ \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left( \sqrt{(D^2+DP_{[a,b]})\sum_{t \in [a,b]}(\|g_t\|^2+λ_t\|g_t\|)} \right) $, where $D$ is the diameter of the decision domain, $P_{[a,b]}$ is the path length of the comparator sequence over $[a,b]$, $g_t$ is the gradient of the loss, and $λ_t$ is the movement-cost coefficient at round~$t$. Key to our approach is a novel reduction to sleeping experts with movement costs, a previously unexplored variant that is of independent interest. As a result of our development, we further obtain strongly-adaptive dynamic regret guarantees under arbitrary delayed feedback with a refined dependence on interval-restricted cumulative delays. Our approach also naturally extends to OCO with time-varying memory, where we obtain strongly-adaptive guarantees which improve the best-known bounds.

items.title: An Integrated Framework for Rule-Based Data Editing
items.summary: Statistical data editing in official statistics must restore consistency while limiting changes to observed data. Exact minimum-change correction can be computationally demanding. This paper develops a general framework for structured data whose dependencies admit a normalized acyclic routing representation. It connects routing metadata and explicitly specified semantic edits to logical admissibility, violation diagnosis, and correction. Under stated record semantics, the generated Horn theory characterizes admissibility without materializing its deductive closure. Canonical indices preserve the origin of each requirement and identify the variables that can affect a violation. With complete diagnostics and strictly positive weights, a nonnegative violation Hamiltonian vanishes exactly on admissible records within the specified domain. This characterization is independent of the correction procedure and provides both an objective for correction and a certificate: a verified zero-energy output is admissible and globally minimizes violation energy within its permitted candidate domain. Minimum modification cost is formulated separately, with sufficient conditions for an equivalent penalized objective and optimality certificates based on attained lower bounds. A household survey application illustrates the construction, the verification of admissible corrections, and minimum-cost certification for a subset of outputs. The framework supports traceable validation and correction in official statistics, while statistical accuracy of replacement values requires separate assessment.

items.title: Coarsening Linear Non-Gaussian Causal Models with Cycles
items.summary: Recent work on causal abstraction, in particular graphical approaches focusing on causal structure between clusters of variables, aims to summarize a high-dimensional causal structure in terms of a low-dimensional one. Existing methods for learning such summaries from data assume that both structures are acyclic. Acyclicity is helpful for causal effect identification and reasoning, but it excludes the many systems of scientific interest that contain feedback loops. We show that in the linear non-Gaussian (LiNG) setting, the acyclicity assumption on the high-dimensional structure can be relaxed while still allowing recovery of a low-dimensional causal directed acyclic graph (DAG). LiNG models with cycles are observationally identifiable only up to an equivalence class whose members differ only within their feedback loops. Our low-dimensional DAG, which is invariant across all members of this class, is therefore identifiable from observational data alone. While existing approaches for learning this equivalence class have exponential time complexity, our low-dimensional summary is learned in worst-case cubic time and comes with finite-sample guarantees. We provide open source code and experiments on synthetic data to corroborate our theoretical results.

items.title: A Geometric Theory for Nonequilibrium Transformer Dynamics
items.summary: We develop a variational and geometric theory based on statistical physics for the joint evolution of Transformer attention and token representations at fixed model parameters. To this end, we introduce a free energy for the attention and model the evolution of the attention weights by its Fisher--Rao gradient flow. At fixed token representations, we prove that the softmax matrix is the unique free-energy minimiser and that every positive attention trajectory converges to it. For prescribed time-dependent representations, we show that the attention dynamics becomes linear after a change to logit variables. This result yields tracking bounds relative to the instantaneous softmax and sufficient conditions for attention to converge to a fixed matrix. Hamiltonian dynamics for the representations and their momenta are then coupled to the attention relaxation driven by the same energy. This coupling results in an energy-dissipation law. We also develop two alternative Hamiltonians incorporating the attention value map. We prove global well-posedness of the attention flow and all three coupled systems.

items.title: Energy-Tweedie: Score meets Score, Energy meets Energy
items.summary: Denoising and score estimation are classically linked through Tweedie's formula, which relates the posterior mean under Gaussian noise to the Stein score of the noisy marginal. In this work, we extend this perspective beyond Gaussian noise to a broad class of Gibbs (energy-based) noise distributions, with the generalized Gaussian family as an example.
