items.summary: The classical tail dependence coefficient (TDC) may fail to capture non-exchangeable features of bivariate tail dependence since it evaluates the underlying copula only along the diagonal. To address this limitation, several measures of strongest manifestation of tail dependence have been proposed in the bivariate case, including a measure based on the tail copula of the underlying bivariate copula. This paper introduces and investigates the multivariate maximal tail concordance measure (MTCM), which extends the bivariate measure to the multivariate case. The MTCM quantifies the largest tail mass over lower hyperrectangles of common unit volume, while the associated maximizer identifies the direction of maximal tail probability. We establish fundamental properties of the MTCM in the multivariate case, including existence of an optimal direction. We also derive analytical representations for several important model classes. Closed-form expressions are further obtained for survival Marshall-Olkin copulas, Archimax and nested Archimedean copulas with regularly varying Archimedean generators. An application to trivariate annual sea-level maxima in England reveals off-diagonal stress directions and differences in extremal dependence that are not summarized by likelihood values or the TDC alone. A basis-risk analysis of a parametric insurance further shows that the fitted model with relatively low values of TDC and MTCM can nevertheless yield the most conservative risk assessment due to its non-exchangeability in the tail.

items.title: Track or Follow? A Jev-Compatible Multi-Agent Trading System When Web News Lags the Market
items.summary: LLM agents increasingly trade on the Web news they read, yet much Web news about listed firms is published after, and about, the price move it reports, so a reader can agree with the market by following it instead of reading the event. We ask whether LLM judgments of Web news track the market's reaction to the reported event or follow it. To answer, we built a multi-agent trading system whose agents share only point-in-time stores and answer typed questions through the interface of Jev, a hosted typed decision model; code sets every position under a proved bound on how far text can move it. In a hash-committed test of a Jev-compatible reader built from a pinned LLM's option probabilities, item judgments track announcement-window abnormal returns (weekly Spearman 0.119), also after the LLM's release, and event types agree with the issuers' 8-K filings (AUC 0.833); Jev's judgments of news published after its own release track the reaction as well (descriptive). Exploratory analyses show where the association comes from: 72% of earnings news items appear after the issuer's filing, contributor-written items often report the price move, and from the first trade after publication the association falls to 0.023. At a weekly horizon, the confirmatory test detects no rank information over code-only features. Under attack, decision cards traced 88% of successful attacks to the planted item. We propose that market-graded tests of Web-text readers report the criterion from publication, not only from the event.

items.title: Implied Volatility Expansions for VIX Options in Forward Variance Models
items.summary: We develop expansions for the implied volatility of VIX options within the class of forward variance models based on weak-approximation techniques for VIX option prices. In single-kernel models, such as the standard and rough Bergomi models, the expansion is fully explicit, and we prove that its error is of the same order as that of the underlying price approximation. In mixed-kernel models, we propose two expansions. The first one is fully explicit and relies on a Hermite expansion of the price, which we rewrite exactly as a Black-Scholes price with a shifted volatility, up to explicit residual terms. The second one uses the implied volatility of a mixed log-normal proxy, computed numerically, as its zeroth-order term, and we prove that it achieves the same order of accuracy as in the single-kernel case. The resulting formulas yield implied volatilities directly, rather than by inverting approximate option prices.

items.title: Optimal Dividend, Reinsurance and Capital-Injection Strategies for Collaborating Business Lines: The Case of Excess-of-Loss Reinsurance
items.summary: This paper considers an insurer with two collaborating business lines that must make three critical decisions: (1) dividend payout, (2) a combination of proportional and excess-of-loss reinsurance coverage, and (3) capital injection between the lines. The reserve level of each line is modeled using a diffusion approximation, and the insurer aims to maximize the weighted total discounted dividends paid until the first ruin time. We obtain the value function and the optimal strategies in explicit or semi-explicit form. We then prove that the optimal dividend payout strategy for bounded dividend rates is of threshold type, while for unbounded dividend rates it is of barrier type. Under the diffusion approximation, the optimal combination of proportional and excess-of-loss reinsurance is shown to be pure excess-of-loss reinsurance. We also show that the optimal level of risk ceded to the reinsurer decreases as the aggregate reserve level increases, and that reinsurance is phased out line by line. The optimal capital-injection strategy involves transferring reserves to prevent the ruin of one line. Finally, numerical examples are presented to illustrate these optimal strategies.

items.title: Rough Heston model as the scaling limit of bivariate cumulative heavy-tailed INAR processes: Weak-error bounds and option pricing
items.summary: We study nearly unstable bivariate cumulative heavy-tailed INAR($\infty$) processes and show that, under a one-factor parameterization and a suitable scaling, they converge to the rough Heston model. This yields a discrete-time microstructural route to the joint price-variance dynamics and gives explicit formulas linking the INAR asymmetry parameters to the leverage correlation and diffusion scale of the limiting volatility process. For pricing, we reduce the exact finite-$τ$ Fourier--Laplace transform recursion to a quadratic discrete Volterra equation and compare it with the rough Heston fractional Riccati equation. Under a transform-strip condition for the continuous model and bounded-Riccati regularity, every fixed bounded frequency window admits a uniform transform-error bound of order $τ^{-α}+τ^{-(1-α)}$. The finite-$τ$ transform is entire, and a uniform exponential-moment estimate then removes the Fourier cutoff and yields convergence of the exact, untruncated call prices. We also develop an FFT-accelerated CDQ simulator with $\mathcal O(τ\log^2τ)$ complexity per path and use it to price European and path-dependent options, benchmark the Markovian case $α=1$, and analyze the model-implied volatility surface.

items.title: The Logic of Factor Portfolios: Boolean Rules, Interactions, and Trading Costs
items.summary: Investors turn signals into holdings through decision rules: buy the top decile, hold stocks with high momentum and low volatility, exclude stocks that fail a screen. Many such rules are Boolean functions of threshold statements about signal ranks, and writing them this way shows both what a rule holds and how often it trades. A Walsh decomposition splits the return of any rule into exposures to individual signals and to interactions among signals; an intersection and a union of the same two screens, for example, have opposite interaction exposures. The same coefficients, together with the persistence of the underlying statements, determine turnover. Interactions are less persistent than their components, so rules that load on higher-order interactions trade more, and thresholds discard information, so at equal risk threshold implementations of interactions trade more than smooth ones. In U.S. stocks from 1973 to 2024, these predictions hold closely: predicted and realized persistence have correlations of at least 0.999, predicted turnover matches realized turnover with a slope of 1.02, and the same interactions are more persistent as products of ranks than as threshold rules. Trading costs rise with order, and because premia fall with order, 58% of single-signal portfolios have absolute premia above their quoted-spread costs over 1995-2024, against 24% of two-signal and 6% of three-signal interaction portfolios. Out of sample, interaction portfolios raise the Sharpe ratio of single-signal tangency portfolios, and over 1995-2024 they reject a six-factor model that conventional sorts on the same signals do not reject.

items.title: Drift-invariant kernels for discount curve models
items.summary: Kernel ridge regression estimates the discount curve as the minimizer of a pricing error plus a penalty given by the norm of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. By the representer theorem, the estimate lies in a finite-dimensional affine space that depends only on the kernel and on the cash flow dates of the instruments. We ask when this space is invariant under the risk-neutral drift of the discount curve, so that the estimated curves can be the states of a continuous-time arbitrage-free model. We show that this holds for every grid of cash flow dates if and only if the kernel is of the form $k(x,y)=\e^{b(x+y)}\big(c\,\e^{axy}+1-c\big)$, apart from kernels whose Hilbert space has dimension at most two. For this kernel the estimated curve is an affine combination of flat discount curves, each corresponding to a constant continuously compounded yield. The drift-invariant subspaces correspond to sub-grids of the cash flow dates, and the discounted coefficients have linear risk-neutral dynamics.

items.title: The Long-Only Minimum Variance Portfolio in a One-Factor Market: Theory and Asymptotics
items.summary: We study the long-only minimum variance (LOMV) portfolio, an object of interest going back to Markowitz, and the simplest non-trivial instance of quantitative portfolio construction. Despite its importance, aspects of the LOMV remain mysterious. Here we examine the base case of a general one-factor covariance model, and provide an explicit characterization of the solution. As a corollary we resolve an open question of Qi (2021) for this setting. In the high-dimensional regime of many assets, we prove that the active ratio (proportion of assets with non-zero weight in the LOMV portfolio) converges in almost all cases to a limit expressed in terms of the distribution of asset betas. In particular, when asset betas are all positive and drawn from a continuous distribution, the active ratio tends to zero in the high dimensional limit, and close to zero when the fraction of negative betas is small.

items.title: Shared AI Decision Interfaces and Credit Allocation in a Simulated Lending Market
items.summary: Language-model agents can choose from a shared menu of actions. I ask whether the order of that menu, which carries no payoff-relevant information, can move credit in a market. Borrowers from three small open-weight model families operate in a simulated collateralized lending market. In each of 12 matched blocks, one market shows all borrowers the same complete action order and the other balances the six orders. An exact randomization test, hash-locked locally before the first model call, rejects the null that common-market net debt does not depend on the assigned order (two-sided p = 2/8,100). The pre-specified lever-up-first versus delever-first estimate is 1.12 units of initial unused borrowing capacity. Every lever-up-first market ended above the balanced market of its block, and every delever-first market ended below it. Exploratory counterfactuals show why the collateral cap does not undo this shock. The cap limits new borrowing, but no rule makes a borrower sell collateral. The market's rules therefore keep 41 percent of the borrowing difference and 93 percent of the repayment difference. Pool-price valuation also returns part of the screened borrowing. Exposure responds more than debt. Lever-up-first markets ended with 58 percent more debt than delever-first markets and about four times the scenario write-offs under a fixed-price shock (exploratory p = 2/8,100). Credit decisions were concentrated as well, because one model family bought 86 percent of the tokens purchased on credit. No market had a liquidation or realized bad debt.

items.title: The End-of-Day Reversal After 2019: A Pre-Registered Test on S&P 500 Stocks Excluding Heavily Traded Names
items.summary: Baltussen, Da and Soebhag (2025) document an end-of-day reversal in U.S. stocks through December 2019: intraday losers outperform intraday winners over the last half hour of trading. We test it on later data, on point-in-time S&P 500 members excluding about 80 heavily traded stocks we had examined in earlier, unpublished work. Under a private pre-registration, the 2016-2019 data had to reproduce the published sign before any statistic linking the sort to the outcome was computed on later primary-sample data. Measured to the last trade before the closing auction, the dollar-volume-weighted reversal is 3.13 bps per day (t = 7.5) in 2016-2019 and 3.05 bps (t = 3.0) in 2023-2026, with a one-sided 95% bound on the decline of 61%. The result depends on the window: the reversal is indistinguishable from zero in 2020-2022, 2023 carries much of the later estimate, and from 2020 onward it is 1.69 bps (t = 2.3), with a bound of 91%. A proxy sample, added after the run, gives 2.81 and 3.86 bps. On the full index the reversal falls from 3.40 to 0.74 bps (t of the change -1.83, short of the registered bar of -3); descriptive comparisons concentrate this weakness in the very largest stocks. No pre-registered mechanism test passes.

items.title: Joint modelling of financial cost and carbon footprint in motor insurance claims: a BINAR(1) decision framework for circular auto parts adoption
items.summary: Motor insurance claims management increasingly faces a dual objective: controlling claim costs while reducing greenhouse-gas emissions associated with vehicle repair decisions. This paper proposes a bivariate, discrete-time modelling framework that links the dynamics of financial claims and repair-related carbon footprint inspired by a BINAR(1) dependence structure, allowing for temporal persistence, cross-dependence and a positive/negative correlation between the two dimensions. Using externally sourced emission factors and cost information for replacement parts, we operationalise the carbon footprint of claims under two repair pathways: new parts versus circular-economy reused parts (PIEC). We then conduct scenario analyses in which the acceptance rate of reused parts varies, and we quantify the joint implications for expected monetary outlays and CO 2 -equivalent emissions. Results show that higher PIEC acceptance can simultaneously reduce expected emissions and average claim cost, and the magnitude of the joint benefit depends on the dependence structure and persistence captured by the BINAR(1) process. The proposed framework provides a transparent, reproducible tool for insurers to evaluate repair-policy levers and to align claims operations with decarbonisation targets while retaining an explicit stochastic risk perspective.

items.title: Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging for uncertainty quantification of electricity price forecasts
items.summary: Quantifying the uncertainty of forecasting models is essential to assess and mitigate the risks associated with data-driven decisions, especially in volatile domains such as electricity markets. In this paper, we propose a computationally efficient isotonic variant of Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA), called Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging (iQRA), for generating probabilistic forecasts from ensembles of point forecasts. Building on QRA, we introduce stochastic order constraints as a hyperparameter-free regularization mechanism that reduces computational complexity while maintaining competitive forecast accuracy. We further demonstrate that the same isotonic regularization principle can be applied to the smoothed estimator of QRA. In an extensive forecasting study of two European day-ahead electricity markets, we show that iQRA and its smoothed variant consistently rank among the top state-of-the-art postprocessing methods in terms of reliability and sharpness. It produces well-calibrated prediction intervals, with smoothed iQRA providing superior reliability even when compared against coverage-oriented conformal prediction. We further introduce a battery arbitrage evaluation, showing that the leading probabilistic methods achieve the highest profit per trade and that probabilistic risk control improves the economic value of trading decisions. Isotonic regularization offers a scalable hyperparameter-free variable selection for linear quantile regression, making iQRA attractive for practical decision-support systems in energy markets.

items.title: Towards Robust Reinforcement Learning Market Making: Lessons from Loss Function Experimentation
items.summary: Market makers play a vital role in ensuring efficient trade within financial markets. Recent literature has delved into training market-making systems using reinforcement learning. This paper delves into the impact of various loss function formulations on risk management behavior within reinforcement-based market making. Through empirical evaluation, we contrast profit-maximizing strategies with risk-averse approaches, finding that penalties for inventory and cash management foster more resilient and adaptable market-making strategies. Our results underscore the significance of striking a balance between profit maximization and risk management in algorithmic trading, providing actionable insights for refining strategies in practical settings.

items.title: Portfolio-aware scenario transfer of reserve movements: evidence from Lloyd's syndicates
items.summary: A claims-development movement on one portfolio may not transfer directly as a stress to another size. We estimate how to transfer such scenarios between portfolio sizes, using 632 syndicate-years from 117 Lloyd's syndicates over 2015-2024. The measured movement is the change in gross claims estimates on selected older underwriting cohorts, divided by opening gross claims outstanding plus reserves taken on in the year whose development it includes; it is not a pure measure of opening-reserve deterioration. Its dispersion falls materially with reserve size, and a size-based scale predicts held-out syndicates far better than a single market scale. But the transferred upper tail understates the smallest books: in the smallest reserve-size quartile, six of 158 held-out observations exceeded the transferred 99.5th percentile, against 0.79 expected, from three syndicates. Square-root scaling has descriptively lower held-out pinball loss at 99% and 99.5%, though more misses among the largest books. For a GBP 500m portfolio the transferred empirical 99.5th percentile is 0.34 of reserves (95% credible interval, conditional on the fitted model, 0.23-0.52), against 0.67 in the raw market pool. Both are Syndicate 5820's 2016 movement. The contribution is inspectable scenario comparability, not a calibrated capital quantile or a next-year forecast.

items.title: Correlation Ambiguity, Diversification Fragility, and Insurance Pricing
items.summary: We study how correlation ambiguity affects insurance supply, investment, and pricing in a competitive market. An insurer jointly chooses underwriting and risky investment under worst-case correlation uncertainty, with the insurance loading determined by insurance supply and household demand. With the correlation midpoint and all other model parameters fixed, widening the correlation interval makes diversification less reliable. With underwriting fixed, absolute financial investment weakly declines; with endogenous underwriting, investment may instead rise as insurance supply contracts. Nevertheless, joint exposure to uncertain dependence, measured by underwriting times absolute financial investment, strictly decreases whenever positive. Once this exposure vanishes, further ambiguity leaves the equilibrium unchanged. Insurance prices redistribute ambiguity costs between insurer and policyholder, while combined local certainty-equivalent surplus declines as long as joint exposure remains positive.

items.title: Quantitative Universal Approximation for Noisy Quantum Neural Networks
items.summary: We prove a quantitative universal approximation theorem for noisy quantum neural networks (QNNs), with explicit non-asymptotic error bounds in terms of the number of accuracy blocks, the qubit count, the number of two-qubit gates, and hardware noise parameters. Motivated by quantitative finance, where target functions are expectations of payoffs, we first extend existing noiseless bounds to expectation functions and derive explicit constants for exponential Levy models, covering the Black-Scholes price of (truncated) European Put options. We then formulate the noisy circuit via quantum channels, obtain a fidelity-based bound for general noise models, and specialise to depolarising noise with readout error, calibrated to real hardware. Finally, we provide a detailed numerical analysis for option pricing in the Black-Scholes model, testing our results on actual noisy quantum hardware.

items.title: Universal Value-at-Risk superadditivity
items.summary: Value-at-Risk (VaR) is a standard regulatory risk measure, and its failure of subadditivity is well known. Much less appreciated is that for sufficiently heavy-tailed losses, VaR can be superadditive uniformly across all probability levels, a phenomenon strictly stronger than the asymptotic superadditivity studied in extreme value theory. We call this property universal VaR superadditivity (UVS). We study UVS and its stronger weighted version (WUVS) as properties of random vectors rather than of marginal distributions. This perspective unifies and extends a recent line of work on iid infinite-mean models. UVS, except for trivial cases, imposes an infinite-mean structure. We establish preservation properties of UVS and WUVS under increasing and convex transformations, weak convergence, and certain distributional mixtures, and use these tools to prove UVS and WUVS for non-identically distributed risks in several large families including completely subscalable, super-Cauchy, and inverted subadditive risks, extending results previously available only in the iid case. In many results, we also establish strict versions of UVS and WUVS, which lead to stronger decision-theoretic implications. As a consequence, for any portfolio satisfying WUVS, every distortion risk measure is superadditive, so an optimal allocation concentrates on a single asset, and diversification is never beneficial.

items.title: Does a Trading Policy Need to Know What It Trades? Microstructure Invariance and Zero-Shot Transfer of Execution Policies
items.summary: Execution algorithms are calibrated asset by asset, because the queues, trade rates and bid-ask spreads they face differ by orders of magnitude across assets. For reinforcement learning this is zero-shot generalisation across contexts of very different scales, and microstructure invariance proposes a normalisation fixed by theory: measured in each asset's own units of time, size and price, markets look alike. In an exact order-by-order replay of public Nasdaq data, we train policies once, on 954 stocks in 2019, to choose between waiting in the queue and crossing the spread, and evaluate them unchanged on 1,964 unseen stocks in 2020-21, 2,629 stocks in 2025-26, crypto pairs and a second exchange. First, a policy that sees a stock only through its recent trade rate, trade size, spread and price increment (tick) costs within 0.015 spreads per share (a fifth of what learning saves) of a policy whose training data included the stock, and the stock's own history does not help it; it comes within a similar margin of policies trained on the second exchange when every episode counts equally, and within a wider one on crypto. Second, in mean cost before fees, invariant units beat raw units, z-scores and asset descriptors, but by under a basis point: most of their advantage is information and a common cost scale that a learner can also take as plain inputs, and none of the representations tested extrapolates to unseen spread regimes. Third, a near-zero transfer gap to a pooled comparator is weak evidence that a representation is right: we show that such a comparator detects only a small share of what a poor representation loses, and confirm it in synthetic markets and on pendulums.

items.title: Portfolio Risk Bounds without Cross-Asset Return Covariances: Distributional Fields from Language-Model Representations
items.summary: Portfolio risk assessment ordinarily relies on reliable estimates of cross-asset return covariances, which are difficult to obtain in short, high-dimensional panels. We show that firm-level distribution-valued characteristics can instead provide one-sided certificates of portfolio risk. Under maintained links from characteristics to systematic exposures and from exposures to returns, multi-firm Wasserstein-2 dispersion yields a sharp upper bound on systematic portfolio variance and a corresponding bound for standardized returns. A weighted pairwise relaxation produces an objective that is convex under a checkable condition and requires marginal volatility scales but no cross-asset return covariances. With zero firm-specific slack, the common-map scale changes the certified variance reduction but not the normalized allocation, which depends only on observed information geometry. In a 100-firm panel from 2018-2022, only 0.09%-0.46% of portfolios across four prespecified capped reference populations have in-sample variance no greater than an allocation constructed from Qwen3-Embedding-8B news representations; the corresponding share for equal risk weighting is 28.3%-34.7%. The lower in-sample variance ranking relative to equal risk also appears across the reported frozen language-model representations. The framework therefore converts distribution-valued firm information into a coherent risk bound and an implementable allocation rule constructed without cross-asset return covariances.

items.title: Who Are a Firm's Economic Peers? Mapping a Latent Information Field with Language Models
items.summary: Identifying a firm's economic peers matters for benchmarking, risk measurement, and understanding return dependence, yet a diversified firm may have no single natural peer. We use language-model representations of corporate news to identify the combination of firms that jointly represents each firm's information environment. Each firm is represented by a distribution of article embeddings, and target-anchored Wasserstein barycentric reconstruction produces a directed map of economic-peer weights. We use this map as the interaction structure in a spatial factor model and ask whether return dependence follows peer relations measured from news without using returns. We construct peer weights from 2018-2022 news for 100 large-cap US traded firms and evaluate their financial relevance in subsequent returns. Relative to a matched model with the Fama-French five factors and momentum, the information field firms' unexpected returns move together after common factor exposures are accounted for. Joint reconstruction contributes substantially more than pairwise Wasserstein proximity or equal weighting of the selected peers, while centroid reconstruction retains most of the gain. Explicit news co-mentions provide complementary information. Language models thus make the interaction structure in spatial asset pricing an object of measurement: economically interpretable peer relations can be constructed from text before their financial relevance is assessed in returns.

items.title: Systematic Covariance Envelopes from Wasserstein Geometry: Evidence from Language-Model Representations
items.summary: Firm characteristics are commonly represented as fixed vectors, even though evidence about firms' operations arrives as heterogeneous collections of articles and reports. We represent firms by distributions and derive restrictions on the systematic covariance their factor exposures can support. Quadratic Wasserstein distance measures the minimum displacement needed to align two distributions; in exposure space, it determines their sharp covariance ceiling. A common characteristic-to-exposure benchmark with bounded distortion and firm-specific departures transfers this restriction to characteristic space. The framework makes explicit how transmission uncertainty widens the range of feasible covariance ceilings. We construct firm distributions from language-model embeddings of financial news, disclosures, and analyst reports for Nasdaq firms over 2018-2022. Greater article-embedding distance is associated with weaker return co-movement after symmetric firm effects: the return-distance coefficient is 1.874, with 95% interval [1.516, 2.250]. The association remains positive after sector, industry, and 10-K product-market controls, and retains its sign in a later return window. A sensitivity grid shows how quickly the covariance restriction loses informativeness as transmission tolerances widen. Together, the framework and evidence support screening firm pairs for shared exposures and assessing covariance under explicit economic scenarios.

items.title: Information Games: Strategic Crowding and Firm Repositioning in Language-Model Space
items.summary: When firms respond to new market opportunities, their capacity choices alter the future discounted free cash flows available to both competitors and investors. In competitive markets, these investment decisions publicized in news articles and analyst reports, measuring the changes in capital structure, product mix, firm leadership, risk exposure and operating procedure made by the firm. Modern search engines rely on Large Language Models to measure the relevancy of source documents to given search query. These measurements let researchers represent these news articles as clouds of dense vectors whose information geometry reflects the dissimilarity of firms over time. Building on Xu et al. (2022), we develop a model of costly competitive adjustment in which firms allocate capacity in which firms make firm capacity adjustment towards free cash flow shocks. Using a novel sandwich estimator, we analyse the sign and magnitude of this predicted adjustment using multi-agent simulation, and validate our findings on a sample of news and analyst reports from Nasdaq-listed companies between 2018-2022.

items.title: On consistency of optimal portfolio choice for state-dependent exponential utilities
items.summary: In a complete Brownian market, we characterize consistency across investment horizons for state-dependent exponential utilities. We show that consistency is equivalent to an explicit relation between the drift and diffusion of risk tolerance and a deterministic absolutely continuous function. Within this family, the forward performance property selects a unique coefficient. More generally, under the stated admissibility conditions, a forward performance is consistent, whereas consistency alone does not imply the forward performance property.

items.title: Deep Neural Operator Learning for Probabilistic Models
items.summary: We propose a deep neural-operator framework for a general class of probabilistic models. Under global Lipschitz conditions on the operator over the entire Euclidean space-and for a broad class of probabilistic models-we establish a universal approximation theorem with explicit network-size bounds for the proposed architecture. The underlying stochastic processes are required only to satisfy integrability and general tail-probability conditions. We verify these assumptions for both European and American option-pricing problems within the forward-backward SDE (FBSDE) framework, which in turn covers a broad class of operators arising from parabolic PDEs, with or without free boundaries. Finally, we present a numerical example for a basket of American options, demonstrating that the learned model produces optimal stopping boundaries for new strike prices without retraining.

items.title: Absolute Continuity of Monotone Aggregations under Positive Regression Dependence
items.summary: In this paper, we provide sufficient conditions for the absolute continuity of one-dimensional push-forwards of dependent random vectors. Suppose that $X$ has an absolutely continuous distribution and that the conditional distribution of an $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued random vector $Y$ given $X=x$ is nondecreasing in $x\in \mathbb{R}$ in the usual stochastic order. For Borel maps $g\colon \mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfying a coordinatewise monotonicity condition in $Y$ and a uniform lower-increment condition in $X$, we prove that $g(X,Y)$ has an absolutely continuous distribution. The result requires neither independence nor a joint density, and allows the marginal law of $Y$ to be completely arbitrary. Moreover, the result remains valid if $\mathbb{R}^d$ is replaced by an arbitrary measurable space endowed with a reflexive binary relation. We discuss consequences for monotone risk aggregation and extensions of the familiar regularization by convolution beyond independent random variables.

items.title: Reaction-boundary variance and adjoint-consistent local-volatility projection
items.summary: We derive an operational-time variance kernel for a latent-order-book reaction boundary and use it to separate three objects usually collapsed in calendar-time volatility models: a structural boundary cumulant, a clock projection, and a pricing-measure choice. The reaction boundary is the zero of a bid--ask imbalance field. For a locally linear book, signed order-flow perturbations displace this zero through a damped Abel response kernel, so the variance of boundary increments is obtained as a finite-scale Green-function cumulant rather than introduced as a primitive diffusion coefficient. For long-memory forcing with exponent $0<γ<1$, the operational variance has a closed asymptotic form involving effective signed-forcing intensity, liquidity slope, resilience, memory, and operational coarse-graining scale. A deterministic activity clock gives the benchmark local-volatility projection. More general, non-unique clocks generate candidate calendar-time pricing systems. We argue that such projections are admissible only when the induced forward density operator and backward valuation operator remain adjoint on the same state space. Adjoint consistency is therefore a reality constraint on operational-to-calendar time projection: it disciplines non-unique time and identifies where incompleteness enters.

items.title: Why financial prices exhibit Brownian motion despite predictable order flow: An exactly solvable nonlinear price impact model
items.summary: In econophysics, there are two enigmatic empirical laws of financial market microstructure: (i) the market-order flow has predictable persistence due to metaorder splitting by institutional investors, as formulated by the Lillo--Mike--Farmer model. However, this phenomenon seems paradoxical given the diffusive and unpredictable price dynamics. (ii) The price impact $I(Q_{\rm tot})$ of a large metaorder $Q_{\rm tot}$ follows the square-root law, $I(Q_{\rm tot})\propto \sqrt{Q_{\rm tot}}$. In this Letter, we reveal why price dynamics follows Brownian motion despite predictable order flow by unifying these enigmas via an exactly solvable model. We generalize the Lillo--Mike--Farmer model to nonlinear price-impact dynamics, which is mapped to a solvable Lévy-walk model. Our exact solution shows that the price dynamics remains diffusive under the square-root law, even under persistent order flow, reflecting the finite variance of metaorder impact; our model is thus a minimal representative of the universality class of nonlinear price-impact models with finite-variance metaorder impact. This work illustrates the crucial role of the square-root law in mitigating price movements by large metaorders, leading to Brownian price dynamics, consistent with the efficient market hypothesis over long timescales.

items.title: Quantifying Repair Risk in Crypto Option Surfaces
items.summary: Option desks adjust crypto option quotes into price surfaces that remain within bid-ask intervals and satisfy standard no-arbitrage restrictions across strikes before computing Greeks, hedge quantities, or risk measures. For the same quote panel, however, these constraints may admit multiple such surfaces, which we call admissible repairs, with different downstream outputs. We define the resulting variation as repair risk and propose repair-risk validation, a matched framework for quantifying dispersion in Greeks, hedge quantities, and risk measures. The mechanism is finite-difference amplification: two admissible repairs within price distance $\varepsilon$ can differ in local normalized-strike curvature by $4\varepsilon/h^2$, where $h$ is local normalized-strike spacing. We evaluate repair risk on Deribit BTC and ETH option chains, using $L_1$ and $L_2$ projections of midpoint prices onto the same admissible set as matched controls. Across 108 matched evaluations spanning 18 sampled calendar months, the median 90th percentile of the scaled spot-gamma gap for $L_2$ versus the $ρ=10$ smoothness-penalized repair is nearly twenty times the matched $L_1$--$L_2$ control. We also instantiate NN-Proj, a neural-projection repair, to test whether learned repairs exhibit repair risk. Despite good held-out fit, its downstream outputs remain distinct from those of classical repairs. Across five seeds with the same training window and architecture, its curvature dispersion exceeds the matched $L_1$--$L_2$ control in 17 of 18 months ($p=1.45\times10^{-4}$). For a USD 1 million risk reversal, switching from $L_2$ to the $ρ=10$ repair shifts the median 90th-percentile hedge notional by 18.62 basis points of gross spot notional. VaR-style estimates also exhibit greater dispersion across repairs. The repair rule is therefore part of the risk model, not merely a feasibility check.

items.title: Proxy-Reliance Control in Conformal Recalibration of One-Sided Value-at-Risk
items.summary: We introduce a proxy-reliance-controlled conformal recalibration framework for one-sided Value-at-Risk (VaR), and study a question that existing state-aware methods do not usually isolate: how strongly should the recalibration adjustment depend on an imperfect volatility proxy? We formalize this through a proxy-reliance parameter that continuously interpolates between an approximately constant-shift correction and a fully proxy-scaled correction. This makes proxy reliance a distinct and practically interpretable design choice in one-sided VaR recalibration. We show theoretically that larger proxy reliance increases the responsiveness of the tail adjustment to proxy scale, but also increases stressed-state fragility when the proxy underreacts. Empirically, in rolling out-of-sample tests on a six-ETF panel with VIX-linked state variables, and with supporting evidence from SPY, we find that the empirical value of proxy-reliance control lies in improved stressed-state robustness rather than uniform overall dominance. In particular, when the baseline forecast remains exposed to proxy imperfection in stressed states, lower or intermediate proxy reliance can outperform fully proxy-scaled recalibration in stressed left-tail VaR control.

items.title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance
items.summary: Language agents increasingly work for users on the open Web, and finance is where trusting them is hardest. The data must come from the Web, the strategy lives in the user's head, and correctness depends on time, so an agent can fail silently: a strategy the user never asked for, unverified data, or a backtest that uses the future yields a report as convincing as a correct one. Existing benchmarks close the world somewhere, fixing the task, the data, or the timeline, and thereby remove these failures instead of measuring them. We introduce FINCOSMOS, an open-world evaluation paradigm for agents doing financial work. A simulated user holds a hidden strategy sampled from a compositional grammar and reveals it only when asked. The agent receives no data, so it must acquire data from the Web, build its own backtest under a data cutoff, and deliver verifiable results. Grading needs no reference answer. Programs verify point-in-time correctness and recompute every reported metric, the delivered strategy is checked against the hidden specification, and a run is accepted only when the user is satisfied and none of 15 veto checks fails. Across four coding agents and a model without tools in 150 sessions, no session is accepted: every session that the simulated user signed off fails a program check, and agents raise only 54--64\% of the details they were not told. Human experts attribute 88.33\% of failures to the agents. With FINCOSMOS feedback, an agent with persistent memory learned all ten tasks.

items.title: Information-Theoretic Model for the Growth Optimal Portfolio of Stocks
items.summary: Drawing on information-theoretic principles and empirical evidence, a proxy for the growth-optimal portfolio of stocks (the benchmark) is constructed and modeled. The derivative of its activity time captures overreactions in trading behavior and follows a fast-moving, quasi-stationary scalar diffusion. The benchmark's log-returns are predicted to follow a Student t distribution with degrees of freedom slightly less than four, and this prediction is tested empirically. With the benchmark as numeraire, the derived model enables benchmark-neutral pricing and hedging.

items.title: Neural Realized Measures: Forecast-Supervised Intraday Aggregation for Volatility Forecasting
items.summary: High-frequency volatility forecasting typically separates measurement from prediction: intraday observations are first compressed into a daily realized measure using a fixed aggregation rule, and the resulting statistic is then passed to a forecasting model. This conventional pipeline therefore treats measure construction as forecast-agnostic preprocessing. We ask whether the aggregation stage itself can instead be learned from the downstream forecasting objective while preserving the statistical structure of established realized measures. We propose Neural Realized Measures (NRM), a primitive-preserving, forecast-supervised aggregation framework that retains the original measure-specific intraday contributions but replaces uniform aggregation with positive, mean-normalized context-dependent weights. Uniform weights exactly recover the corresponding raw realized measure (RRM), so the classical construction is nested as a special case. Because NRM remains an explicit weighted sum of established primitive contributions, it also retains direct bar-level attribution. Across SF, HAR, and MIDAS forecasting specifications, NRM is evaluated against corresponding RRM specifications under controlled comparisons. In Heston simulations, NRM reduces RMSE for both contemporaneous and next-day latent integrated variance across all evaluated primitive--regime combinations. On six cryptocurrencies using five-minute data, NRM improves QLIKE in all 54 paired out-of-sample comparisons, with mean gains of 7.23\%, 8.15\%, and 9.22\% under SF, HAR, and MIDAS, respectively. Validation-selected NRM specifications also achieve the lowest mean QLIKE across the six assets among the evaluated approaches. Ablation and SHAP analyses reveal systematic time-of-day and nonlinear local-context effects in the learned allocation.

items.title: A Rough Instantaneous Squared VIX Model for Term Structure and Option Pricing
items.summary: The VIX term structure provides forward-looking measures of market uncertainty across horizons, while VIX options allow investors to hedge volatility risk. This paper proposes a rough instantaneous squared VIX (RISVIX) model by introducing fractional memory into the conventional Markovian framework. We derive an explicit representation of the VIX term structure governed by Mittag--Leffler decay and a semi-closed-form pricing formula for VIX options based on an affine Fourier--Laplace transform. These results support a two-step calibration procedure that estimates memory, mean reversion, and date-specific initial states from VIX term-structure indices before calibrating the remaining distributional parameters to VIX option prices. Using daily VIX term-structure indices and VIX option quotes from January 2018 to June 2025, we find that RISVIX improves upon the Markovian benchmark in fitting the VIX term structure, with larger gains during elevated-volatility periods and for its slope and curvature. RISVIX also improves out-of-sample option pricing, reducing MSE and MAE by 13.06\% and 6.33\%, respectively, with larger gains at shorter maturities and in high-VIX states. These findings suggest that the gains from fractional memory are particularly pronounced when volatility is elevated and can be obtained within a tractable direct model of VIX derivatives. Comparisons with additional benchmarks from the recent literature also show improvements to varying degrees in both VIX term-structure fitting and option pricing.

items.title: Credibility Clustering for Experience Rating: An Automated Approach to Risk Group Allocation in Group Life Insurance
items.summary: In insurance, experience rating plays a crucial role in mitigating adverse selection by adjusting premiums according to historical claims experience. A key step in this process is the classification of insured collectives into homogeneous risk groups. Within group life insurance, this classification traditionally relies on manual decisions and arbitrary thresholds, which may lead to inefficiencies and inconsistent outcomes. This paper proposes a data-driven methodology for automating risk group allocation based on a combination of the multidimensional Bühlmann-Straub model and k-means clustering -- referred to as credibility clustering. By incorporating credibility weights, the method accounts for the varying statistical significance of experience data and ensuresthat risk classifications are both actuarially sound and practically implementable. Empirical results based on real-world group life insurance data from a major European insurer demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms the two k-means benchmark variants considered in the empirical application in terms of viability, temporal stability and accounting for statistical reliability.

items.title: FinMultiHopQA: A KG-Grounded Multi-Hop Financial QA Benchmark for Evidence-Driven Reasoning
items.summary: Multi-hop financial question answering often requires composing evidence distributed across filing sections, fiscal years, and peer companies. Prior financial QA benchmarks address parts of this problem individually, but none jointly support controlled multi-hop taxonomies, document topologies, motif-level reproducibility, and provenance-linked auditability at scale. We introduce FinMultiHopQA, a benchmark of 15,600 qualitative and quantitative questions, grounded in FinReflectKG, a temporally indexed financial knowledge graph derived from SEC 10-K filings with 17.5M+ triples. The pipeline instantiates statistically salient 2-3 hop typed KG motifs across intra-document, inter-year, and cross-company regimes. Beyond closing this gap, the same construction lets us hold each question's underlying evidence constant while varying only its presentation - embedding it in noisy surrounding context or changing its order - giving a controlled instrument to study a secondary question at scale: using six such presentations, we test whether reasoning LLMs' performance depends on evidence structure. Results confirm this: despite their reasoning capacity, judged correctness remains consistently lower under less-structured presentations of the same evidence - most sharply for quantitative cross-company reasoning and 3-hop branch motifs - indicating that reasoning alone does not fully offset how evidence is structured; KG-linked presentation also uses fewer input tokens by design. We release the benchmark, provenance annotations, model outputs, evaluation records, and supporting technical documentation.

items.title: AIDA: An AI Outage Registry with Evidence from On-Chain MEV
items.summary: Generative AI coding tools have lowered the cost of writing trading software, but no systematic dataset records when these services fail. We introduce the AI Incident and Disruption Archive (AIDA), a multi-vendor registry of 5,868 deduplicated outage incidents across 30 providers from 2025 to 2026, with foundation-model incidents verified against primary status-page or postmortem URLs. Pairing AIDA with 5,041,034 verified maximal extractable value (MEV) transactions by 8,516 Ethereum addresses, their contract creations, and a 22-month Base Layer-2 panel of 1,099,593,191 swaps and 29,120 private executors, we establish two findings. First, entry into MEV expanded where code and public state suffice, as active arbitrage addresses quadrupled from late 2024 to late 2026 and liquidators grew by a third, while sandwich attackers, who need private order flow and builder access, declined. Execution nonetheless remained concentrated, with the top fifty addresses executing two thirds of verified trades. Second, AI outages stall new trading code while deployed bots keep trading. On Ethereum, addresses releasing a private executor fall to 0.67 on the day of an eight-hour disruption (0.68 for executor creations during OpenAI outage hours) and to 0.66 at lag two before rebounding on day three; on Base, operator top-level creations fall to 0.76 during OpenAI hours and executor-deploying operators to 0.88 at lag two. Non-trading creations, automated factory clones, and live arbitrage and sandwich execution across both chains remain unchanged. Cheaper code thus lowers the barrier to building MEV contracts, while private order flow, latency and capital still determine who wins execution.

items.title: Dynamic Strategy Selection
items.summary: We consider the problem of dynamically selecting among competing strategies using observable predictors. To mitigate estimation noise and excessive switching, we regularise the estimated policy with a switching cost, which may exceed actual transaction costs when these are too small to provide sufficient regularisation. Since switching costs make current choices affect future decisions, we formulate the problem using dynamic programming. The optimal policy is estimated using a reinforcement learning algorithm based on iterated regressions, making the procedure simple to implement. We apply the method to monthly rotation among momentum, value, profitability, and defensive U.S. equity factors over a sample of about 60 years. Using a parsimonious set of state variables, the estimated policy outperforms both the myopic dynamic policy and the best fixed factor in hindsight in out-of-sample evaluation. Under weak conditions, we show theoretically that the decision rule estimated from empirical data is asymptotically consistent for the unknown optimal decision rule. Simulation results illustrate the finite-sample relevance of these asymptotic results.

items.title: Hard to Fool: A Bounded LLM Research Loop for Quantitative Finance, and What Two Dozen Campaigns Found
items.summary: Agentic research loops that let a language model propose a change, run a fixed experiment and keep whatever improves the metric work well in machine learning. In trading research the same loop is a machine for producing false discoveries: a backtest that "improves the metric" is, by default, overfit, look-ahead, a multiple-comparisons artifact, cost-free, or market drift wearing a strategy. We describe Autonomous Quant Researcher, an open-source loop built on the opposite premise: the model proposes, and only trusted code decides. Proposals are strict declarative JSON over a fixed vocabulary, so there is no model-written code to sandbox. Evaluation runs on immutable chronological stores split into discovery, validation and a final holdout that can be opened exactly once, after a durable receipt is written. Acceptance is a conjunction of absolute gates (positive edge and net P&L after costs, a positive weekly-cluster bootstrap lower bound, survival at elevated costs, per-year stability and sample floors), never a single score. Duplicates are refused before they spend a trial, and every formulation, refusal, crash and result is kept in a hash-chained, append-only ledger. We report every campaign run to date, across 0DTE options priced from traded option bars, overnight SPX verticals, daily ETF rules, technical-analysis premises, Kalshi crypto binaries, earnings options, off-exchange volume and a pre-registered alternative-data campaign. Most hypotheses fail, and we report them. Two results survive their pre-registered bars. The clearest example of the loop working is a failure: a language-model survivor that passed discovery and validation with Sharpe ratios near 3 and fell to 0.26 on its single holdout use. The value of such a loop lies less in what it finds than in how hard it is to make it report something that is not there.

items.title: Constrained defined-contribution pension management: A reparameterized neural network approach
items.summary: This paper studies constrained defined contribution (DC) pension management under a two-factor financial market model. The pension participant is allowed to invest in cash, two nominal bonds, an inflation-linked bond, and a stock index. Moreover, they can also purchase term life insurance to manage pre-retirement death risk. Unlike traditional literature, we consider a pension member restricted to a general non-empty, closed, and convex trading constraint set that includes no short-selling, no borrowing, and portfolio-mix constraints as special cases. Such restrictions reflect common limits on pension-account trading. To solve the problem, we construct a family of unconstrained artificial markets, in which the original trading constraints are satisfied by adjusting the drift terms of the risky assets. Using a duality transformation, we derive the Lagrangian dual problem and propose a reparameterized neural network method to compute lower and upper bounds on the primal value function. We calibrate our model with U.S. data using a Kalman filter method, and find that our method produces a smaller duality gap than the benchmark methods. We also compare the constrained results with the unconstrained explicit solution and find that trading constraints substantially change wealth accumulation, portfolio strategies, and insurance demand. This highlights that unconstrained solutions may provide misleading guidance for pension management in practice.

items.title: Geometric Observables for Financial Regime Detection
items.summary: We extract four geometric observables -- Berry Phase Rate, Spectral Entropy, Reduced State Purity, and Hamiltonian Sensitivity -- from a learned spectral embedding of equity-index returns and evaluate them as regime-shift detectors against 46 classical and machine-learning baselines on 17 historical crises spanning 2000-2024. Under walk-forward nested hyperparameter selection on nine labelled windows, the Berry Phase Rate achieves an unbiased out-of-sample median Cohen's $d = 0.72$ (95% percentile-bootstrap CI $[0.34, 1.18]$, 10,000 resamples) and produces approximately 67% fewer false alarms per year than a label-supervised Random Forest (1.2 vs. 3.6 per year). Reduced State Purity attains the highest in-sample separability of any method ($d = 0.83$), tied closely by the Absorption Ratio ($d = 0.80$); geometric and classical channels are largely uncorrelated (mean $|ρ| \approx 0.22$), suggesting they capture distinct risk signals. Score construction is unsupervised; hyperparameter selection is the only supervised step.

items.title: A general technique for explicit quantile representations
items.summary: This work proves existence of contours independent of probability level for exact quantile integrals of strictly positive real-analytic densities. Explicit constructions cover five broad distribution families and yield a finite-interval representation of Black-Scholes implied volatility using forward functions.

items.title: Market-Based Probability of Stock Returns
items.summary: This paper describes the dependence of market-based statistical moments of returns on statistical moments and correlations of the current and past trade values. We use Markowitz's definition of value weighted return of a portfolio as the definition of market-based average return of trades during the averaging period. Then we derive the dependence of market-based volatility and higher statistical moments of returns on statistical moments, volatilities, and correlations of the current and past trade values. We derive the approximations of the characteristic function and the probability of returns by a finite number q of market-based statistical moments. To forecast market-based average and volatility of returns at horizon T, one should predict the first two statistical moments and correlation of current and past trade values at the same horizon. We discuss the economic reasons that limit the number of predicted statistical moments of returns by the first two. That limits the accuracy of the forecasts of probability of returns by the accuracy of the Gaussian approximations. To improve the reliability of large macroeconomic and market models like BlackRock's Aladdin, JP Morgan, and the U.S. Fed., the developers should use market-based statistical moments of returns.

items.title: Price-Volume Correlations Are Always Zero
items.summary: We argue that the use of the empirical time series of values, volumes, and prices of consecutive trades made during the averaging interval to calculate the price-volume correlation in a way that follows the definition of correlation always gives zero correlation. We show that the usual expression for the empirical calculation of the correlation misleads the researchers and doesn't fulfill the definition of price-volume correlation. The mistake has its origin in the dependence of volume weighted average price on the mean values and volumes of trades during the averaging interval but not on time series of prices only. The true sense of the declared positive or negative results of the empirical calculations of price-volume correlations made by numerous researchers in reality is determined by the difference between the volume weighted average price and its limiting expression of average price, which is correct only when all volumes of consecutive trades are constant, and multiplication of this difference by the mean trade volume. To empirically determine the statistical dependence between time series of prices and trade volumes, one should calculate the correlations between prices and squares of trade volumes or correlations between squares of prices and squares of volumes. We derive the expressions for empirical calculations of these correlations.

items.title: Valuation Model of Chinese Convertible Bonds Based on Monte Carlo Simulation
items.summary: We tackle the problem of pricing Chinese convertible bonds(CCBs) using Monte Carlo simulation and dynamic programming. At each exercise time, we use the state variables of the underlying stock to regress the continuation value, and apply standard backward induction to get the coefficients from the current time to time zero. This process ultimately determines the CCB price. We then apply this pricing method in simulations and evaluate an underpriced strategy: taking long positions in the 10 most undervalued CCBs and rebalancing daily. The results show that this strategy significantly outperforms the benchmark double-low strategy. In practice, CCB issuers often use a downward adjustment clause to prevent financial distress when a put provision is triggered. Therefore, we model the downward adjustment clause as a probabilistic event that triggers the put provision, thereby integrating it with the put provision in a straightforward manner.

items.title: Exponential Seniority Weighting Chain-Ladder Reserving
items.summary: We develop a tractable state-space version of the chain-ladder model. The state-space dynamics acts on the accident year axis which, in contrast to the classical chain-ladder model, makes accident years dependent. This state-space version yields an exponential seniority weighting in the chain-ladder factor estimation, and it admits an analytical likelihood representation that enables us to compute the seniority weighted chain-ladder reserves and their prediction uncertainty: the one-year uncertainty is available in closed form and the total uncertainty requires a Monte Carlo simulation from the fully tractable likelihood representation.

items.title: A Financial Brain Scan of the LLM
items.summary: We use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to "brain scan" large language models, mapping internal activations to interpretable concepts and enabling targeted "steering" of specific features. We show that prompting models to adopt specific preferences activates many unintended concepts, complicating causal inference. In contrast, SAEs permit smooth, more isolated steering of target concepts. Furthermore, our scans reveal a stark disconnect between the model's internal feature contributions and its self-generated explanations, showing that these explanations are unreliable guides to its reasoning. Finally, SAEs provide a lightweight intervention for existing models, producing interpretable embeddings and allowing researchers to attenuate specific economic biases.

items.title: Valuation Reveals Uncertainty
items.summary: This paper studies the recovery of uncertainty from dynamic sublinear valuation rules. Robust valuation assigns each payoff its worst-case expected value over a family of plausible models, thereby inducing a dynamic sublinear valuation rule. While valuation rules are observable in practice, the underlying uncertainty structure remains latent. Under suitable conditions, we show that an uncertainty structure can be recovered from an observed valuation rule and provide an explicit recovery procedure. The construction characterizes the joint uncertainty in the discount factor and the law of the state process.

items.title: Mitigating Return Drag and Regime Whipsaws in Sector Rotation: An Asymmetric Downside-Aware Nested Clustered Optimization Framework
items.summary: Hierarchical clustering and Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) mitigate the mathematical ill-conditioning of classical Markowitz covariance matrices. However, two structural vulnerabilities persist in equity markets: (1) symmetric variance penalizes upside and downside return dispersion identically, inducing acute return drag against soaring momentum sectors; and (2) unconstrained Hidden Markov Models (HMM) exhibit hyper-active regime switching (whipsaw instability), incurring excessive turnover and transaction drag. We propose Asymmetric Downside-Risk Nested Clustered Optimization with Sticky Regime Dynamics (Asym-Sticky-NCO) for tactical sector rotation across all 11 S&P 500 GICS sectors. The framework substitutes symmetric covariance with the Bawa-Lindenberg downside semi-covariance matrix across both hierarchical tree clustering and two-stage allocation. Furthermore, we introduce a Sticky Gaussian HMM incorporating a diagonal self-transition persistence prior (\k{appa}) and confidence-adaptive boundaries (δ) to enforce macroeconomic persistence. Strictly non-anticipative walk-forward backtesting across 65 out-of-sample months (August 2020 to December 2025) demonstrates that the architecture elevates CAGR from 10.65% (Plain NCO) to 13.41% (+276 bps/year), delivers a 97.74% total return versus 72.99%, suppresses maximum drawdown to 14.22% (versus 23.93% for the S&P 500), and achieves a Calmar ratio of 0.94 (+38.2% over S&P 500; +84.3% over Baseline Regime-NCO). Crucially, sticky dynamics cut regime whipsaws by 75.0% (from 16 to 4 switches) and reduce monthly turnover from 60.78% to 30.48%, addressing core limitations of machine learning asset allocation.

items.title: Beyond Anonymous Order Flow: Wallet Identity as a Feature for Short-Horizon Return Prediction
items.summary: Conventional public order-book data summarize trading without identifying the accounts behind it. Hyperliquid's Level-4 record also exposes persistent pseudonymous wallet addresses. We reconstruct full-depth books from consensus-ordered messages and evaluate wallet identity as a feature for short-horizon return prediction. The July 1-27, 2026 record covers 17.1 billion messages, 14.3 million aggressive orders by 147,113 wallets, and $84.3 billion in taker notional across ten markets. In the three model markets, notional-weighted ten-second markout rankings persist across adjacent ten-day windows (Spearman rho = 0.52); covariate-adjusted validation markouts reach 3.11 basis points in the top ventile. On a 100-millisecond grid, eleven features describing previously scored top-decile wallets raise one-second out-of-sample R2 from 10.88% to 12.

items.title: Walraswap: equilibrium-based decentralized exchange integrating external AMM liquidity
items.summary: This article advocates the development of a decentralized exchange protocol for Ethereum based on Walrasian equilibrium. Building on previous work (arXiv:2111.02719, arXiv:2210.04929), it develops a mathematical framework that incorporates liquidity from independent automated market makers (AMMs). Trade orders are represented by continuous monotonic pairwise supply functions and external AMMs are represented by concave swap functions. Under a connectivity condition, we establish the existence of a common clearing-price vector and external swaps that jointly fulfill the prescribed orders while leaving a nonnegative surplus of every token. External AMMs execute ordinary swaps according to their own pricing rules, including swap fees. For the selected clearing-price vector, the prescribed external swaps maximize the value of the batch surplus. We also establish structural properties of equilibrium, including invariance of individual net trades across equilibria, and formulate equilibrium computation as a convex optimization problem. We then outline Walraswap, an exchange protocol for Ethereum with off-chain batch construction and on-chain settlement. Its proposed governance and solver accountability mechanisms aim to encourage public order disclosure and discourage censorship. The protocol design explores how the mathematical construction could support decentralized trading with reduced opportunities for maximal extractable value.

items.title: Breaking the Trend: How to Avoid Cherry-Picked Signals
items.summary: Our empirical results show an excellent fit with the theoretical Sharpe formula of a trend-following strategy depending on the parameter of the signal, which was derived by by Grebenkov and Serror (2014). That empirical fit convinces us that a mean-reversion process with only one time scale is enough to model, in a precise way, the reality of the trend-following mechanism at the average scale of CTAs and as a consequence, using only one simple EMA, appears optimal to capture the trend. As a consequence, using a complex basket of different sophisticated indicators as signal, does not seem to be so rational or optimal and exposes to the risk of cherry-picking.

items.title: Safe Portfolio Learning from Untrusted Predictions: Signed Trust, Abstention, and Cross-Universe Polarity Failure
items.summary: Portfolio use of machine predictions must often proceed while the predictions' economic direction, reliability, and timing remain untrusted, and while feedback from overlapping multi-period positions arrives with delay. A controller chooses among Safe, Follow, and Reverse portfolio actions, so signal orientation is learned rather than assumed. A share-adaptive master updates action probabilities from matured Safe-relative rewards, an evidence gate can abstain by transferring unsupported directional probability to Safe, a delayed collateral budget reserves worst-case loss capacity before exposure is funded, and a protected split account caps the capital adaptive decisions may touch. The architecture carries a dual certificate, tracking regret against switching action sequences under delay and one-sided intervention, together with a pathwise collateral safety bound that holds when predictions fail. On a 24-stock development universe a conservative prediction-assisted overlay stays near equal-weight performance at a fraction of the turnover. On a frozen 82-stock holdout, the pre-specified Reverse orientation fails to outperform Equal Weight; a separately labeled post-holdout diagnostic shows that permanently flipping the sign to Follow also does not recover a return edge. Under the post-holdout controller, protected wealth remains within 15.9 basis points of the Safe benchmark throughout. The contribution is safe adaptive use of untrusted predictions, not demonstrated alpha.

items.title: Does the Market Anticipate? Can it? Should it?
items.summary: A nuance to 'no arbitrage' is studied: it can be suboptimal to act upon an arbitrage immediately; in such cases optimised trading can suppress the anticipation of predictable risk-outcomes, creating an apparent Status Quo Bias. This is shown for asset-pricing under model- or event-risk. Unlike standard treatments, we allow pre-horizon revelations of risk-outcomes; the associated technical challenges are addressed through results from the weak viability and (in)side-information literature. The conflict between 'anticipation', 'no arbitrage' and 'information efficiency', and the competition between the 'signal-to-noise of data' and the 'inference-free risk-premium drift', are exposed.

items.title: Stablecoin Integration and Stress Transmission Through Crypto-Asset Service Providers: Evidence from Austria
items.summary: Stablecoins are increasingly entangled with traditional finance, making their response to stress a financial stability concern. However, blockchain pseudonymity and the lack of geographic identifiers force existing work to rely on indirect proxies to infer and locate market participants. In this paper, we exploit a regulatory registry that directly identifies the on-chain addresses of every crypto-asset service provider (CASP) registered in Austria at the end of 2024, reconstructing their Bitcoin, Ether, USDT, and USDC activity through May 2025. Austrian CASPs intermediate roughly $30 billion in cumulative external transfers, while transfers among them are negligible. Combining two transaction-level signals, interaction with CASP cold wallets and on-chain transaction frequency, we classify CASP counterparty activity as retail-like or institutionally mediated. Around stress events, the two groups exhibit distinct flow responses that are obscured in aggregate data. After the FTX bankruptcy, we observe retail-like withdrawals and institutional deposits across assets. After Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) failure, retail-like USDC deposits and institutionally mediated withdrawals are consistent with USDC's asymmetric redemption access. Registry-based, transaction-level measurements thus offer a reproducible basis for cross-jurisdictional monitoring of how cryptoasset markets transmit risk.

items.title: A mathematical study of the excess growth rate
items.summary: The excess growth rate, defined as the gap in Jensen's inequality for the logarithm, is a fundamental functional in portfolio theory. In this paper, we present a mathematical study motivated by information theory. We begin by establishing its properties and showing that it has rich connections with information-theoretic concepts such as the Helmholtz free energy, L. Campbell's measure of average code length and large deviations. Our main results consist of three axiomatic characterization theorems of the excess growth rate, in terms of (i) the relative entropy, (ii) the gap in Jensen's inequality, and (iii) the logarithmic divergence that generalizes the Bregman divergence. Furthermore, we study maximization of the excess growth rate and compare it with Kelly's growth optimal portfolio. Our results not only provide theoretical justifications of the significance of the excess growth rate, but also establish new connections between information theory and quantitative finance.

items.title: CosmosAlpha: Multi-Relational Graph Search with Pareto-Guided Exploration for LLM-Driven Alpha Mining
items.summary: Discovering predictive alpha factors from noisy financial data is a fundamental yet challenging problem in quantitative finance. LLM-driven formulaic alpha mining offers an attractive paradigm by combining interpretable symbolic expressions with iterative generation and refinement guided by quantitative feedback. However, existing generation-centric and tree-based search strategies primarily organize factors through generation lineage, leaving structural and statistical relationships across search branches underutilized. Consequently, information remains localized along parent--child trajectories, which can confine exploration to redundant regions. Moreover, effective factor discovery must account for multiple distinct objectives that cannot be adequately captured by a single search criterion. We introduce CosmosAlpha, a graph-based LLM factor-mining framework that represents discovered factors as a multi-relational graph encoding generation lineage, expression-structure similarity, and cross-sectional exposure correlation. A Graph Flow mechanism propagates search utilities across the graph, allowing each factor to be assessed using relational evidence from nearby factors rather than in isolation. Pareto-guided selection jointly considers quality, fertility and diversity, explicitly modeling their trade-offs within a multi-objective search framework. Across CSI 300 and CSI 500, CosmosAlpha-Graph achieves the best mean rank over seven predictive and portfolio metrics and outperforms its controlled CosmosAlpha-MCTS counterpart on every reported metric, showing a consistent advantage for relational graph search in LLM-driven factor mining. The source code is available at https://github.com/wzhmtldswz/CosmosAlpha

items.title: How market volatility responds to a preceding price trend: a lag-resolved measurement in cryptocurrencies and equities
items.summary: We quantify the response of market volatility to a preceding price trend as a function of lag at minute resolution. The asymmetry of the response is investigated. The sample consists of trades in three of the largest cryptocurrencies on a single exchange and in three large US stocks and the S&P 500 exchange-traded fund between 2020 and 2026. For the cryptocurrencies the asymmetry is positive, matching the sign of the leverage effect. It follows the trend: it is greatest at the first measurable lag, 20 minutes, and weak at negative lags, where the trend follows the volatility. At those lags a scan over window lengths resolves a small component of opposite sign that has not yet been disentangled from what the statistic itself generates. For Bitcoin and Ether the asymmetry decays to one half by a lag of roughly an hour and a half. Decomposition under time reversal divides the asymmetry into a T-even part and a T-odd part. Only the latter carries an arrow of time. For Bitcoin and Ether the T-odd part is detected. At the first lag it is between 0.4 and 0.9 of the T-even part at windows of 10 and 20 minutes. At 20 minutes this is the ratio produced by a purely one-sided response in this statistic: at that window the response is consistent with being wholly one-sided in time. None of the equities exhibits a detectable T-odd part at 20 minutes in the straight-line fit over 2.5 trend scales. This fit is the shared instrument of comparison. The fund's return-variance correlation displays an arrow of time; the cryptocurrencies' asymmetry is independent of the shapes of the fits, and Bitcoin's and Ether's of their ranges. On simulated and shuffled data without coupling, the analysis yields zero with errors of the correct size. It also recovers the time scale of a one-sided response embedded in a simulated market.

items.title: Partially Active Automated Market Makers
items.summary: We introduce a new class of automated market maker (AMM), the \emph{partially active automated market maker} (PA-AMM). PA-AMM divides its reserves into two parts, the active and the passive parts, and uses only the active part for trading. At the top of every block, such a division is done again to keep the active reserves always being \(λ\)-portion of total reserves, where \(λ\in (0, 1]\) is an activeness parameter. We show that this simple mechanism reduces adverse selection costs, measured by loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR), and thereby improves the wealth of liquidity providers (LPs) relative to plain constant-function market makers (CFMMs). As a trade-off, the asset weights within a PA-AMM pool may deviate from their target weights implied by its invariant curve. Motivated by the optimal index-tracking problem literature, we also propose and solve an optimization problem that balances such deviation and the reduction of LVR.

items.title: FinTech Adoption, Bank Profitability, and Stability: The Mediating Role of Operational Cost Efficiency in Bangladesh's Commercial Banking Sector
items.summary: While financial technology (FinTech) is seen as a contributor to bank performance, the empirical evidence of digitization's ability to translate into improved profit and stability outcomes and efficiency gains, within emerging systems dominated by banks is not conclusive. The direct impact of a composite FinTech Adoption Index (FTI) on the profitability (ROE) and stability (ln(Z-score)) of Bangladesh's commercial banks is explored in this study along with whether operational cost efficiency (CIR) acts as a mediator. The study is conducted using a balanced panel of 30 commercial banks between 2015 and 2024, supplemented by an entropy-weighted index of FinTech as a robustness check, using a two-step System GMM to address dynamic persistence and endogeneity issues. The adoption of FinTech presents no significant relationship with profitability, stability or cost efficiency, while cost efficiency does not significantly transmit the effect of FinTech to either outcome. The alternative measure suggests that adoption is not only significantly negatively related to profitability, but is also associated with a significantly improved (not worse) cost-to-income ratio, which indicates the sensitivity to measurement rather than any one consistent effect on performance. These findings qualify the expected performance benefits of FinTech and have implications for investment sequencing and regulation of digital transformation in emerging banking markets.

items.title: Aggregate Calibration Can Mask Stress-State Undercoverage: Bounded-Memory Forecast Intervals under Recurrent Financial Stress
items.summary: Sequential forecast intervals are often evaluated by aggregate coverage even when calibration memory is bounded.
